2.01 Clinical Reasoning (Decision Making in Clinical Medicine) 19 items

Dr. Gentry Dee · Recall 6 / Comp 5 / App 4 / Analysis 4 · Past-exam style source: 2028 LE2 #1–18 (same professor); 2027 LE2 #1–18 for topics only · Bring a standard calculator

How Dr. Dee asks
  • Case → which heuristic / reasoning (representative, availability, anchoring, simplicity). 2028 #3, #4
  • 2×2 table → compute one parameter (sensitivity, NPV), usually 2 items on the SAME table. 2028 #6, #7
  • Multi-part chain: pre-test probability → pre-test odds → post-test odds (→ probability). 2028 #13, #14
  • Threshold rapid-fire: "High-risk treatment → raise / lower / unaffected?" 2028 #11, #12
  • Forest plot: "Which study is definitely (NOT) beneficial?" 2028 #17, #18
  • Definitions: clinical reasoning, CI, RR, prevalence-dependent parameter, SnNOut/SpPIn. 2028 #1, 5, 9, 10, 15, 16

The 4 heuristics: case → name HIGH-YIELD MUST KNOW 2028 #3, #4 2027 #1

Heuristic = pattern recognition / rule-of-thumb shortcut. Four types: Representative, Availability, Anchoring, Simplicity ("RAAS").

TypeWhat the doctor doesClue words in the stemFailure mode
RepresentativeMatches the presentation to a disease that "looks like" it"typical / classic presentation", "because of the features", fever + jaundice → hepatitisNot all symptoms fit
AvailabilityRecalls a similar past case"I've seen this before", "case conference / grand rounds", "since then he always…", recent memorable missRecall bias
Anchoring (= conservatism, stickiness)Sticks to the first diagnosis"orders MORE tests to confirm even though a test already ruled it out", "insists", "refuses to revise"Neglects other test results
SimplicityTakes the simplest explanation"attributes everything to…", "disregards / dismisses" other symptomsPremature exclusion of symptoms
MUST KNOW Nothing is wrong with a heuristic diagnosis as long as it is backed up by diagnostic tests that confirm or negate it. p. 1
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: short case, "What kind of clinical reasoning / cognitive shortcut is applied?"
  • Trap: representative vs availability → how to tell: representative = matches THIS patient's features to a textbook picture; availability = driven by a PAST case/memory.
  • Trap: anchoring vs simplicity → anchoring ignores test results; simplicity ignores symptoms.
  • Trap: "Premature conclusion" / "Bayesian updating" / "evidence-based practice" are not heuristic types in the trans.

A 40/M had a missed dengue case last month that went into shock. Today the same doctor sees a 30/F with 1 day of fever and sore throat and immediately orders dengue NS1, CBC every 6 hours, and admission "because the last one crashed." What heuristic is at work?

  1. Representative
  2. Availability
  3. Anchoring
  4. Simplicity

B. Decision is driven by a memorable prior case (recall). Not representative: sore throat + day-1 fever is not a classic dengue picture.

Clinical reasoning: definition, heuristic vs analytical MUST KNOW 2028 #1, #2

Clinical reasoning = the cognitive and analytical PROCESS to collect, interpret and integrate patient info → differentials → diagnostic/therapeutic decisions → evaluate outcomes. Not just data collection.

Heuristic / intuitiveAnalytical
SpeedQuick, easySlow, methodical, deliberate, effortful
BasisPattern recognition, rules of thumbDefined steps, testable predictions
WhoExperienced clinicians, often subconsciousInfluenced by acuteness/severity of a possibility; experts generate & discard as they go
  • Process order: collect (history + PE) → differentials → tests based on differentials → interpret in clinical context (tests are confirmatory) → treatment plan.
  • Hypothetico-deductive model starts with collecting cues/data (2028 #2 key).
  • Elements (Fig 1): centre = clinical reasoning; top = clinical skills (history + PE); plus diagnostic tests ("very critical"), cognitive biases/human factors, thinking about thinking, patient-centred EBM, shared decision-making.
  • Factors affecting decisions: physician traits/practice style, practice setting, economic incentives (fee-for-service vs capitation vs value-based).
  • Medical errors: 250,000–440,000 US deaths/yr (Johns Hopkins 2022), 50% preventable.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "Which describes analytical reasoning?" / "best defines clinical reasoning".
  • Trap: "relying solely on intuition", "applying statistical formulas", "memorizing guidelines" → all wrong definitions.

Which statement correctly describes analytical clinical reasoning?

  1. It is used mainly subconsciously by experienced clinicians
  2. It relies on rules of thumb to reach a quick conclusion
  3. It must always follow a fixed sequence even among experts
  4. It is slow and effortful and generates testable predictions

D. A and B describe heuristic reasoning; C is wrong because experts do not follow a fixed pattern.

Stepwise approach + VINDICATE MUST KNOW

Gather → Identify key findings → Generate differentials (heuristic + VINDICATE) → Prioritize with EBM → Plan tests → Implement & reassess.

  • Identify: first 2–3 key findings are most important.
  • Prioritize with EBM: narrow to top 3 using prevalence and likelihood ratios.
  • VINDICATE widens the differential: Vascular, Infectious/Inflammatory, Neoplastic, Degenerative, Iatrogenic/Intoxication, Congenital, Autoimmune/Allergy, Trauma, Endocrine.
  • Lecture cases: chest pain → ACS (r/o PE, dissection) → ECG + troponin → NSTEMI; fever + cough + crackles → CAP → CURB-65 + CXR → home on amoxicillin/doxycycline.

A resident has listed peptic ulcer disease, AAA, DKA and gastric cancer for a 55/M with epigastric pain, and now uses local prevalence and likelihood ratios to keep only the three most probable. Which step is this?

  1. Identify key clinical findings
  2. Generate differential diagnoses
  3. Prioritize using EBM
  4. Implement and reassess

C. Prevalence + LR to narrow to top 3 = prioritize. Listing them (VINDICATE) was the "generate" step.

EBM: 3 circles, 4 areas, 5 A's, PICO(M) MUST KNOW 2027 #10

EBM = conscientious, explicit, judicious use of current best evidence for individual patients = clinical judgment + scientific evidence + patient values/preferences.

  • 4 areas: diagnostic test, treatment, harm & prognosis, meta-analysis (combined RCTs).
  • 5 A's: Ask (PICO/PICOM) → Acquire (UpToDate, PubMed; meta-analyses, RCTs) → Appraise (validity, relevance) → Apply (evidence + expertise + values) → Assess (outcomes).
  • PICOM: Patient, Intervention (diagnostic test / drug), Comparator (gold standard for diagnosis; standard treatment / placebo for therapy), Outcome, M = Methodology. LECTURER slides showed PICOM, lecture discussed PICO.
  • Therapeutic EBM asks: is it beneficial (effective)? is it harmful (adverse events limiting use)? It is the best way to avoid harmful treatments.
TRAP "Treatment effectiveness over patient values", "pathophysiology is the single most important factor", "clinical experience adds no value" = all FALSE.

After starting a drug chosen from a meta-analysis, the physician reviews the patient's BP log and side effects two weeks later to decide whether to continue. Which "A" of EBM is this?

  1. Assess
  2. Apply
  3. Appraise
  4. Acquire

A. Evaluating outcomes after treatment = Assess. Apply was the act of integrating evidence with the patient's values when choosing.

The 2×2 table + Sensitivity HIGH-YIELD MUST KNOW 2028 #6

Disease across the TOP, test down the SIDE. Sensitivity = A/(A+C) = among the diseased, how many test positive (read DOWN the disease(+) column).

Disease (+)Disease (−)Row total
Test (+)A = TPB = FPA+B (all positives)
Test (−)C = FND = TNC+D (all negatives)
Col totalA+C (all diseased)B+D (all non-diseased)
Formula Sens = A / (A + C) = TP / (TP + FN)
Solved example (use this "card table" for the next cards): TP 90, FP 20, FN 10, TN 80. Sens = 90 / (90 + 10) = 90/100 = 90%.
  1. Find A (top-left) and C (bottom-left). Add: 90 + 10 = → 100. Write it down (or press M+).
  2. 90 ÷ 100 = (or 90 ÷ MR =) → 0.9
  3. × 100 = → 90%
Shortcut / trap Sensitivity and PPV share numerator A: sens divides by the column (A+C), PPV by the row (A+B). Always check the table orientation — if the exam puts Disease on the side, transpose before computing. C = FN = diseased but test negative. 1 − sens = false-negative rate.

Pleural-fluid ADA was validated against pleural biopsy for TB pleurisy. ADA (+): 48 with TB, 12 without TB. ADA (−): 16 with TB, 124 without TB. What is the sensitivity of ADA?

  1. 75%
  2. 80%
  3. 89%
  4. 91%

A. 48/(48+16) = 48/64 = 75%. 80% = PPV (48/60); 91% = specificity (124/136); 89% = NPV (124/140).

Specificity + false-positive rate MUST KNOW

Specificity = D/(B+D) = among the non-diseased, how many test negative (read DOWN the disease(−) column). False-positive rate = B/(B+D) = 1 − specificity.

Formula Spec = D / (B + D) = TN / (FP + TN)
Solved example (card table): TN 80, FP 20 → Spec = 80/(20+80) = 80%; FP rate = 20/100 = 20%.
  1. 20 + 80 = → 100 (M+)
  2. 80 ÷ MR = → 0.8 → × 100 → 80%
  3. FP rate: 1 − 0.8 = 0.2 → 20%
Shortcut / trap "Probability of labeling as positive those WITHOUT disease" = false-positive rate (not PPV, not sensitivity, not LR+) — trans review Q5. B/(A+B) is NOT the FP rate.

A rapid strep test: Test (+): 30 with strep, 15 without. Test (−): 10 with strep, 45 without. What proportion of patients WITHOUT strep pharyngitis were incorrectly called positive?

  1. 15%
  2. 33%
  3. 25%
  4. 75%

C. FP/(FP+TN) = 15/60 = 25% (= 1 − specificity 75%). 33% = 15/45, the fraction of positives that are false (1 − PPV).

PPV and NPV (prevalence-dependent) HIGH-YIELD 2028 #7, #9 2027 #4

Read ACROSS the rows. PPV = A/(A+B): a positive test → chance of disease. NPV = D/(C+D): a negative test → chance of NO disease.

Formulas PPV = TP/(TP+FP) · NPV = TN/(FN+TN)
Solved example (card table): PPV = 90/(90+20) = 90/110 = 81.8%. NPV = 80/(10+80) = 80/90 = 88.9%.
  1. PPV: 90 + 20 = 110 (M+) → 90 ÷ MR = 0.818 → 81.8%
  2. Press MC. NPV: 10 + 80 = 90 (M+) → 80 ÷ MR = 0.889 → 88.9%
Prevalence effect (same test, sens 90%, spec 90%, 1,000 people):
PrevalenceTP / FP / FN / TNPPVNPV
50%450 / 50 / 50 / 45090%90%
10%90 / 90 / 10 / 81050%98.8%
1%9 / 99 / 1 / 8918.3%99.9%
Shortcut / trap Prevalence ↓ → PPV ↓, NPV ↑. Sens, spec and LR do NOT change. "Directly influenced by prevalence" = PPV or NPV. To build a table from sens/spec/prevalence: diseased = N × prev; TP = sens × diseased; TN = spec × non-diseased.

A screening test (sensitivity 90%, specificity 90%) is used in a barangay of 1,000 adults where the disease prevalence is 10%. A patient tests positive. What is the probability she truly has the disease?

  1. 90%
  2. 50%
  3. 10%
  4. 98.8%

B. TP 90, FP 90 → PPV 90/180 = 50%. 90% is sensitivity (confusing test property with PPV); 98.8% is NPV.

SnNOut / SpPIn + "which parameter is…" HIGH-YIELD 2028 #5, #9, #10

Sensitive + Negative → rule OUT (no further testing). Specific + Positive → rule IN (disease very likely).

Stem says…Answer
Inherent property of the test; hard to turn into a patient probabilitySensitivity / specificity
Depends on prevalence; less reliable for the individualPPV / NPV
Independent of test and prevalence, individualizable, works with ranged results (2×4 table)Likelihood ratio
Computed vertically (columns)Sens, spec
Computed horizontally (rows)PPV, NPV
TRAP Flip-trap: a highly SENSITIVE test that is POSITIVE does not rule in; a highly SPECIFIC test that is NEGATIVE does not rule out.

Which pairing is INCORRECT?

  1. Highly specific test, positive result — disease is likely present
  2. Highly sensitive test, negative result — no further testing usually needed
  3. PPV — changes when the test is moved to a lower-prevalence population
  4. Specificity — falls when the test is moved to a lower-prevalence population

D. Specificity is an inherent test property and does not change with prevalence; only PPV/NPV do.

Likelihood ratios (LR+ and LR−) HIGH-YIELD MUST KNOW 2027 #7

LR+ = sens / (1 − spec). LR− = (1 − sens) / spec. LR multiplies ODDS.

Formulas LR+ = [A/(A+C)] ÷ [B/(B+D)] = Sens/(1 − Spec) · LR− = [C/(A+C)] ÷ [D/(B+D)] = (1 − Sens)/Spec
Solved example (card table, sens 0.90, spec 0.80): LR+ = 0.90/(1 − 0.80) = 0.90/0.20 = 4.5. LR− = (1 − 0.90)/0.80 = 0.10/0.80 = 0.125.
Trans review Q4: sens 80%, spec 90% → LR− = 0.20/0.90 = 0.22.
  1. Convert to decimals first (80% → 0.8).
  2. LR+: 1 − 0.8 = 0.2 (M+) → 0.9 ÷ MR = 4.5
  3. LR−: MC, 1 − 0.9 = 0.1 → ÷ 0.8 = 0.125 (numerator first, so no memory needed)
Shortcut / trap LR+ > 1 (bigger = better rule-in); LR− < 1 (closer to 0 = better rule-out); LR = 1 → useless test. Flipping LR− to spec/(1 − sens) or (1 − spec)/sens gives a distractor (0.89 in review Q4). LR does not change with prevalence.

Using the ADA table (TB+: 48 test+, 16 test−; TB−: 12 test+, 124 test−), what is the positive likelihood ratio of ADA?

  1. 0.27
  2. 4.0
  3. 8.5
  4. 10.3

C. Sens 48/64 = 0.75; 1 − spec = 12/136 = 0.088; 0.75/0.088 = 8.5. 0.27 is LR−; 4.0 = 48/12 (raw counts, wrong).

Odds ↔ probability HIGH-YIELD MUST KNOW 2028 #13

Odds = P / (100 − P). Probability = Odds / (1 + Odds) × 100. Odds ≠ probability.

Solved examples 20% → 20/80 = 0.25. 60% → 60/40 = 1.5. Odds 0.25 (1:4) → 0.25/1.25 = 20%. Odds 3:1 → 3/4 = 75%.
  1. P → odds: 100 − 60 = 40 (M+) → 60 ÷ MR = 1.5
  2. Odds → P: 1 + 1.5 = 2.5 (M+) → 1.5 ÷ MR = 0.6 → ×100 = 60%
  3. Ratio form (a:b): probability = a/(a+b). 1:4 → 1/5 = 20%.
Probability20%25%40%50%60%75%80%
Odds0.250.330.6711.534
Shortcut / trap 50% = odds 1 (not 0.5). Odds can exceed 1; probability cannot exceed 100%. If the question asks for odds, stop — do not convert to %.

After a positive test, a patient's post-test odds of disease are 1:4. What is the post-test probability?

  1. 20%
  2. 25%
  3. 75%
  4. 80%

A. 1/(1+4) = 20%. 25% is the odds value read as a percentage (0.25).

Pre-test → post-test probability (3 steps) HIGH-YIELD MUST KNOW 2028 #13, #14 2027 #8, #9

(1) probability → odds; (2) odds × LR = post-test odds; (3) odds → probability.

Solved example (lecture): pre-test 25%, LR+ 5, LR− 0.2.
  1. Odds: 25 ÷ 75 = 0.333
  2. Positive: × 5 = 1.667 (M+) → 1 + MR = 2.667 → MR ÷ 2.667 = 0.625 → ≈ 62%
  3. Negative: 0.333 × 0.2 = 0.0667 → ÷ 1.0667 = 0.0625 → ≈ 6%
Pre-testOddsLR+ 5 → postLR− 0.2 → post
25%0.3362%6%
40%0.6777%12%
50%183%17%
75%394%38%
Shortcut / trap Never multiply LR by the PROBABILITY (25% × 5 = 125% → impossible). If the stem gives sens/spec, compute LR first. If the result is negative use LR−, not LR+. Rounding 0.33 vs 0.333 gives 62% vs 62.5% — pick the nearest choice.

A 50/F has a pre-test probability of DVT of 30%. A D-dimer with LR− 0.1 comes back negative. What is her post-test probability of DVT?

  1. 3%
  2. 4%
  3. 10%
  4. 30%

B. Odds 30/70 = 0.43 → × 0.1 = 0.043 → 0.043/1.043 = 4.1%. 3% = multiplying probability directly (30% × 0.1).

Test and treatment thresholds HIGH-YIELD MUST KNOW 2028 #8, #11, #12 2027 #5, #6

A = test/diagnostic threshold (floor), B = treatment threshold (ceiling). Below A → excluded, stop testing. A–B → uncertain, test further. Above B → established, treat.

LOWER the treatment threshold (treat sooner)RAISE it (need more certainty)
Life-threatening / emergency; high cost of missingSelf-limiting or low-risk disease
Low-risk, high-benefit treatmentHigh-risk treatment; costly treatment
Test unavailable or delayedTests available and reliable
High prevalence (rainy season → leptospirosis); vulnerable patient; patient preferenceLow clinical suspicion
  • Post-test probability stuck between A and B → cannot diagnose, cannot treat yet → find another test that moves it past a threshold.
  • Treatment threshold is set by the physician and the disease type.
  • Troponin case (pre-test 70%): positive → above B → treat; negative → below A → excluded.
  • 2027 key: the more fatal the disease, the lower the testing threshold (pancreatic cancer < chronic pancreatitis).
Formula? The 2026 trans gives NO threshold formula — exam asks location (excluded / test / treat) and raise vs lower. Harrison's background only: treatment threshold ≈ Harm / (Harm + Benefit) (e.g. harm 1, benefit 9 → 10%): low harm or high benefit → low threshold.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: one-word scenario + "treatment threshold should be lowered / increased / unaffected", or "at which level do you reconsider and investigate other diseases" (= diagnostic/test threshold).
  • Trap: "test available and reliable" sounds like "treat sooner" — it RAISES the threshold (you can afford to confirm first).

A 6-year-old in a remote clinic has fever, stiff neck and petechiae; lumbar puncture and cultures are not available for 12 hours. Ceftriaxone is safe and highly effective. How should the treatment threshold be adjusted?

  1. Raised, because the diagnosis is not yet confirmed
  2. Raised, because the patient is a child
  3. Unchanged, because thresholds depend only on prevalence
  4. Lowered, because the condition is life-threatening, the test is delayed and the treatment is low-risk/high-benefit

D. Three "lower" triggers at once. A vulnerable patient (child) also lowers, not raises.

Full worked case: 2×2 → LR → post-test → threshold decision HIGH-YIELD

Exam chains 2–4 items on ONE scenario. Do every step on paper; the next item reuses your last answer.

Scenario A 35/F has 2 days of fever and joint pains in the rainy season (trans dengue scenario). A rapid NS1 test was validated against RT-PCR (gold standard) in 300 patients:
Dengue (+)Dengue (−)Total
NS1 (+)A 85B 1095
NS1 (−)C 15D 190205
Total100200300
Clinician's pre-test probability: 40%. Test threshold A = 15%, treatment threshold B = 80%.
  1. Sens = 85/100 = 0.85 · Spec = 190/200 = 0.95
  2. PPV = 85/95 = 89.5% · NPV = 190/205 = 92.7% (study prevalence 33% — not this patient's)
  3. LR+ = 0.85 ÷ (1 − 0.95) = 0.85 ÷ 0.05 = 17 · LR− = 0.15 ÷ 0.95 = 0.158
  4. Pre-test odds = 40 ÷ 60 = 0.667
  5. NS1 positive: 0.667 × 17 = 11.33 → 11.33 ÷ 12.33 = 91.9% → above B (80%) → diagnosis established, manage as dengue
  6. NS1 negative: 0.667 × 0.158 = 0.105 → 0.105 ÷ 1.105 = 9.5% → below A (15%) → excluded, stop testing for dengue
Shortcut / trap Use the CLINICIAN's pre-test probability (40%), not the study prevalence (33%), for the patient. PPV 89.5% from the table ≠ this patient's post-test probability (91.9%) because prevalence differs — that is exactly why the lecture prefers LR.

Same scenario: what are the post-test ODDS of dengue if the NS1 is positive?

  1. 0.67
  2. 6.8
  3. 11.3
  4. 17

C. 0.667 × 17 = 11.3. 6.8 = 0.40 × 17 (multiplied probability, not odds); 17 is LR+ alone.

Same scenario, but now the patient's NS1 is negative. Which is the correct interpretation?

  1. Post-test probability ≈ 9.5%, below the test threshold — dengue is excluded
  2. Post-test probability ≈ 9.5%, between thresholds — order another test
  3. Post-test probability ≈ 26%, between thresholds — order another test
  4. Post-test probability ≈ 7.3%, the 1 − NPV — dengue is excluded

A. 0.667 × 0.158 = 0.105 → 9.5% < 15%. D uses the study's NPV (prevalence-dependent), not the patient's pre-test probability.

RR, RRR, ARR, NNT HIGH-YIELD MUST KNOW 2028 #15

RR = Rt/Rc · RRR = 1 − RR · ARR = Rc − Rt · NNT = 1/ARR. RR compares the risk in the treatment group to the control group.

Solved example Mortality: placebo (Rc) 30/200 = 0.15; drug (Rt) 18/200 = 0.09.
  1. Risks: 30 ÷ 200 = 0.15; 18 ÷ 200 = 0.09
  2. RR = 0.09 ÷ 0.15 = 0.6
  3. RRR = 1 − 0.6 = 0.4 (40%)
  4. ARR = 0.15 − 0.09 = 0.06 (6%)
  5. NNT = 1 ÷ 0.06 = 16.7 → round UP to 17
Lecture analogy: weight 100 → 80 kg: RR 0.8 ("80% of previous weight"), RRR 0.2 ("lost 20%"), ARR 20 ("lost 20 kg").
Shortcut / trap NNT = 1/ARR, never 1/RRR. Use ARR as a decimal (6% → 0.06) or NNT = 100 ÷ ARR%. RR < 1 beneficial, > 1 harmful. State outcomes as NEGATIVE (mortality, recurrence, not survival). RR/RRR/ARR are point estimates. Trans prints ARR as "Rc = Rt" and "100 − 80 = 80" — typos; intended Rc − Rt = 20.

In an RCT, stroke occurred in 20% of the placebo group and 15% of the anticoagulant group. How many patients must be treated to prevent one stroke?

  1. 4
  2. 20
  3. 25
  4. 5

B. ARR = 0.20 − 0.15 = 0.05 → 1/0.05 = 20. 4 = 1/RRR (RRR = 25%); 5 = ARR% read as NNT.

Forest plots and 95% CI: reading guide HIGH-YIELD MUST KNOW 2028 #16, #17, #18 2027 #11, #13

Diamond = RR (point estimate); bar = 95% CI; vertical line = RR 1 (no difference). LEFT favors treatment, RIGHT favors placebo. Does the bar cross the line?

Whole CI for RR (ratio, null = 1)Verdict
Entirely < 1Definitely beneficial → give
Crosses 1 (e.g. 0.2–1.2)Neither beneficial nor harmful / inconclusive / not significant → do not give
Ends exactly at 1Beneficial but not "definite"; worst case = no effect (lecture: no harm in giving)
Entirely > 1Definitely harmful / definitely NOT beneficial, favors placebo
  • Null value depends on the measure: ratios (RR, OR) → 1; differences/reductions (ARR, RRR) → 0. RRR CI −10% to 50% crosses 0 → inconclusive. 2027 #11, #13
  • For RRR/ARR the direction flips: CI entirely > 0 = beneficial; entirely < 0 = harmful.
  • 95% CI = range likely to contain the true population value with 95% certainty; used because you cannot test the whole population.
  • Fig 6 (comparative plot): all outcomes sit right of 1 → not better than placebo; only total joint replacement dipped below 1.
TRAP A small RR (0.2) does not mean "definitely beneficial" if the upper limit passes 1. Judge the WHOLE bar, not the diamond. "Somewhat beneficial" needs a narrow CI entirely < 1.

Four RCTs of a new anti-arrhythmic report mortality. Which result shows the drug is DEFINITELY beneficial?

  1. RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.25–1.15
  2. ARR 4%, 95% CI −1% to 9%
  3. RRR 22%, 95% CI 8% to 35%
  4. RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.05–1.60

C. RRR CI entirely above 0 → benefit. A crosses 1 and B crosses 0 (inconclusive); D is entirely > 1 → definitely harmful.

Practice drill — Dr. Dee style

A urine antigen test for pneumococcal pneumonia: Test (+): 36 with pneumonia, 14 without. Test (−): 4 with pneumonia, 146 without. What is the negative predictive value?

  1. 90.0%
  2. 97.3%
  3. 91.3%
  4. 72.0%

B. D/(C+D) = 146/150 = 97.3%. 91.3% = specificity (146/160); 72% = PPV; 90% = sensitivity.

Of 80 biopsy-proven cases, 68 had a positive ultrasound; of 120 patients without disease, 24 had a positive ultrasound. What is the negative likelihood ratio?

  1. 0.19
  2. 0.81
  3. 4.25
  4. 5.33

A. Sens 0.85, spec 96/120 = 0.80 → (1 − 0.85)/0.80 = 0.1875. 4.25 is LR+; 5.33 = spec/(1 − sens) (flipped).

A 62/M with exertional chest pain has a pre-test probability of CAD of 60%. A stress test with LR+ 4 is positive. What is his post-test probability?

  1. 60%
  2. 75%
  3. 86%
  4. 240%

C. Odds 60/40 = 1.5 → × 4 = 6 → 6/7 = 85.7%. 60% = LR never applied; 240% = LR × probability (impossible — LR multiplies odds).

Same patient (pre-test 60%), but the stress test is negative (LR− 0.25). The physician's test threshold is 30% and treatment threshold is 75%. What is the next best step?

  1. Start anti-anginal treatment; post-test probability is above the treatment threshold
  2. Repeat the same stress test to confirm the negative
  3. Order coronary angiography; probability is between thresholds
  4. No further CAD testing; post-test probability (~27%) is below the test threshold

D. 1.5 × 0.25 = 0.375 → 0.375/1.375 = 27% < 30% → excluded. B = anchoring behavior.

A clinician estimates an 80% probability of appendicitis. Expressed as pre-test odds, this is:

  1. 0.8
  2. 1.25
  3. 4
  4. 0.25

C. 80/20 = 4 (4:1). 0.25 is the inverse (20/80); 0.8 is just the probability.

In a trial, 30 of 200 controls and 18 of 200 treated patients died. What is the relative risk reduction?

  1. 40%
  2. 6%
  3. 60%
  4. 17%

A. RR = 0.09/0.15 = 0.6 → RRR = 1 − 0.6 = 40%. 6% = ARR; 60% = RR; 17 = NNT.

A test with sensitivity 90% and specificity 90% is moved from a referral hospital (prevalence 50%) to community screening (prevalence 1%). Which statement is correct?

  1. PPV stays 90% because sensitivity did not change
  2. PPV falls to about 8%, while LR+ stays at 9
  3. LR+ falls because there are more false positives
  4. NPV falls because the disease is rarer

B. At 1%: TP 9, FP 99 → PPV 8.3%. LR+ = 0.9/0.1 = 9 regardless of prevalence. NPV rises, not falls.

A 68/M smoker has weight loss, a hilar mass on CXR, and hyponatremia. The physician immediately labels it small-cell lung cancer because the picture "fits the textbook." Which reasoning is this?

  1. Representative heuristic
  2. Availability heuristic
  3. Anchoring heuristic
  4. Analytical reasoning

A. Matching features to a classic presentation. No past case is invoked (not availability); no test result is being ignored (not anchoring).

A patient admitted as "community-acquired pneumonia" has a clear CXR and normal procalcitonin. Instead of reconsidering, the resident orders a chest CT and sputum cultures ×3 "to find the pneumonia." Which heuristic, and what is its typical failure?

  1. Simplicity — premature exclusion of symptoms
  2. Availability — recall bias
  3. Representative — not all symptoms fit
  4. Anchoring — neglect of other test results

D. Sticking to the first diagnosis and testing more after tests ruled it out = anchoring (conservatism/stickiness).

A 45/F has fatigue, a 7-kg weight loss, and night sweats. The doctor attributes everything to "work stress" and sends her home with vitamins without addressing the weight loss. Which heuristic?

  1. Anchoring
  2. Simplicity
  3. Availability
  4. Representative

B. Simplest explanation while disregarding important symptoms. Anchoring would require ignoring a test that ruled it out.

Which situation would RAISE the treatment threshold?

  1. Suspected leptospirosis during a flood in the rainy season
  2. Suspected sepsis in an immunocompromised patient
  3. Suspected viral URTI when a reliable rapid test is available and the proposed drug has serious toxicity
  4. Suspected meningitis with CT and LP delayed for 24 hours

C. Self-limiting disease + reliable test + high-risk treatment all raise it. A, B, D are high prevalence, vulnerable patient, delayed test → lower.

Which RCT result for a cholesterol drug (outcome: MI) is definitely NOT beneficial (i.e., harmful)?

  1. RR 1.4, 95% CI 1.1–1.8
  2. RR 1.2, 95% CI 0.7–1.9
  3. RR 0.8, 95% CI 0.6–1.0
  4. RRR 15%, 95% CI −5% to 30%

A. Whole CI > 1 → favors placebo. B and D cross the null (1 and 0) → inconclusive; C touches 1 → beneficial but not definite.

A resident frames: "In adults with suspected dengue (P), does NS1 antigen (I), compared with RT-PCR (C), accurately detect dengue (O)?" Which statement is correct?

  1. This is the Acquire step; RT-PCR is the placebo
  2. This is the Appraise step; RT-PCR is the outcome
  3. This is the Apply step; NS1 is the comparator
  4. This is the Ask step; RT-PCR is the gold-standard comparator

D. Framing PICO = Ask. In diagnostic EBM, C = gold standard; placebo is the comparator in therapeutic EBM.

Which parameter answers the question, "Of all patients WITH the disease, what proportion will the test detect?"

  1. Positive predictive value
  2. Sensitivity
  3. Specificity
  4. Positive likelihood ratio

B. Sensitivity = A/(A+C), the disease-positive column. PPV starts from the test-positives instead.

Last-look cram sheet

  • "Typical/classic presentation" → representative; "seen before / case conference / since that case" → availability; "more tests after it was ruled out" → anchoring (conservatism, stickiness); "ignores other symptoms" → simplicity.
  • Heuristic OK only if backed by diagnostic tests. Analytical = slow, methodical, deliberate, effortful, testable predictions.
  • Steps: Gather → Identify → Generate (VINDICATE) → Prioritize (prevalence + LR) → Plan → Implement/Reassess.
  • EBM = judgment + evidence + patient values. 5 A's: Ask (PICO/M) · Acquire · Appraise · Apply · Assess. C = gold standard (dx) / placebo or standard tx (therapy).
  • Sens A/(A+C) · Spec D/(B+D) (columns, test property) · PPV A/(A+B) · NPV D/(C+D) (rows, prevalence-dependent).
  • SnNOut · SpPIn · FP rate = 1 − spec · prevalence ↓ → PPV ↓ NPV ↑.
  • LR+ = sens/(1 − spec) · LR− = (1 − sens)/spec · LR independent of prevalence.
  • Odds = P/(100 − P) → × LR → P = odds/(1 + odds). 50% = odds 1; 75% = 3; 20% = 0.25.
  • Below A excluded · between A and B test more · above B treat. Emergency / delayed test / safe drug / high prevalence / vulnerable → LOWER. Risky or costly drug / self-limiting / reliable test / low suspicion → RAISE.
  • RR = Rt/Rc · RRR = 1 − RR · ARR = Rc − Rt · NNT = 1/ARR (round up).
  • Forest: diamond = RR, bar = 95% CI, line = 1. Whole bar left → definitely beneficial; crosses → inconclusive; whole bar right → definitely harmful. Differences (ARR/RRR) null = 0.

2.02 Hypo-/Hyperthermia and Fever of Unknown Origin 19 items

Dr. Claro Antonio · Recall 2 / Comp 4 / App 6 / Analysis 7 · Past-exam style source: 2028 LE2 #37–56 (same professor); 2027 #39–58 for topics only · Trans 2.02 V1 (15 p.)

How Dr. Antonio asks
  • Mechanism items (2028 had 5 in a row): fever vs hyperthermia (set point), which cytokine, which brain area, why the arrhythmia / afterdrop happens.
  • Short cases ("60/F, hot dry skin after time outdoors…", "30/M given haloperidol…") ending in mechanism / diagnosis / how to tell apart.
  • FUO block (8 of 20 items in 2028): classic vs revised definition (asked in BOTH 2027 and 2028), most common cause, first imaging, role of PET/CT, what to do before invasive tests, clues to NIID.
  • Some 2028 keys were built from Harrison's rather than the trans. Where they clash with the current trans, this section flags it.
  • The trans says most exam questions come from the slides and synchronous lecture p. 14. 📌 "Must know" pins = lecturer emphasis.
Past-exam concept map (2027 / 2028)
Concept20282027Covered in
Thermoregulatory center / heat-loss mechanism / SNS response to cold#42#43, #44Thermoregulation
Fever vs hyperthermia (set point), cytokine, PGE2#37, #38, #39, #40, #41#41, #42Fever vs hyperthermia
Temperature measurement site—#39, #40Measurement
Drug-induced hyperthermia vs infection (antipsychotic)#43#48 (CCB)Drug hyperthermia
Heat edema / cramps / exhaustion type—#49, #51, #52Heat-illness spectrum
Heat stroke triad#37#50Heat stroke
Hypothermia stages, rewarming arrhythmia, afterdrop#44, #46, #47#45Hypothermia, Rewarming
Frostbite vs trench foot vs chilblain#45#46, #47Cold injuries
FUO definition (classic vs revised)#53, #55#53FUO definitions
FUO most common cause / NIID clue#50, #54#56FUO causes
FUO workup: first imaging, PET/CT, before invasive tests, liver biopsy, sequence#49, #51, #52, #56#54, #55, #58FUO workup
Factitious vs fraudulent fever—#57not in current trans
(blank placeholder)#48——

Fever vs hyperthermia: did the thermostat move? HIGH-YIELD MUST KNOW 2028 #37–41 2027 #41–42

Fever = REGULATED rise because the hypothalamic set point goes UP (via PGE2). Hyperthermia = UNREGULATED rise with a NORMAL set point (heat gain or production beats heat loss).

  • Fever chain: exogenous pyrogen (microbe, toxin) → monocytes/macrophages release IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α (endogenous pyrogens) → COX-2 in hypothalamus → PGE2 → preoptic area raises set point Harrison's; trans: set point ↑ "usually via PGE2" p. 3.
  • Then the body "chases" the new set point: vasoconstriction (cold hands/feet) + shivering + liver heat. So shivering and vasoconstriction are responses, not the cause.
  • IL-1 = key cytokine of the febrile response (anakinra blocks it) p. 13.
  • Hyperpyrexia = still a fever (set point driven) but >41.5°C; most common cause CNS injury, also severe infection p. 3.
  • Trap: hypothalamic damage usually gives SUBnormal temperature, not fever p. 3.
FeatureFeverHyperthermia
Set point↑ (PGE2)Normal, hypothalamus not involved
PyrogensYesNone
SkinCan be cold (vasoconstriction)Hot, dry (heat stroke syndromes)
AntipyreticsLower tempNo effect
Onset / maxGradual or rapid; usually +1–2°CUsually rapid; can exceed 40.5°C
Preceding eventInfectionHeat exposure, exertion, drugs
TRAP 2027 #42 keyed cAMP as the "immediate trigger" of the set-point rise (PGE2 acts via EP3 receptors → cAMP, Harrison's). The current trans only names PGE2 as the mediator. If both PGE2 and cAMP appear and the stem says "immediate/final signal in the neuron," cAMP; if it asks "mediator," PGE2. Cytokines do NOT act directly; they make the hypothalamus make PGE2 (2028 #39 rationale).
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: case + "mechanism of her condition?"; "which interleukin"; "correct statement on fever vs hyperthermia."
  • Trap: "excessive sweating" or "↑PGE2" offered for a heat-stroke case → how to tell: heat exposure + hot dry skin + no antipyretic response = normal set point.

Four ER patients all have a core temperature of 40.2°C. Acetaminophen is most likely to lower the temperature of which patient?

  1. A 72/F found in a non-air-conditioned room during a heat wave, hot dry skin
  2. A 19/M recruit who collapsed during a noon run
  3. A 30/M who became rigid during halothane anesthesia
  4. A 45/F with flank pain, pyuria and chills

D. Pyelonephritis = pyrogen-driven fever with raised set point, so COX inhibition works. A–C are hyperthermia (normal set point): antipyretics have no role.

Thermoregulation: center, feedback, heat transfer MUST KNOW 2028 #42 2027 #43–44

Center = preoptic nuclei of the ANTERIOR hypothalamus; it runs a NEGATIVE feedback loop around a set point.

  • Inputs: peripheral (skin) + central thermoreceptors + blood → compare with set point → error signal p. 1.
  • Cold → heat retention: vasoconstriction, shivering, non-shivering thermogenesis (sympathetic; brown fat in infants, who can't shiver), thyroid axis. Immediate cold defense is sympathetic (norepinephrine; 2027 #44).
  • Warm → heat loss: vasodilation + sweating; evaporation does most of the cooling.
MechanismRole (trans p. 2)
ConductionMinimal (contact: cold floor, cold water)
Convection"Most common" (fan, wind)
RadiationMajor at rest (no contact)
EvaporationMajor when hot; fails in high humidity
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "primary thermoregulation center", "main mechanism of heat loss at rest / in heat."
  • Trap: "most common" (convection) vs "major at rest" (radiation) vs "major when hot" (evaporation). Read the setting.

A 50/M has a small hemorrhage confined to the preoptic area of the anterior hypothalamus. Which temperature pattern is most expected?

  1. Sustained hyperpyrexia above 41.5°C
  2. Subnormal body temperature
  3. Fever that responds briskly to acetaminophen
  4. Normal temperature, since peripheral thermoreceptors take over

B. Trans: most patients with hypothalamic damage have SUBnormal temperatures. "Hypothalamic fever" exists but is rare (A is the near-miss).

Temperature measurement and normal values MUST KNOW 2027 #39–40

Most accurate = lower ESOPHAGEAL (closest to core). Rectal = highest baseline. Oral 0.4°C lower than rectal; unadjusted tympanic 0.8°C lower than rectal.

  • Normal range 35.7–37.3°C, mean oral 36.6°C; fever >37.7°C (99th percentile) p. 2.
  • Lowest 8 AM, peak 4 PM. Higher in winter, LOWER in summer. Ovulation +0.6°C (progesterone).
  • Oral falsely low with mouth breathing / rapid breathing. Tympanic: check wax, otitis externa first.
  • Hypothermia: measure core at 2 sites; rectal probe 15 cm (not in cold feces); esophageal 24 cm below larynx (falsely high with heated inhalation); never tympanic alone p. 8.
TRAP 2027 #40 (different professor) keyed temporal artery as closest to core. The current trans says esophageal is closest to core and calls external (axillary, temporal) thermometers unreliable in hypothermia. Follow the trans.

A 70/M has a rectal temperature of 38.4°C. If the same patient were measured at the same time with other methods, which reading would MISS the fever (fever = >37.7°C)?

  1. Esophageal
  2. Oral
  3. Unadjusted tympanic
  4. None; all would still show fever

C. 38.4 − 0.8 = 37.6°C (not >37.7). Oral would be 38.4 − 0.4 = 38.0°C, still febrile.

Drug-induced hyperthermia: NMS vs serotonin syndrome vs malignant hyperthermia vs heat stroke HIGH-YIELD 2028 #43 2027 #48

Drug + rigidity + ↑CK + no infection source = drug-induced hyperthermia, not infectious fever. Match the drug and timing to the syndrome.

NMSSerotonin syndrome Harrison'sMalignant hyperthermiaHeat stroke
TriggerAntipsychotics (haloperidol, chlorpromazine); trans also lists SSRIsSerotonergic drug combos (SSRI + tramadol, MAOI, linezolid)General anesthesia: succinylcholine, "-flurane"/halogenated agents (Ca channel, RYR1)Heat stress ± exertion; anticholinergics, CCB, β-blockers raise risk
OnsetDays–weeksHours (<24 h)Minutes–hours, intra-/post-opDuring heat wave or exertion
MusclesLead-pipe rigidity, ↓ reflexesClonus, hyperreflexia, tremorRigidity (masseter), ↑ETCO2, metabolic acidosisNo rigidity (EHS: rhabdo)
OtherAltered mental status, autonomic instability, ↑↑CKAgitation, diarrhea, diaphoresis, mydriasisHyperkalemia, ↑CKCNS dysfunction, hot dry (CHS) or sweaty (EHS) skin
Specific RxStop drug; bromocriptine/dantrolene Harrison'sStop drug; benzos, cyproheptadine Harrison'sStop agent; dantrolene Harrison'sCooling + fluids; dantrolene NOT established p. 6
  • All four: normal set point → antipyretics useless.
  • Drug mechanisms in heat illness p. 4: anticholinergics block sweating + blunt CV response + disturb preoptic nucleus; CCBs ↓ peripheral blood flow (2027 #48); β-blockers limit vasodilation; stimulants ↑ muscle heat.
  • Trans DDx of heat stroke also includes thyroid storm, pheochromocytoma crisis, infection.
TRAP Trans Table 8 lists "antipsychotics, SSRIs" under NMS. Harrison's separates serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, fast onset). If the stem gives an SSRI + clonus and "serotonin syndrome" is a choice, pick it; if only NMS is offered, NMS (per trans).
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "fever after antipsychotic — how to tell from infectious fever?" (2028 #43: CK + rigidity). New angles: anesthesia case, drug-combo case, next step.
  • Trap: diaphoresis/tachycardia or ↑WBC → present in infection too, not discriminating.

A 24/M undergoing appendectomy under sevoflurane, intubated with succinylcholine, develops masseter rigidity, rising end-tidal CO2, temperature of 40.4°C and metabolic acidosis 30 minutes into surgery. What is the best next step?

  1. IV acetaminophen and blood cultures
  2. Stop the triggering anesthetic and give dantrolene
  3. Bromocriptine via nasogastric tube
  4. Cyproheptadine and a benzodiazepine

B. Malignant hyperthermia (halogenated agent + succinylcholine). Bromocriptine is for NMS; cyproheptadine for serotonin syndrome; antipyretics useless (normal set point).

Heat-illness ladder: minor → cramps → exhaustion → stroke HIGH-YIELD 2027 #49, #51, #52

The dividing line is the BRAIN: heat exhaustion = CNS and thermoregulation intact, <40.5°C. Any significant CNS dysfunction = heat stroke until proven otherwise.

SyndromeKey clueDo / don't
Heat edemaFirst days of heat; swollen hands/feet/ankles; vasodilation + fluid pooling + ↑ADH/aldosteroneElevate, stockings. No diuretics
Miliaria rubra (bungang araw)Itchy red papules/vesicles in clothed areas; pores blocked by macerated stratum corneumAntihistamine, chlorhexidine, loose clothes
Heat syncopeElderly, prolonged standing → postural hypotensionRemove from heat, cool, rehydrate
Heat crampsSalty sweat replaced with plain water → intracellular Na/K/fluid deficit → painful spasmsORS or 650 mg salt dissolved in 1 quart water; not undissolved tablets
Heat exhaustion 📌<40.5°C, CNS intact, orthostatic hypotension, sinus tachy; dx of exclusionFluids by electrolytes; cool nonresponders to 39°C
Heat stroke 📌Triad: heat stress + CNS dysfunction + >40.5°CCool immediately (next cards)
Heat exhaustion typeWater depletionSalt depletion
StoryWorked in heat, drank too little ("voluntary dehydration", drink only 2/3 of losses)Unacclimated, drank lots of plain/hypotonic fluid
Tempo / labs—Develops more slowly; hyponatremia, hypochloremia
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: worker/hiker case with temp and mental status → which heat illness / which type.
  • Trap: "slightly slow but coherent" at 39.5°C = still exhaustion (2027 #52). Confused/combative or >40.5°C = stroke. Some impending heat strokes look lucid at first.

A 32/M construction worker newly arrived from a cool province has worked outdoors for a week, drinking several liters of plain water daily. Over 2 days he develops malaise, nausea, headache and muscle cramps. He is alert and oriented; temperature 38.9°C, HR 118 with orthostatic drop. Na 128, Cl 92. Most likely diagnosis?

  1. Exertional heat stroke
  2. Water-depletion heat exhaustion
  3. Salt-depletion heat exhaustion
  4. Heat syncope

C. Unacclimated + plenty of hypotonic fluid + slow onset + hyponatremia/hypochloremia. Intact CNS and <40.5°C excludes heat stroke.

Heat stroke: triad and classic vs exertional HIGH-YIELD MUST KNOW 2028 #37–38 2027 #50

Triad: heat stress + CNS dysfunction + core >40.5°C. Classic = old/sick in a heat wave with hot DRY skin; exertional = young athlete/recruit, often SWEATING, with rhabdo + renal failure.

Classic (CHS)Exertional (EHS)
Who / whenElderly, chronic disease, heat-impairing meds, summer heat wavesAthletes, laborers, military recruits; anytime
SkinHot, dry, anhidroticProfusely diaphoretic
Labs↑AST/ALT (>100x), hypernatremia, stress leukocytosisRhabdo + ARF, ↑CK/LDH, myoglobinuria, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, ↓Ca ↑PO4, coagulopathy
FluidsDeceptively modest (CVP 12–14)More active crystalloid
Immersion coolingNOT recommendedBest for young healthy EHS
  • Why sudden: to keep perfusion, skin vessels clamp → skin heat loss stops → core shoots up p. 5.
  • >42°C: direct cell injury, uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation → SIRS, DIC, multiorgan failure. 📌 Initial core >42°C = worse prognosis.
  • Labs grade severity; they do NOT diagnose heat stroke. O2 curve shifts RIGHT (hot = right).
TRAP Hypotension is NOT part of the triad (2027 #50). Sweating does NOT exclude heat stroke (EHS).

A 19/M cadet collapses at the 8th km of a morning run. He is combative, drenched in sweat, core temperature 41.3°C. Urine is cola-colored. Which laboratory profile is most expected?

  1. Markedly ↑CK, hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypoglycemia
  2. Hypernatremia with normal CK
  3. Normal labs, since he is still sweating
  4. Low ESR and procalcitonin-driven leukocytosis

A. Exertional heat stroke: rhabdomyolysis pattern + hypoglycemia. Hypernatremia with isolated liver injury fits classic heat stroke.

Heat stroke management: cool first, avoid the wrong drugs MUST KNOW

Start cooling right away, even while you are still working up the cause. Evaporative cooling works for every heat stroke patient. Ice-water immersion is only for young patients with exertional heat stroke (EHS). Stop active cooling once the core reaches 38–39°C.

  • Evaporative cooling is the go-to method p. 6.
    • How: spray cool water (about 15°C) on exposed skin and keep a fan blowing over the moist skin. Ice packs on the neck, armpits (axillae) and groin are an add-on.
    • Why it is preferred: it is the most practical method, it still lets you monitor and treat the patient, and it works for both classic heat stroke (CHS, the elderly or sick person in a heat wave) and exertional heat stroke (EHS, the young person exercising hard).
    • Rapid cooling matters because many heat stroke patients already meet SIRS (systemic inflammatory response syndrome) criteria.
  • Immersion cooling (ice-cold water bath) is fast, but has drawbacks.
    • It can first cause peripheral vasoconstriction and shivering, which work against heat loss.
    • It is best for young, healthy EHS patients and is not recommended for CHS.
    • Stop active cooling at 38–39°C. If you keep going, the temperature can overshoot downward (hypothermic afterdrop).
  • Supportive care
    • Monitor the core temperature continuously and check the glucose.
    • Intubate if there is altered mental status (AMS), since aspiration is common.
    • For low blood pressure, give repeated isotonic crystalloid boluses. CHS patients often need only modest fluid, while EHS patients need more.
  • 📌 Drugs to AVOID, and why
    • α-agonist inotropes such as norepinephrine: they cause vasoconstriction, which blocks heat loss and slows cooling.
    • Depolarizing agents (for airway management).
    • Chlorpromazine: it lowers the seizure threshold and has anticholinergic effects.
    • Barbiturates when there is liver dysfunction.
    • Atropine and other anticholinergics: they block sweating.
    • Antipyretics: they work by blocking pyrogens at the hypothalamus, and in heat stroke there are no pyrogens to block. Acetaminophen also stresses the liver, and salicylates can worsen coagulopathy.
  • Complications
    • Arrhythmias and seizures usually settle once the patient is cooled and hydrated.
    • Delay electrical cardioversion until the heart muscle has been cooled.
    • Shivering or agitation is treated with a short-acting benzodiazepine.
    • Every heat stroke patient belongs in a monitored setting or ICU.

A 78/F with heart failure is brought in during a heat wave: disoriented, hot dry skin, core temperature 41.0°C, BP 82/50. Which order is INCORRECT?

  1. Spray with cool water under a fan and apply ice packs to the axillae and groin
  2. Give isotonic crystalloid boluses for the hypotension
  3. Immerse in ice water and continue until core temperature reaches 37°C
  4. Give a short-acting benzodiazepine for shivering-related agitation

C. This elderly woman in a heat wave has classic heat stroke, and immersion is not recommended for classic heat stroke. On top of that, active cooling should stop at 38–39°C, not 37°C, to avoid hypothermic afterdrop.
The other orders are all correct: evaporative cooling with ice packs works for everyone, crystalloid boluses are the right fix for hypotension (not norepinephrine), and a short-acting benzodiazepine is the recommended drug for shivering or agitation.

Hypothermia: definition, stages, primary vs secondary HIGH-YIELD 2028 #47 2027 #44–45

Accidental hypothermia means a core temperature below 35°C. In the mild stage the body is still fighting back with vasoconstriction and shivering. Below 32°C the body can no longer hold a steady temperature, and its temperature simply follows the surroundings (poikilothermia).

Stage Harrison'sCore tempHallmarksTrans thresholds / rewarming
Mild32–35°CThe body is still compensating: shivering and vasoconstriction.
Also fast heart rate, fast breathing, cold diuresis, ataxia and apathy.		Below 35°C is the definition.
A healthy patient with an acute, primary case gets passive external rewarming (0.5–2°C per hour).
Moderate28–32°CShivering stops.
Lower level of consciousness, weak reflexes, atrial fibrillation or slow heart rate, Osborn J wave, paradoxical undressing.		Below 32°C is poikilothermia, so active rewarming is needed.
Below 30°C, drugs are generally withheld and VF gets only one shock.
SevereBelow 28°CComa, no reflexes, VF or asystole, no breathing.Below 28°C, intermittent CPR is acceptable in the field.
Needs advanced core rewarming or ECLS (extracorporeal life support).
  • Primary vs secondary hypothermia
    • Primary: a healthy person who simply got too cold. The fix is removing them from the cold and rewarming.
    • Secondary: hypothermia as a complication of another disease, such as sepsis, hypoglycemia, myxedema (severe hypothyroidism), adrenal insufficiency, spinal cord injury or a drug overdose.
    • Secondary hypothermia has a much higher mortality, so you must find and treat the underlying cause, not just warm the patient.
  • Who is at risk, and why
    • Neonates: they have a large surface area for their mass and cannot shiver effectively.
    • The elderly and the malnourished (less fat and fewer energy stores for making heat).
    • Ethanol: it causes vasodilation, so heat is lost even though the person feels warm.
    • Psychiatric drugs (antipsychotics, antidepressants, anxiolytics): they reduce the brain-driven vasoconstriction that normally conserves heat.
    • Anesthesia: it blocks shivering.
  • Red flags for a secondary cause p. 7. These are findings that do not fit the temperature:
    • Heart rate too fast for how cold the patient is. Think of hypoglycemia, low volume (hypovolemia) or overdose.
    • Persistent fast breathing. Normally the breathing rate falls as CO2 production drops, so think of a brain lesion or metabolic acidosis.
    • Deep coma with only mild hypothermia. Think of overdose or a CNS problem (infection, trauma).
TRAP The stage cut-offs (32°C and 28°C) come from Harrison's. The trans instead lists functional thresholds: 35, 32, 30, 28 and 33°C.
  • In a staging question, "mild" means the body is still fighting: shivering and vasoconstriction.
  • Altered mental status or VF does not describe the mild stage (this was the 2028 #47 key).

A 58/M is found in a wet alley at dawn. Core temperature is 33.6°C, HR 134, RR 14, GCS 7. He is not shivering much. Which is the most appropriate next step?

  1. Passive external rewarming only, as for mild primary hypothermia
  2. Check capillary glucose and search for a secondary cause (toxins, sepsis, hypovolemia)
  3. Amiodarone for the sinus tachycardia
  4. Temperature-corrected ABG to guide bicarbonate

B. At 33.6°C he only has mild hypothermia, yet his heart rate is very fast and he is in deep coma (GCS 7). Those findings are out of proportion to the temperature, so they point to secondary hypothermia, for example hypoglycemia or an overdose. Check the glucose and look for the cause.
A is tempting because the temperature is in the mild range, but passive rewarming alone is only for healthy, primary cases. The ABG should NOT be temperature-corrected, and antiarrhythmics are used only with extreme caution in hypothermia.

Rewarming: who needs active warming, afterdrop, rewarming arrhythmias HIGH-YIELD 2028 #44, #46

Warm the TRUNK, not the limbs. Putting heat on the arms and legs opens up (dilates) the cold vessels there. Cold, acidotic blood from the limbs then flows back to the core, and the core temperature keeps dropping (afterdrop), which can trigger arrhythmias.

  • Who needs ACTIVE rewarming p. 9. Think of it as "below 32°C, or anything that means the patient cannot rewarm alone":
    • Core temperature below 32°C (poikilothermia).
    • Cardiovascular instability (low blood pressure, arrhythmia, arrest).
    • Age extremes (elderly, neonates).
    • CNS dysfunction.
    • Hormone deficiency (thyroid, adrenal, pituitary).
    • Suspected secondary hypothermia.
  • Passive rewarming (cover, insulate, warm room) is enough for a previously healthy person with mild, acute, primary hypothermia. The patient needs enough glycogen to make their own heat.
  • Active external rewarming
    • Use forced-air heating blankets (the most effective), circulating-water pads or radiant heat.
    • Avoid a heated tub, because monitoring the patient becomes extremely difficult.
    • Avoid electric blankets, because they burn the cold, vasoconstricted skin.
  • Active core rewarming (heat delivered inside the body)
    • Heated, humidified oxygen at 40–45°C.
    • Warmed IV fluids at 40–42°C.
    • Warm irrigation of body cavities (GI tract or bladder) adds little heat and is reserved for cardiac arrest.
    • Closed thoracic lavage is very efficient in arrest, but is not done in the LEFT chest of a patient who still has a perfusing rhythm.
    • Hemodialysis and peritoneal lavage are other options.
    • ECLS (extracorporeal life support) or bypass is for non-perfusing patients or those with frozen limbs.
  • Why arrhythmias happen during rewarming (2028 #44)
    • Abrupt changes in the cell membranes cause abnormal depolarization and repolarization.
    • Reperfusion of tissues adds to this.
    • Old ectopic beats can reappear as the heart warms up.
    • The cold right atrium is easily irritated by a deeply placed central line or pacing wire.
  • 📌 There is no evidence that extremely rapid rewarming improves survival in patients who still have a perfusing rhythm.
  • 📌 Use antiarrhythmics only with extreme caution.
  • Rewarming toxicity: drugs like digoxin and insulin can build up while the patient is cold and then act all at once on rewarming.
TRAP Afterdrop is a circulation problem (cold blood returning to the core). It is not a change in the hypothalamic set point, and it is not caused by cold diuresis.
  • Afterdrop shows up in two settings:
    • Rewarming hypothermia, when the limbs are heated and their vessels dilate.
    • Over-cooling heat stroke, which is why you stop at 38–39°C.

A 66/M rescued after a night outdoors has a core temperature of 30.5°C with a perfusing rhythm. Staff wrap hot packs around his arms and legs, and 20 minutes later his core temperature falls to 29.6°C and he develops ventricular ectopy. Which change would best have prevented this?

  1. Forced-air warming of the trunk with heated humidified O2 and warmed IV fluids
  2. Passive blankets only, since he is still perfusing
  3. Immersion of the limbs in a hot tub to speed rewarming
  4. Prophylactic class I antiarrhythmic before rewarming

A. At 30.5°C he is below 32°C, so he needs active rewarming aimed at the core and trunk. Heating his limbs dilated the cold vessels there, so cold blood returned to the core and caused the afterdrop and ectopy.
B is wrong because passive warming is not enough below 32°C, even with a pulse. A heated tub is avoided, and no class I antiarrhythmic has been proven safe in hypothermia.

Hypothermic arrest and lab pitfalls MUST KNOW

"Not dead until warm and dead": do not stop CPR until the patient has been rewarmed past 33°C. For VF below 30°C, give one shock, then rewarm by 1–2°C before shocking again.

  • When to do CPR
    • Start CPR unless there is a DNR order, an obviously lethal injury, or a chest wall too frozen to compress.
    • Survival has been reported after more than 7 hours of arrest p. 8, which is why you keep going.
  • Signs of a poor prognosis
    • Potassium above 10–12 mmol/L.
    • Core temperature below 10–12°C.
    • pH below 6.5.
    • Fibrinogen below 0.5 g/L.
    • The worst mechanism is asphyxia first, then cooling, as in avalanche victims.
  • ECG: the Osborn J wave (at the QRS–ST junction) suggests hypothermia. Automated machines often misread it as an injury current.
  • Fluids and oxygen
    • Use normal saline (NSS) instead of lactated Ringer's (LR), because the cold liver cannot clear lactate well.
    • The oxygen–hemoglobin curve shifts LEFT, so hemoglobin holds on to oxygen and tissues get less.
    • Pulse oximetry is often unreliable because of vasoconstriction.
  • Lab pitfalls
    • ABG (arterial blood gas): do not correct it for temperature.
    • Hematocrit rises about 2% for every 1°C drop, so anemia is underestimated.
    • WBC (white cell count) may stay low and hide an infection.
    • Clotting tests look normal because the lab runs them at 37°C, which rewarms the clotting enzymes. In the patient, the cold still blocks those enzymes and the platelets.
    • Platelets and FFP (fresh frozen plasma) will not work until the patient is rewarmed.
  • Hormones and infection
    • Do not give levothyroxine to a hypothermic patient with normal thyroid function. Give it only if there are real clues to myxedema, such as slow relaxation of the Achilles reflex.
    • Hypothermia can hide fever and a high WBC, so take cultures.
    • Give empiric antibiotics to the elderly, neonates and immunocompromised patients.

A 40/M hiker in cardiac arrest has a core temperature of 26°C. VF persists after one biphasic shock at 2 J/kg. ECLS is being prepared. What is the best course now?

  1. Repeat shocks every 2 minutes with IV amiodarone
  2. Terminate resuscitation, since VF persists below 28°C
  3. Give lactated Ringer's boluses and atropine
  4. Continue CPR and core rewarming, defer further shocks until warmed by 1–2°C

D. Below 30°C, the rule is one shock, then rewarm by 1–2°C before trying again, while CPR and core rewarming continue.
A is wrong because repeated shocks are deferred and antiarrhythmics are generally avoided. B is wrong because you do not stop until the patient is warmer than 33°C ("not dead until warm and dead"). C is wrong because normal saline is preferred over lactated Ringer's.

Frostbite vs immersion (trench) foot vs chilblain (pernio) HIGH-YIELD 2028 #45 2027 #46–47

If the tissue actually froze (below 0°C), it is frostbite. If the cold stayed above freezing, look at the type of exposure: WET cold points to trench foot, while DAMP cold with itchy blue nodules and a Raynaud's history points to chilblain.

FrostbiteImmersion (trench) footChilblain (pernio)
TempTissue below 0°C (it freezes)Repeated WET cold above 0°CRepeated DAMP cold above 0°C
MechanismIce crystals destroy cells.
After thawing, the dermis becomes ischemic, small vessels collapse and edema forms.
Damaged vessels then clot (thrombosis).		Prolonged wet coldDamage to nerves and vessel lining.
Vasospasm and vasculitis.
LookNumb, like a "chunk of wood".
Waxy, mottled, violet-white skin.
Blisters (blood-filled blisters mean severe injury).		Feet start cyanotic, cold and swollen.
Later bullae and ulcers, which can progress to liquefaction gangrene.		Itchy redness and plaques.
Blue nodules on the backs of the hands and feet.
WhoContact with metal, high wind, tight boots, previous cold injurySoldiers, fishermen, people in wet bootsYoung women, families with a history of Raynaud's
RxSee the steps below the tableSupportiveSupportive.
If refractory: nifedipine, steroids, limaprost.
  • Frostbite treatment, in order
    • Treat the hypothermia first.
    • Thaw the tissue quickly and completely in circulating water at 37–40°C for 30–60 minutes. Do not use hot air.
    • Give parenteral narcotics (opioids), because reperfusion is intensely painful.
    • Iloprost (a prostacyclin analogue) within 48 hours after rewarming.
    • tPA with heparin within 24 hours for severe, deep frostbite. This can reduce amputations.
    • Delay amputation until the dead tissue clearly separates from living tissue (demarcation), which can take weeks to months. Operate early only if infection develops.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: a type of cold exposure plus how the skin looks, then "which injury is this?", "which pathophysiologic event is NOT consistent?", or "what is the next step?"
  • Trap: the bullae of trench foot can look just like frostbite.
    • How to tell them apart: ask whether the tissue was actually frozen (below 0°C) or only wet and cold above freezing.

A 35/M mountaineer has white, waxy, numb toes after a night at −15°C. After he is rewarmed and his core temperature is normal, the toes develop hemorrhagic blisters and remain dusky. Which step is INAPPROPRIATE?

  1. Parenteral opioids for reperfusion pain
  2. tPA with heparin if within 24 hours of severe injury
  3. Early amputation of the dusky toes within the first 48 hours
  4. Iloprost within 48 hours after rewarming

C. In frostbite you let the dead tissue declare itself (natural demarcation), which takes weeks to months. Early amputation can remove tissue that would have survived, so debridement or amputation is done early only if infection develops.
The other choices are all correct steps: opioids for reperfusion pain, tPA with heparin within 24 hours for severe injury, and iloprost within 48 hours.

FUO definitions: classic vs revised, IUO, recurrent fever HIGH-YIELD MUST KNOW 2028 #53, #55 2027 #53

FUO (fever of unknown origin) needs all of the following: fever lasting more than 3 weeks, temperature of at least 38.3°C on at least 2 occasions, a patient who is NOT immunocompromised, and no diagnosis after a thorough history, physical exam and the obligatory tests. The revised definition replaced "1 week of inpatient evaluation" with "obligatory investigations", so the workup can be done as an outpatient.

Classic (original)Revised (current)
Temp≥38.3°C on several occasions≥38.3°C on at least 2 occasions
DurationMore than 3 weeksMore than 3 weeks
Workup neededNo diagnosis after 1 week of inpatient evaluationNo diagnosis after a thorough history and PE plus the obligatory investigations.
Hospitalization is not required.
Immune status—Known immunocompromised patients are EXCLUDED
Look-alikeDefinition
IUO (inflammation of unknown origin)Same as FUO, except the temperature is normal while ESR and CRP are high. The workup is the same.
ESR and CRP are NOT infection markers, because inflammation can happen without infection p. 11.
Recurrent fever 📌Repeated fever episodes separated by fever-free gaps of at least 2 weeks, with the disease seeming to go into remission in between.
A cause is found in fewer than half of cases. Examples are malaria and Hodgkin lymphoma p. 12.
Durack–Street subtypes Harrison'sClassic, nosocomial, neutropenic and HIV-associated.
Low yield, and not in the current trans.
Do not mix up the two thresholds.
  • Above 37.7°C is the definition of fever (the 99th percentile of healthy people).
  • 38.3°C or higher is the FUO criterion.
  • The trans's "original definition" list already includes "no immunocompromised state" together with "about 1 week inpatient".
    • So when a past item asks which is NOT part of the revised definition, the answer is "known immunocompromised patients". They are excluded from FUO, not included in it 2028 #53 2027 #53.

Which patient meets the revised definition of FUO?

  1. A 30/F with 2 weeks of fever up to 39°C and negative initial labs
  2. A 55/M kidney transplant recipient on tacrolimus with 5 weeks of fever ≥38.3°C
  3. A 42/M with 4 weeks of fever ≥38.3°C on several days, unrevealing outpatient history, PE, CXR, abdominal ultrasound and basic labs
  4. A 60/F afebrile for 4 weeks with persistently high ESR and CRP and no diagnosis

C. He has more than 3 weeks of fever at 38.3°C or higher, he is not immunocompromised, and the obligatory tests were unrevealing. Under the revised definition, an outpatient workup is enough, so hospitalization is not needed.
A is too short (only 2 weeks). B is immunocompromised (transplant on tacrolimus), so he is excluded. D has no fever, so she has inflammation of unknown origin (IUO), not FUO.

FUO causes: infection (TB) here, NIIDs in the West, NIID clues HIGH-YIELD 2028 #50, #54 2027 #56

In non-Western countries like the Philippines, INFECTION is the most common cause of FUO, and up to half of those infections are TB. In Western cohorts, the top causes are non-infectious inflammatory diseases (NIIDs, more than 1/3) and "unexplained" (more than 1/3).

  • The five categories of FUO causes p. 11
    • Infections: TB, endocarditis, abscesses.
    • NIIDs (non-infectious inflammatory diseases): autoimmune and autoinflammatory diseases, granulomatous diseases, and vasculitis.
    • Malignancy, especially lymphoma.
    • Psychosomatic.
    • Unexplained.
  • Why more cases are now "unexplained"
    • Better imaging (CT, MRI, PET/CT) catches the easier causes early, before they ever meet FUO criteria.
    • Abscesses, tumors and endocarditis are now diagnosed sooner.
    • So only the hardest cases are left to be called FUO.
  • Clues that point to an NIID
    • Very high ESR, above 100 mm/h (2028 #50 key, Harrison's).
    • Tender temporal artery, suggesting giant cell arteritis (GCA).
    • Retinal vasculitis seen on fundoscopy.
    • Palpable petechiae or purpura on the legs, suggesting vasculitis (2027 #56 key).
    • Fever that goes away with a naproxen challenge.
    • Recurrent fever lasting more than 2 years. Infection or malignancy is very unlikely after that long.
  • Clues that point to infection instead: chills or rigors, a high procalcitonin, and a fever that rises in the evening (TB).
TRAP If the question says "worldwide" or "most common" without naming a region, 2028 #54 keyed infection.
  • If the stem says Western or European cohort, the answer is NIID.

A 38/F from Batangas has had fever ≥38.3°C for 5 weeks. Obligatory tests are unrevealing and she is not immunocompromised. Which single cause is statistically most likely?

  1. Mycobacterium tuberculosis
  2. Epstein-Barr virus
  3. Sarcoidosis
  4. Hodgkin lymphoma

A. She is from the Philippines, a non-Western setting, where infection is the most common cause of FUO and up to half of those infections are TB.
Sarcoidosis (C) is a classic FUO cause in Western textbooks, but the lecturer noted it is uncommon in the Philippines. Hodgkin lymphoma is a possible cause but much less likely statistically.

FUO workup: PDCs first, stop drugs, obligatory tests, then PET/CT HIGH-YIELD MUST KNOW 2028 #49, #51, #52, #56 2027 #54, #55, #58

The most important step is searching for Potentially Diagnostic Clues (PDCs), which are any localizing signs, symptoms or abnormalities that point toward a diagnosis. You find them by taking the history and doing the exam REPEATEDLY. Before ordering more tests, STOP antibiotics and glucocorticoids. Before any invasive test, repeat the history and exam.

  1. Take a complete history and do a focused exam, plus the obligatory tests.
    • History: travel, animal contacts, sexual history, drugs and family history.
    • Exam: eye grounds (fundi), deep axillary lymph nodes, temporal arteries, liver and spleen, the whole skin, mucous membranes and old surgical sites.
  2. 📌 Stop antibiotics and steroids.
    • Antibiotics make cultures falsely negative.
    • Steroids shrink lymph nodes and hide inflammation, whatever the cause.
    • Repeat blood cultures only if the earlier ones were drawn while on antibiotics or within 1 week after stopping them.
  3. Obligatory tests
    • Chest X-ray (CXR) for everyone.
    • Abdominal ultrasound, preferred over CT because it is cheap and has no radiation.
    • TST or IGRA for TB.
    • 2–3 sets of blood cultures. More than 3 sets is useless without PDCs.
    • Cryoglobulins as a screening test.
  4. If PDCs are present, follow them with targeted tests.
    • Example: FUO with headache calls for a CSF (spinal fluid) exam.
    • Example: suspected miliary TB calls for a liver biopsy, which has the highest yield.
  5. If there are no PDCs, go step by step:
    • Rule out drug fever: stop all drugs and watch for 72 hours.
    • Repeat the history and physical exam.
    • Have an ophthalmologist do fundoscopy (looking for retinal vasculitis).
    • Then ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT, the first choice, especially when ESR or CRP is high.
    • Leukocyte scintigraphy only if PET/CT is not available.
TRAP 2028 #49 keyed "chest and abdominal CT" as the first-line imaging (from Harrison's). The current trans says CXR plus abdominal ultrasound are obligatory, and ultrasound is preferred over CT.
  • If ultrasound is among the choices, choose ultrasound.
  • If the only options are CT versus echo, gallium scan or MRI, choose CT.
  • PET/CT has high sensitivity but low specificity. It tells you where the process is.
    • It is done after the first-stage tests fail, not after invasive biopsies fail (2028 #51).

A 47/M with 4 weeks of fever ≥38.3°C has been on co-amoxiclav and prednisone 20 mg/day from a private clinic for 10 days. Two blood cultures drawn this week are negative. What is the best next step?

  1. FDG PET/CT now, since cultures are negative
  2. Stop the antibiotic and steroid, then repeat cultures at least a week later
  3. Add empiric anti-TB drugs
  4. Bone marrow biopsy

B. His cultures were drawn while he was taking an antibiotic, so they may be falsely negative. The prednisone can also hide the disease. Stop both drugs first, then repeat the cultures at least a week later.
A is tempting, but the negative cultures cannot be trusted yet, and imaging comes after the first-stage tests are done properly. Empiric anti-TB drugs and bone marrow biopsy come much later.

FUO special cases, treatment and prognosis MUST KNOW

Avoid empiric antibiotics, steroids or anti-TB drugs UNLESS the patient is rapidly getting worse after the tests have failed to give a diagnosis. If the FUO stays unexplained, the prognosis is FAVORABLE.

  • Why avoid empiric treatment?
    • Antibiotics can permanently ruin your chance of culturing fastidious bacteria or mycobacteria, and they add risks of resistance and blood-count complications.
    • Early steroids lower the chance of reaching a diagnosis that may have a specific, life-saving treatment.
  • When empiric antibiotics or anti-TB drugs ARE acceptable
    • Hemodynamic instability.
    • Neutropenia.
    • Positive TST or IGRA plus granulomas, when sarcoidosis is unlikely.
    • If there is no response after 6 weeks of anti-TB drugs, rethink the diagnosis.
  • 📌 NSAID (naproxen) challenge
    • If the fever goes away with naproxen, the cause is most likely inflammatory rather than infectious.
    • NSAIDs can work dramatically in adult-onset Still's disease.
  • Other targeted treatments
    • Colchicine for suspected FMF (familial Mediterranean fever). It is very good at preventing attacks.
    • Steroids for GCA (giant cell arteritis) or PMR (polymyalgia rheumatica), but only after infection and lymphoma have been largely ruled out.
    • Anakinra for FUO that is still undiagnosed after the later-stage tests. It is an IL-1 receptor antagonist that blocks both IL-1α and IL-1β.
  • FUO with headache: check the CSF for HSV-2, Cryptococcus (India ink stain) and TB (AFB smear). Collect all samples in a single tap.
  • TB tests (TST and IGRA)
    • They can be falsely negative in miliary TB, malnutrition and immunosuppression.
    • IGRA detects latent TB and does not help diagnose active TB.
    • A negative result does not rule out TB.
  • Recurrent fever: do imaging only during an episode and only when inflammatory markers are abnormal, because the findings may disappear between episodes.

A 50/M with FUO has a positive IGRA, and liver biopsy shows non-caseating-looking granulomas but sarcoidosis is considered unlikely. AFB smear and PCR are negative and he is stable. What is the most appropriate plan?

  1. High-dose prednisone for granulomatous hepatitis
  2. Anakinra, since the work-up is complete
  3. Observe only, positive IGRA means latent TB
  4. Empiric anti-TB therapy, reassessing the diagnosis if no response after 6 weeks

D. A positive TST or IGRA plus granulomas, with sarcoidosis unlikely, is one of the listed exceptions where empiric anti-TB treatment is allowed. If he has not responded after 6 weeks, reconsider the diagnosis.
A is harmful because giving steroids before TB is excluded can let it spread. B is for FUO still undiagnosed after later-stage tests, not when there is a treatable lead. C ignores the granulomas, and a negative smear or PCR does not rule out TB.

Practice drill — Dr. Antonio style

A patient with adult-onset Still's disease refractory to NSAIDs is started on anakinra and his fever settles. The drug blocks the cytokine that is a key endogenous pyrogen. Which cytokine is it?

  1. IL-2
  2. IL-10
  3. IL-1
  4. IL-4

C. Anakinra is a recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist that blocks both IL-1α and IL-1β. IL-1 is a key cytokine in inflammation and the fever response.
The others do not fit: IL-10 is anti-inflammatory, IL-2 drives T-cell growth, and IL-4 drives the switch to IgE.

A 76/F on chlorpromazine and benztropine is found confused at home during a heat wave. Core temperature 41.2°C, skin hot and DRY, no rigidity, CK normal. What best explains her loss of heat dissipation?

  1. Muscarinic blockade impairing sweating and evaporative heat loss
  2. Dopamine blockade causing lead-pipe rigidity and muscle heat production
  3. Cytokine-induced elevation of the hypothalamic set point
  4. β-adrenergic blockade preventing tachycardia

A. This is classic heat stroke made worse by anticholinergic drugs. Blocking muscarinic receptors stops sweating, so she cannot lose heat by evaporation, and these drugs also interfere with the preoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus.
B describes NMS (neuroleptic malignant syndrome), but she has no rigidity and a normal CK. C describes fever, but there is no pyrogen here, so the set point is normal.

A 28/M develops agitation, tremor, diarrhea, profuse sweating, inducible ankle clonus and hyperreflexia 6 hours after tramadol was added to his sertraline. Temperature is 39.8°C. Most likely diagnosis?

  1. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
  2. Malignant hyperthermia
  3. Exertional heat stroke
  4. Serotonin syndrome

D. Harrison's Symptoms came on within hours of combining two serotonergic drugs (sertraline and tramadol), and he has clonus and brisk reflexes. That is serotonin syndrome.
NMS (neuroleptic malignant syndrome) is the main distractor. It follows an antipsychotic, develops over days, and causes lead-pipe rigidity with decreased reflexes.

A daughter gave her 80/M father paracetamol every 4 hours for a temperature of 41°C after he was found in a hot attic, confused with dry skin. Why is this inappropriate?

  1. Paracetamol raises the hypothalamic set point in the elderly
  2. There are no pyrogens to block in heat stroke, and acetaminophen adds hepatic stress
  3. Paracetamol causes rhabdomyolysis
  4. It is appropriate, but should be combined with aspirin

B. Antipyretics work by blocking pyrogens at the hypothalamus. In heat stroke caused by the environment there are no pyrogens, so they do nothing, and acetaminophen adds stress to the liver.
D is wrong because salicylates (aspirin) are also avoided: they further uncouple oxidative phosphorylation and can worsen coagulopathy.

A 68/F tourist arrives from Canada and, on her 2nd day in Manila, notices swollen ankles and feet. Vitals and heart, liver and kidney exams are normal. What is the best management?

  1. Furosemide for 3 days
  2. Admit for IV fluids and electrolyte monitoring
  3. Leg elevation or compression stockings, expect resolution in several days
  4. Oral salt tablets taken whole

C. This is heat edema: mild swelling of the feet and ankles in someone not yet used to the heat, with a normal heart, liver and kidney exam. It settles on its own in several days with leg elevation or compression stockings.
A is wrong because diuretics do not work for heat edema and can cause volume depletion.

Which patient can be managed with PASSIVE external rewarming alone?

  1. An 82/F with core temperature 34.2°C found on her bathroom floor
  2. A healthy 24/M hiker, core temperature 34.0°C, shivering, after 3 hours in cold rain
  3. A 30/M with core temperature 31.5°C after falling into a river
  4. A 45/F with known hypothyroidism off levothyroxine, core temperature 34.5°C

B. He is healthy, the exposure was acute, the hypothermia is mild and primary, and he is still shivering, which shows he has enough glycogen to make his own heat.
The others all need active rewarming. A is at an age extreme (elderly). C is below 32°C. D has a hormone deficiency (hypothyroidism).

A 61/M with core temperature 29°C is oozing from IV sites. His PT/aPTT come back normal and platelets are adequate. What best explains the discrepancy?

  1. Coagulation tests are run at 37°C, which rewarms the cold-inhibited clotting enzymes
  2. Hypothermia causes hemoconcentration that falsely shortens PT
  3. He has DIC from heat-shock proteins
  4. The bleeding is from hyperkalemia

A. Inside the cold patient, the clotting enzymes and platelets are slowed down, so he bleeds. The lab warms the blood sample to 37°C, which brings the enzymes back to normal, so the tests look normal.
This is also why platelets and FFP (fresh frozen plasma) will not work until the patient is rewarmed.

Which pairing in the management of severe hypothermia is INCORRECT?

  1. IV fluid — normal saline rather than lactated Ringer's
  2. ABG — interpret without temperature correction
  3. Central line — avoid deep insertion into the right atrium
  4. Euthyroid patient — empiric IV levothyroxine to speed rewarming

D. Giving levothyroxine to a hypothermic patient whose thyroid is normal is potentially hazardous. Give it only when there are real clues of hypothyroidism.
The other pairings are correct: normal saline is used because the cold liver cannot clear lactate, the ABG is not temperature-corrected, and a deep central line can irritate the cold right atrium and trigger arrhythmias.

A 26/F call-center agent who commutes in cold, damp weather in Baguio has itchy, burning, reddish-blue nodules on the backs of her fingers and toes every rainy season. Her mother has Raynaud's. What is the most likely diagnosis?

  1. Chilblain (pernio)
  2. Immersion foot
  3. Superficial frostbite
  4. Heat edema

A. Damp cold above freezing, itchy blue nodules on the backs of the hands and feet, and a family history of Raynaud's together point to chilblain.
Immersion foot comes from wet cold and causes swollen, cyanotic feet. Frostbite requires the tissue to actually freeze, which does not happen in Baguio weather.

A 33/M with 4 weeks of fever now has headache. CSF is being collected in a single tap. Which test–organism pair is INCORRECT?

  1. AFB smear — M. tuberculosis
  2. India ink — Cryptococcus neoformans
  3. Gram stain and culture — meningococcus
  4. India ink — herpes simplex virus 2

D. India ink stains the capsule of Cryptococcus, so it is not a test for a virus. HSV is detected by PCR.
The other pairs are correct: AFB smear for TB, India ink for Cryptococcus, and Gram stain with culture for bacteria like meningococcus.

A 29/F has had 1-week fever episodes about every 5 weeks for 18 months, completely well in between. Exam and tests done between episodes are normal. What is the best next step?

  1. PET/CT now while she is well, to avoid inflammation artifacts
  2. Empiric glucocorticoid trial
  3. Have her return during an episode to repeat history, exam and tests (with imaging if inflammatory markers are abnormal)
  4. Reassure, recurrent fever is never diagnosable

C. In recurrent fever, the findings may only be present during an episode and can vanish in between. So examine and test her while she is febrile, and do advanced imaging only during fever with abnormal inflammatory markers.
A gets the timing backwards. D is wrong because a cause is found in fewer than half of cases, which is not the same as never.

A 73/F with 5 weeks of fever has new temporal headache, jaw claudication, a tender cord-like temporal artery and ESR 112 mm/h. Blood cultures and CXR are negative. Which FUO category is most likely, and what is the treatment role?

  1. Infection, empiric antibiotics
  2. Non-infectious inflammatory disease (vasculitis), glucocorticoids once infection and lymphoma are reasonably excluded
  3. Malignancy, empiric chemotherapy
  4. Drug fever, stop all drugs for 72 hours

B. Temporal headache, jaw claudication and a tender temporal artery point to giant cell arteritis, which is a vasculitis and so an NIID. An ESR above 100 also favors an NIID.
Steroids are the supportive treatment for GCA and PMR, but only after infection and lymphoma are largely ruled out, so that a treatable cause is not hidden.

A 52/M with FUO has elevated CRP. Obligatory tests, repeat history and PE, drug-fever exclusion and fundoscopy reveal no PDCs. Which is the best next investigation?

  1. ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT
  2. Radiolabeled leukocyte scintigraphy
  3. Exploratory laparotomy
  4. Empiric anakinra trial

A. After the first-stage steps find no clues, FDG PET/CT is the first-choice advanced imaging, especially when ESR or CRP is high.
Leukocyte scintigraphy (B) is only the backup if PET/CT is not available. Surgery and drug trials come much later.
