A patient with suspected drug fever stops all medications, including supplements. His temperature is still 38.6°C at 96 hours. How should this be interpreted?

  1. Drug fever is confirmed, restart one drug at a time
  2. Observe for another 2 weeks before deciding
  3. Drug fever is unlikely, continue the search for PDCs
  4. This is IUO

C. Drug fever should clear within the 72-hour wash-off period after all drugs are stopped. A fever still present at 96 hours makes drug fever unlikely, so go back to searching for PDCs.
D is wrong because IUO means a normal temperature with high ESR and CRP, and this patient is febrile.

The family of a stable 44/M whose FUO is still unexplained after complete workup asks for "strong antibiotics just in case." Which statement is CORRECT?

  1. Empiric antibiotics are standard after 3 weeks of fever
  2. Unexplained FUO carries a high mortality, so treat empirically
  3. Empiric steroids are preferred because they shrink lymph nodes
  4. Avoid empiric therapy unless he deteriorates rapidly, the prognosis of unexplained FUO is generally favorable

D. He is stable, so empiric therapy should be avoided. Empiric antibiotics spoil future cultures and add risks of resistance and blood-count problems.
C is wrong because steroids shrinking the nodes is exactly the problem: they hide the disease. B is wrong because the risk of death depends on the underlying disease, and it is low when the FUO stays unexplained.

Last-look cram sheet

  • The temperature control center is the preoptic anterior hypothalamus, which works by negative feedback. Damage to the hypothalamus usually causes a subnormal temperature.
  • Heat loss: conduction is minimal, convection is the most common, radiation is the major route at rest, and evaporation is the major route when hot.
  • Esophageal temperature is the most accurate, and rectal reads the highest. Oral reads about 0.4°C lower and unadjusted tympanic about 0.8°C lower. Fever is above 37.7°C, and the FUO criterion is 38.3°C or higher.
  • Fever pathway: a pyrogen triggers IL-1, IL-6 and TNF, which induce COX-2 to make PGE2. PGE2 raises the set point (through cAMP).
  • Fever means a raised set point. Hyperthermia means a normal set point with hot, dry skin, and antipyretics do not work.
  • Hyperpyrexia is above 41.5°C and is most often from CNS injury.
  • Antipsychotic plus rigidity plus high CK means NMS (neuroleptic malignant syndrome).
  • Anesthesia (succinylcholine or the "-flurane" gases) means malignant hyperthermia, treated with dantrolene.
  • An SSRI combination plus clonus means serotonin syndrome Harrison's.
  • Anticholinergics stop sweating. Calcium channel blockers reduce blood flow to the skin. Beta-blockers prevent vasodilation.
  • Heat edema: no diuretics. Heat cramps: salt dissolved in water or ORS. Heat exhaustion: the brain is intact and the temperature is below 40.5°C.
  • Water-depletion heat exhaustion comes from drinking too little. Salt-depletion comes from drinking plain water and causes hyponatremia.
  • Heat stroke triad: heat exposure, CNS dysfunction and a temperature above 40.5°C. Above 42°C is a bad sign.
  • Classic heat stroke: elderly, dry skin, liver injury, high sodium. Exertional heat stroke: young, sweaty, rhabdomyolysis with kidney failure, low glucose.
  • Cooling: evaporative for everyone. Immersion only for young EHS patients, stopping at 38–39°C.
  • Heat stroke hypotension gets crystalloid, NOT norepinephrine. No antipyretics, no chlorpromazine and no depolarizing agents.
  • Hypothermia is a core temperature below 35°C. Mild (32–35°C) still has shivering and vasoconstriction.
  • Below 32°C means poikilothermia and active rewarming. Below 30°C, give one VF shock and hold drugs. Below 28°C, intermittent CPR is acceptable.
  • A heart rate too fast or a coma too deep for mild hypothermia means a secondary cause. Check glucose, toxins and sepsis.
  • Warm the trunk. Heating the limbs causes afterdrop, because cold blood returns to the core.
  • Rewarming arrhythmias come from abnormal depolarization and repolarization. Use antiarrhythmics only with extreme caution.
  • In hypothermia, use normal saline instead of lactated Ringer's, do not temperature-correct the ABG, and remember that clotting tests look falsely normal.
  • Hematocrit rises 2% per 1°C drop. Look for the Osborn J wave. The patient is not dead until warm (above 33°C) and dead.
  • Frostbite (tissue below 0°C): treat the hypothermia first, thaw in 37–40°C water for 30–60 minutes, give iloprost within 48 hours and tPA within 24 hours, and delay amputation.
  • Wet cold above freezing means trench foot, which can lead to liquefaction gangrene. Damp cold with itchy blue nodules and a Raynaud's family history means chilblain.
  • Revised FUO: more than 3 weeks, 38.3°C or higher at least twice, not immunocompromised, and no diagnosis after history, exam and obligatory tests. No hospitalization needed. The classic definition required 1 week as an inpatient.
  • IUO is a normal temperature with high ESR and CRP.
  • Recurrent fever has fever-free gaps of at least 2 weeks. A diagnosis is found in fewer than half, and testing is done during an episode.
  • In the Philippines, the top FUO cause is infection (TB). In the West it is NIID.
  • NIID clues: ESR above 100, temporal artery findings, retinal vasculitis and a response to naproxen.
  • The most important step is the search for PDCs. Stop antibiotics and steroids first. Repeat the history and exam before invasive tests.
  • Obligatory tests include CXR and abdominal ultrasound (preferred over CT). For miliary TB, liver biopsy has the highest yield.
  • With no PDCs, the order is fundoscopy, then FDG PET/CT, then leukocyte scintigraphy only if PET/CT is unavailable.
  • No empiric therapy unless the patient is deteriorating. Exceptions are instability, neutropenia, and a positive IGRA with granulomas (give anti-TB drugs and reassess at 6 weeks).
  • The prognosis of unexplained FUO is favorable.

2.05 Approach to Fever and Rash 19 items

Dr. Carmela Co-Buenviaje · Recall 3 / Comp 5 / App 7 / Analysis 4 · Past-exam style source: 2027 #78–95 AND 2028 #76–94 (same professor all years) + trans formative quiz (p. 15)

How Dr. Co-Buenviaje asks
  • She describes a rash, adds one exposure clue, and asks for the diagnosis, the cause (etiology) or the mode of transmission.
    • Typical exposure clues: recent travel, a mosquito (Aedes), a drug started about 2 weeks ago, raw seafood, sexual contact, a hot tub, a tick, mite or louse, or flood water.
    • So for every disease, learn both the rash AND the exposure that goes with it.
  • Her stems copy the trans wording almost word for word.
    • Example: "0.25 cm papules with rim of erythema… football-shaped erosions" is lifted straight from the HFMD (hand-foot-and-mouth disease) entry.
    • Learn the signature phrase of each disease, because that phrase is usually the whole question.
  • One-line etiology matching. "Which has drugs / GAS (group A Streptococcus) / EBV (Epstein-Barr virus) as etiology?" (2028 #83, #86 and 2027 #84).
  • Category questions. "Which belongs to the vesiculobullous / central maculopapular group?" You need to know which disease sits in which of the 8 eruption categories.
  • Mpox appears every year: the best test and specimen, and when isolation ends (2027 #91, #92 and 2028 #85).
  • Picture items (2 to 3 per exam): rubella, erythema infectiosum, HSV (herpes simplex virus) and target lesions.
  • Her trans formative quiz items come back.
    • 2027 #92 is quiz Q1 (mpox).
    • 2028 #82 is quiz Q3 (dengue).
    • 2028 #88 is nearly quiz Q4 (syphilis).

Approach & the 8 eruption categories MUST KNOW 2028 #76 2027 #78

The diagnosis comes from two things together: the distinctive look of the eruption and the clinical syndrome around it. Rashes are grouped by lesion MORPHOLOGY (what the lesions look like) into 8 types. Centrally distributed maculopapular is the most common type.

#Eruption typeMembers she likes to test
ACentrally distributed maculopapular
Mainly on the trunk. The most common type.		Measles, rubella, fifth disease, roseola, infectious mononucleosis, drug exanthem, typhus, leptospirosis, Lyme disease, typhoid, dengue, erythema marginatum, SLE, Still's disease, Zika
BPeripheral
Starts on the hands and feet (acral areas), then moves inward toward the trunk (centripetal).		RMSF, secondary syphilis, chikungunya, HFMD, erythema multiforme, Haverhill fever, endocarditis, COVID-19
CConfluent desquamative erythema
Diffuse redness that is often followed by peeling.		Scarlet fever, Kawasaki disease, strep and staph toxic shock syndrome, SSSS, exfoliative erythroderma, DRESS, SJS/TEN
DVesiculobullous or pustular
Lesions filled with fluid or pus.		Varicella, variola, hot-tub folliculitis, HSV, rickettsialpox, AGEP, Vibrio, ecthyma gangrenosum, MIRM, mpox
EUrticaria-like

FNodular

GPurpuric

An ulcer or a black crust dominates.		Tularemia, anthrax
  • How to read the category clue words in a stem
    • "Truncal", "starts on the trunk" or simply "maculopapular" with no special site points to group A (central).
    • "Wrists and ankles first", "palms and soles", "acral" or "spreads centripetally" points to group B (peripheral).
    • "Diffuse erythema", "sandpaper", "peeling" or "desquamation" points to group C (desquamative).
    • "Vesicles", "bullae", "pustules" or "dewdrops" points to group D.
    • "Wheal", "hive-like" or "urticaria-like" points to group E. "Nodules" points to F. "Petechiae", "purpura" or "ecchymoses" points to G. "Ulcer" or "black crust" points to H.
  • Look-alikes that land in the wrong group
    • HFMD, erythema multiforme and secondary syphilis can look widespread, but they belong to B (peripheral) because the palms, soles and limbs are where they are most prominent.
    • Rubella spreads from the face down, but it is central (A), not peripheral.
    • Variola (smallpox) is prominent on the limbs and palms, but its lesions are vesicles and pustules, so it is D.
    • Kawasaki disease and scarlet fever start as diffuse redness and then peel, so they are C, not A.
  • History items to ask (p. 1)
    • Immune status, drugs taken in the past month, travel, immunizations, pets and other animals, and bites (including arthropods such as ticks and mites).
    • Recent diet, heart disease, prosthetic material, and contact with ill or sexual partners.
    • The site where the rash started, and the direction and speed of its spread. These alone often separate look-alikes, for example measles versus rubella.
  • Size cut-offs for lesions
    • 1 cm separates the small and large forms: macule versus patch (flat), papule versus plaque or nodule (raised and solid), vesicle versus bulla (fluid-filled).
    • 5 mm separates petechiae (smaller) from purpura (larger). Both are flat bleeding into the skin.
    • Palpable purpura means vasculitis. It is raised because the vessel wall itself is inflamed and then bleeds.
  • Direction of spread
    • Craniocaudal (head to toe): measles and rubella.
    • Centripetal (limbs inward to the trunk): RMSF (Rocky Mountain spotted fever) and erythema multiforme.
    • Centrifugal (trunk outward to the limbs): the dengue maculopapular rash and variola.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "Which condition would present as a ___ eruption?" One choice is from the correct group and three are from other groups.
  • Trap: diseases that look "spread out" but belong to a specific group.
    • HFMD, erythema multiforme and syphilis are peripheral.
    • Rubella is central.
    • Variola is vesiculobullous.
    • Kawasaki disease and scarlet fever are desquamative, not central.
    • How to tell them apart: first ask what the lesion IS (flat red spots, blisters, peeling redness), then ask WHERE it is most prominent.

Which of the following is classified under the PERIPHERAL eruptions, i.e., beginning in acral areas before spreading centripetally?

  1. Rubella
  2. Typhoid fever
  3. Rocky Mountain spotted fever
  4. Kawasaki disease

C. RMSF begins on the wrists and ankles and then spreads inward toward the trunk (centripetally). The palms and soles are involved only later. That is the textbook peripheral pattern.
Rubella and typhoid fever are central maculopapular eruptions. Rubella starts on the face and moves down, and typhoid gives rose spots on the trunk.
Kawasaki disease is a confluent desquamative erythema (diffuse redness then peeling), so it belongs to group C.

Measles vs rubella vs erythema infectiosum vs roseola HIGH-YIELD 2028 #78, #79, #90, #93 2027 #79, #93

Four quick rules. A rash that is faster (reaches the trunk in 1 day), shorter (lasts 2 to 3 days) and clears as it spreads is RUBELLA. Slapped cheeks followed by a lacy rash is PARVOVIRUS B19. A rash that appears after the fever breaks, spares the face, in a child under 3 years is ROSEOLA. Koplik spots mean MEASLES.

Measles (rubeola)Rubella (German, 3-day)Erythema infectiosum (5th)Roseola (exanthem subitum, 6th)

  • Measles versus rubella (both start on the face and move down)
    • Rubella is the "faster and shorter" one. It reaches the trunk in 1 day (measles takes 2 to 3 days) and lasts 2 to 3 days (measles lasts 3 to 5 days).
    • Rubella clears from the face as it spreads to the body. Measles does not do this, it becomes confluent instead.
    • Measles patients look sick, with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and severe prostration. Rubella has only a short, mild prodrome.
    • Rubella gives tender nodes behind the ear (postauricular) and at the back of the head (suboccipital).
  • Koplik spots, the one sign that proves measles
    • Tiny 1 to 2 mm white or bluish spots, like "grains of sand", on the inner cheek (buccal mucosa) opposite the premolars.
    • They appear 1 to 2 days BEFORE the skin rash, so they can make the diagnosis early.
  • Roseola versus fifth disease (both: the rash comes after the fever is gone)
    • Roseola spares the face. Fifth disease starts ON the face (slapped cheeks).
    • Roseola is a child under 3 years with a high fever, sometimes a febrile seizure, and a rash gone within 2 days.
    • Fifth disease is a child 3 to 12 years, and its lacy rash keeps coming and going for about 3 weeks, especially with temperature changes.
  • Why each one matters in pregnancy
    • Rubella crosses the placenta. In the first trimester it causes microcephaly, congenital heart disease and deafness.
    • Parvovirus B19 causes fetal hydrops. It can also cause an aplastic crisis in people with high red cell turnover and chronic anemia in the immunocompromised.
TRAP
  • Forchheimer spots (petechiae on the soft palate) are NOT specific to rubella. They also occur in infectious mononucleosis, scarlet fever and Zika. Only Koplik spots are pathognomonic.
  • Picture items: 2028 #93 showed rubella (discrete pink papules, no lacy pattern, no "dewdrop" vesicles). 2027 #93 showed slapped cheeks.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as:
    • How fast and how long the rash spreads, then name the disease.
    • "What complication in pregnancy?"
    • A picture, then name the disease.
  • Trap: roseola versus fifth disease, since both have the rash after the fever.
    • How to tell them apart: face spared means roseola, face first means fifth disease.
  • Trap: fetal hydrops is parvovirus B19, NOT rubella. Rubella gives microcephaly, heart disease and deafness.

A 19/F unvaccinated college student has low-grade fever and sore throat, then pink macules on the face that reached her trunk and extremities within one day. By day 2 her face had cleared. She has tender postauricular and suboccipital nodes and petechiae on the soft palate. What is the most likely diagnosis?

  1. Measles
  2. Rubella
  3. Exanthem subitum
  4. Erythema infectiosum

B. The rash reached the trunk in 1 day, the face cleared as the rash moved down, and she has postauricular and suboccipital nodes. All three are classic rubella.
Measles is the tempting choice because it also starts on the face and moves down. But measles takes 2 to 3 days to reach the trunk, does not clear as it spreads, and has Koplik spots. The palatal petechiae here are Forchheimer spots, which are not specific.
Exanthem subitum (roseola) is a child under 3 with a rash after the fever that spares the face. Erythema infectiosum starts with slapped cheeks and a lacy rash.

Mode of transmission — her favorite "flip" HIGH-YIELD 2028 #80 2027 #80, #83

She gives the textbook rash description, then asks HOW it spread instead of what it is. So you must first recognize the disease, then recall its route. Memorize one transmission line per disease.

DiseaseMode of transmission (trans wording)
MeaslesPerson-to-person contact or airborne respiratory droplets
RubellaDirect or droplet contact with nose and throat (nasopharyngeal) secretions
Also transplacental spread to the fetus
Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19)Respiratory droplets
Also blood transfusion and blood products
Also vertical, from mother to fetus
Roseola (HHV-6 or HHV-7)Shared saliva
VaricellaHighly contagious

HFMDOral-oral and fecal-oral
Less commonly respiratory

  • Routes that are easy to swap, and how to keep them straight
    • "Transplacental" belongs to rubella. That is why rubella is famous for congenital defects.
    • "Blood transfusion" belongs to parvovirus B19 (and Zika and West Nile, less commonly).
    • "Shared saliva" belongs only to roseola.
    • "Oral-oral and fecal-oral" belongs to HFMD, which is why it spreads among siblings and family members.
    • "Airborne droplets or aerosols" is varicella (and measles). These two are the most contagious.
    • "Water with animal urine" is leptospirosis. "Contaminated food or water" is typhoid.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "0.25 cm papules… football-shaped erosions… what is the mode of transmission?" or "mixed-stage vesicles… mode of transmission?"
  • Trap: the wrong choices are the OTHER exanthems' routes, copied word for word.
    • Shared saliva is roseola. Transplacental is rubella. Fecal-oral is HFMD. Airborne is varicella.
    • How to avoid it: name the disease from the rash first, and only then look for its route among the choices.

Which disease–mode of transmission pair is INCORRECT?

  1. Erythema infectiosum – respiratory droplets, blood transfusion, mother to fetus
  2. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease – oral-oral and fecal-oral
  3. Varicella – airborne droplets or aerosols, also direct contact
  4. Exanthem subitum – transplacental infection of the fetus

D. Exanthem subitum (roseola, HHV-6 or HHV-7) spreads by shared saliva. Transplacental spread is rubella's line, which is why rubella causes congenital defects.
The other three pairs are copied correctly from the trans: parvovirus B19 spreads by droplets, transfusion and mother to fetus, HFMD spreads oral-oral and fecal-oral, and varicella spreads mainly by airborne droplets or aerosols.

A · Central maculopapular: infections with an exposure clue HIGH-YIELD 2028 #82, #91 2027 #82, #83, #84

Many infections give a similar maculopapular rash on the trunk with fever. What separates them is the EXPOSURE in the stem: lice, flea, mite, tick, flood water, food or the Aedes mosquito. The exposure names the disease.

  • The vector is the key clue word
    • Body lice means epidemic typhus. Think crowding, war or disaster.
    • Rat or cat flea means murine (endemic) typhus, in cities.
    • Mites in Asia mean scrub typhus. Look for an eschar.
    • Ticks mean spotted fevers, ehrlichiosis, RMSF or (with Ixodes) Lyme disease.
    • Aedes means dengue, Zika or chikungunya. Culex means West Nile. Tsetse fly means African trypanosomiasis.
    • Flood or urine-contaminated water means leptospirosis. Contaminated food or water means typhoid.
  • Telling the look-alikes apart
    • Typhoid versus typhus: the names sound alike but typhoid is Salmonella from food and water with rose spots, while typhus is a rickettsial disease from lice or fleas.
    • Scrub typhus versus spotted fevers: both have an eschar. Scrub typhus is mites in Asia with a rash that starts on the trunk. Spotted fevers are ticks with a rash that starts on the upper limbs.
    • Leptospirosis versus dengue: leptospirosis has red eyes with scleral hemorrhage and aseptic meningitis after water exposure. Dengue has leukopenia, breakbone pain and the 3-stage rash after a mosquito bite.
    • Infectious mononucleosis versus drug exanthem: a teenager with pharyngitis who gets a rash after ampicillin has EBV. The rash rate jumps from 5% to 30 to 90% with ampicillin.
    • Lyme disease versus STARI: Lyme is an Ixodes tick with a larger (about 15 cm) ring. STARI is the Lone Star tick, a smaller (about 8 cm) ring, a remembered bite and a milder illness.
TRAP (past-key conflict)
  • The rationales for 2028 #83 and 2027 #84 say the etiology of rat-bite fever is Borrelia.
  • The current trans says rat-bite fever is Spirillum minus (Sodoku) or Streptobacillus moniliformis (Haverhill fever).
  • Borrelia causes relapsing fever and Lyme disease. Follow the trans.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as:
    • "Positive for S. typhi, what rash is expected?" The answer is rose spots.
    • "Aedes exposure with biphasic fever, what rash?" The answer is the 3-stage dengue rash.
    • "Conjunctival or scleral hemorrhage with aseptic meningitis, how was it transmitted?" The answer is water contaminated with animal urine.
  • Trap: typhoid is not typhus.
    • How to tell the typhus family apart: lice means epidemic typhus, flea means murine typhus, mite means scrub typhus, and tick means spotted fever, Lyme disease or RMSF.

A 34/M farm worker from rural Asia has fever, headache, myalgia, tender inguinal nodes, a black crusted lesion on his groin and a diffuse macular rash that started on his trunk. Which vector most likely transmitted his infection?

  1. Body louse
  2. Rat flea
  3. Mite
  4. Ixodes tick

C. An eschar (the black crusted lesion), a macular rash that starts on the trunk, and nearby enlarged nodes in a farm worker from Asia add up to scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi). It is transmitted by mites, and the eschar marks the bite site.
A body louse causes epidemic typhus, which starts in the armpits and has no eschar. A rat flea causes murine typhus, also without an eschar. An Ixodes tick causes Lyme disease, which gives a single large ring rather than an eschar with a truncal rash.

Timing of rash vs fever (dengue 3 stages, Still's, roseola) LECTURER 2028 #82 trans quiz Q2, Q3

The lecturer marked this as "important to note". The dengue rash comes in 3 stages. First there is diffuse flushing. Midway through the illness a maculopapular rash appears on the trunk and spreads to the limbs and face. Finally, petechiae appear on the limbs AFTER the fever breaks (defervescence).

When the rash appearsDisease
After the fever resolvesRoseola, erythema infectiosum
At the height of each fever spike (salmon-colored 2 to 5 mm papules that come and go)Still's disease (ESR above 100, polyarthritis, enlarged spleen)
At the end of a fever episodeRelapsing fever
Midway through the illness, with petechiae after the fever breaksDengue
1 to 2 days after Koplik spotsMeasles
Weeks after a chancre at the bite siteAfrican trypanosomiasis
  • Why timing is such a strong clue
    • Several of these rashes look alike on the skin, so the moment the rash appears relative to the fever is often the only thing that separates them.
    • In a stem, watch for words like "after the fever lysed", "with each fever spike", "at the end of the episode" or "after defervescence".
  • Pairs that are easy to mix up
    • Dengue petechiae come AFTER the fever breaks. Still's rash comes WITH the fever peak. Do not reverse them.
    • Relapsing fever gives its rash at the END of an episode, not at the start.
    • Roseola and fifth disease both appear after the fever. Separate them by the face (spared in roseola, first in fifth disease).
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: a dengue syndrome with a mosquito exposure, then "what is the expected dermatologic presentation?" The wrong choices are the rashes of erythema marginatum, Lyme disease and typhoid.
  • Trap: dengue petechiae are NOT at the fever peak.
    • How to tell them apart: a rash at the fever peak is Still's disease, petechiae after the fever breaks is dengue.

A 16/M with dengue (Aedes exposure, leukopenia, saddleback fever) had a maculopapular rash on his trunk that spread to his limbs. On day 6 his fever lyses. Which skin finding is now most expected?

  1. Petechiae on the extremities
  2. Diffuse flushing of face and trunk
  3. Salmon-colored papules that appear with each fever spike
  4. Rose spots on the trunk

A. He has already passed through stage 2 (the maculopapular rash). Now that the fever has broken, stage 3 follows: petechiae on the extremities after defervescence.
Diffuse flushing is tempting because it is also part of dengue, but it is stage 1 and comes at the start, not after the fever breaks.
Salmon papules with fever spikes belong to Still's disease. Rose spots belong to typhoid.

Erythema migrans vs multiforme vs marginatum, plus SLE & Still's MUST KNOW 2028 #83 2027 #84, #89

Three "erythema M" words to separate. MIGRANS is one big (about 15 cm) bull's-eye after a tick bite, and it means Lyme disease. MULTIFORME is many small (2 cm or less) target lesions on the knees, elbows, palms, soles and face, triggered by HSV, Mycoplasma or drugs. MARGINATUM is polycyclic rings that vanish within HOURS, and it means rheumatic fever from group A Streptococcus (GAS).

Erythema migransErythema multiformeErythema marginatum
CauseB. burgdorferi (from an Ixodes tick)HSV, M. pneumoniae
Drugs: sulfa, phenytoin, penicillin		Group A Strep (rheumatic fever)
LesionOne expanding ring with central clearing, average 15 cmTarget lesions 2 cm or less, symmetric, spreading inward (centripetal)Rings joined in wavy (polycyclic) patterns on the trunk and upper limbs
CourseFades in about 1 month (may persist over 1 year)EM major involves the mucosa but has no SJS-type sloughingEach lesion resolves within hours
  • What a target lesion is: a red center, then a ring of clearing, then an outer red rim, up to 2 cm in size.
  • How to separate the three from the stem
    • A tick bite, then one large ring: migrans (Lyme disease).
    • Recent cold sore, pneumonia or a new sulfa, phenytoin or penicillin, then many small targets on the hands, feet and limbs: multiforme.
    • Recent sore throat, then joint pain, carditis or chorea, with rings that come and go within hours: marginatum (rheumatic fever).
SLEStill's disease
WhoYoung to middle-aged women
Flares with sun exposure		Children and young adults
RashButterfly (malar) rash on the cheeks
Discoid lesions with atrophy and scale
Telangiectasia around the nails
Oral erosions		Short-lived 2 to 5 mm salmon-colored papules that appear at the fever spikes
ClueArthritis plus heart, lung, kidney, blood or vasculitic diseaseHigh spiking fever, polyarthritis, enlarged spleen, ESR above 100
  • SLE versus Still's disease: both are autoimmune and both have arthritis.
    • A young woman whose rash flares in the sun, with organ involvement, is SLE.
    • A child or young adult with salmon papules that show up with each fever spike and a very high ESR is Still's disease.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "Which has GAS or EBV as etiology?" or "autoimmune, young women, flares with sun" (the answer is SLE).
  • Trap: the three "erythema M" words.
    • How to tell them apart: one big ring after a tick is migrans, small targets on the limbs is multiforme, rings gone in hours after strep throat is marginatum.
  • Trap: Still's disease versus SLE.
    • How to tell them apart: salmon papules with fever spikes means Still's disease.

A 12-year-old with recent sore throat now has migratory polyarthritis, a new murmur and chorea. Over his trunk are annular, polycyclic pink plaques that shift and disappear within a few hours. What is the etiology of this rash?

  1. Borrelia burgdorferi
  2. Group A Streptococcus
  3. Herpes simplex virus
  4. Mycoplasma pneumoniae

B. A sore throat followed by polyarthritis, carditis (new murmur) and chorea is rheumatic fever. Its rash, erythema marginatum, is made of polycyclic rings that shift and disappear within hours. The cause is group A Streptococcus.
Borrelia is tempting because its rash is also a ring, but erythema migrans is a single large ring that lasts weeks.
HSV and Mycoplasma trigger erythema multiforme, which gives small target lesions on the limbs.

B · Peripheral eruptions (palms & soles) HIGH-YIELD 2028 #77, #88, #89, #92 2027 #86–88, #95

These rashes start on the hands and feet (acral) and spread inward (centripetally). Sexual contact with copper-colored scaly palms is secondary syphilis. Football-shaped erosions with mouth erosions is HFMD (hand-foot-and-mouth disease). Target lesions 2 cm or smaller is erythema multiforme.

Painless chancre that healed weeks ago

  • Key clue words
    • "Wrists and ankles first" means RMSF. The palms and soles come late.
    • "Copper-colored", "scaly", "papulosquamous" plus a sexual history means secondary syphilis.
    • "Football-shaped erosions" or "0.25 cm papules with a rim of erythema" means HFMD.
    • "Target lesions" on knees, elbows, palms and soles means erythema multiforme.
    • "Tender finger pad nodules" (Osler) or "painless palm macules" (Janeway) plus IV drug use or a murmur means endocarditis.
    • "Chilblains" or "retiform purpura" means COVID-19.
  • Telling the look-alikes apart
    • Syphilis versus HFMD: both involve the palms and soles. Syphilis lesions are scaly and NEVER vesicular in adults. HFMD lesions are tender vesicles that turn into erosions, often in a child with mouth sores.
    • RMSF versus meningococcemia: both become petechial. RMSF has a tick history and starts at the wrists and ankles.
    • Osler versus Janeway: "Osler = Ouch". Osler nodes are tender and go with a subacute course (viridans strep). Janeway lesions are painless and go with an acute course (S. aureus).
    • Erythema multiforme versus SJS: EM major can involve the mouth and give fever, but the skin does not slough. Sloughing skin means SJS.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as:
    • Sexual history with copper scaly papules, asking for the organism. The answer is T. pallidum (trans quiz Q4).
    • IV drug use with hand and foot lesions, which points to endocarditis.
    • A picture of target lesions, which is erythema multiforme.
  • Trap: tender versus painless lesions in endocarditis.
    • How to tell them apart: "Osler = Ouch" (tender, subacute).
  • Trap: vesicles on the palms of an adult.
    • How to tell them apart: this is not syphilis, because secondary syphilis is never vesicular in adults.

A 24/M has fever and a rash on the trunk, palms and soles two months after unprotected sex. Which additional finding would argue AGAINST secondary syphilis?

  1. Copper-colored papules topped with scale
  2. Patchy "moth-eaten" hair loss
  3. Condyloma latum and mucous patches
  4. Tender vesicles on the palms evolving into erosions

D. The rash of secondary syphilis is never vesicular in adults. Tender palmar vesicles that turn into erosions fit HFMD instead, so this finding argues against syphilis.
Choices A to C are all features of secondary syphilis listed in the trans: copper-colored scaly papules, moth-eaten alopecia, and condyloma latum with mucous patches.

C · Confluent desquamative erythemas (scarlatiniform look-alikes) MUST KNOW 2027 #90

These start as diffuse redness and then peel. Sandpaper skin with Pastia's lines and a strawberry tongue is scarlet fever. Fissured lips with inflamed coronary arteries is Kawasaki disease. Very tender skin with a positive Nikolsky sign and NO tongue signs is SSSS (staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome).

    • "Sandpaper", "Pastia's lines" and "circumoral pallor" are scarlet fever only.
    • "Strawberry tongue" is in BOTH scarlet fever and Kawasaki disease, so it does not decide alone.
    • "Fissured lips", "hand and foot edema" and "coronary aneurysm" are Kawasaki disease.
    • "TSST-1", "palms red" and "colonization only" are staph TSS.
    • "Phage group II", "Nikolsky" and "profound skin tenderness" are SSSS.
  • Telling the look-alikes apart
    • Scarlet fever versus SSSS: both look scarlatiniform early. SSSS has painful skin and blisters with light pressure, but NO strawberry tongue and NO circumoral pallor.
    • Scarlet fever versus Kawasaki disease: Kawasaki has no known cause, affects children under 8, and threatens the coronary arteries.
    • Staph TSS versus strep TSS: staph TSS needs only colonization with a toxin-producing S. aureus. Strep TSS needs a severe, deep GAS infection such as necrotizing fasciitis.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: a long description (phage group II, Nikolsky sign, under 10 years or kidney dysfunction), then name the disease. The answer is SSSS.
  • Trap: the two toxic shock syndromes.
    • How to tell them apart: staph TSS needs only colonization, strep TSS needs a severe deep infection.

A 22/F has fever of 40°C, hypotension, conjunctival and oral mucosal erythema, and diffuse erythema that involves her palms. No deep soft-tissue infection is found, and cultures show only colonization with a toxin-producing organism. Which toxin is most likely responsible?

  1. TSST-1
  2. Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin A from necrotizing fasciitis
  3. Exfoliative toxin of phage group II S. aureus
  4. Shiga toxin

A. Fever above 39°C, hypotension, red mucosa, diffuse redness that includes the palms, and only colonization (no deep infection) is staphylococcal TSS. Its toxin is TSST-1.
Streptococcal exotoxin A is tempting because strep TSS looks similar, but strep TSS requires a severe GAS infection such as necrotizing fasciitis, and none was found here.
The phage group II exfoliative toxin causes SSSS (tender, blistering skin). Shiga toxin is linked to HUS.

SSSS vs SJS vs TEN (Nikolsky-positive sloughing) HIGH-YIELD 2027 #85, #90

SSSS and TEN both have a positive Nikolsky sign (the skin blisters or peels with light sideways pressure). SSSS is caused by a toxin, affects children, splits the skin superficially and spares the mucosa. SJS and TEN are caused by drugs in 80% of cases, involve the mucosa, and kill the whole thickness of the epidermis. They are graded by the body surface area (BSA) detached: SJS under 10%, overlap 10 to 30%, TEN over 30%.

SSSSSJSTEN
CauseS. aureus toxin (from colonization)Drugs in 80%: allopurinol, anticonvulsants, antibiotics
Also infection
WhoUnder 10 years, newborns, kidney failureAdults, especially with HIV, SLE, certain HLA types or slow acetylation
Uncommon in children
CleavageSuperficial, within the epidermisDeeper, with necrosis of the entire epidermis
MucosaNot involved (only nasal or eye secretions)Involved
BSA detached—Under 10%Over 30% (10 to 30% is overlap)
SkinVery tender, scarlet-fever-like redness that turns into blistersPurple-red macules, sometimes target-like, that turn into blisters and sloughing
  • Why the depth of the split matters
    • In SSSS the toxin splits the skin high up in the epidermis, so the damage is shallow.
    • In TEN the whole epidermis dies and comes off. The patient loses skin integrity, which leads to dehydration and sepsis. That is why mortality reaches up to 30%.
  • How to separate them in a stem
    • A young child, a staph source, very painful skin and no mouth or eye erosions points to SSSS.
    • An adult, a new drug (especially allopurinol) and erosions in the mouth or eyes points to SJS or TEN.
MUST KNOW
  • Estimate BSA with the patient's own palm, which equals 1%.
  • Add two kinds of skin together:
    • Detached skin: areas that are already bullae or erosions.
    • Detachable skin: areas that are Nikolsky-positive but have not blistered yet.
  • SJS and TEN are the most serious skin reactions to drugs, with mortality up to 30%. p. 9–10
TRAP
  • EM major (erythema multiforme major) involves the mucosa and often has fever, but it has no prominent sloughing. So it is not SJS.
  • MIRM (Mycoplasma-induced rash and mucositis) has mucositis at 2 or more sites, bloody crusts on the lips and a sparse rash on under 10% of the body. It is a separate condition from SJS/TEN and has a good prognosis.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "what percent of the skin is necrotic", then classify as SJS, overlap or TEN. Or "which finding favors TEN over SSSS".
  • Trap: the Nikolsky sign is positive in BOTH SSSS and TEN, so it cannot separate them.
    • How to tell them apart: look at the age, the drug history and whether the mucosa is involved.

Both a 3-year-old and a 45-year-old have fever, painful skin and a positive Nikolsky sign. Which finding most favors TEN over SSSS in the adult?

  1. Diffuse erythema preceding the bullae
  2. Profound skin tenderness
  3. Oral and conjunctival erosions after starting allopurinol 3 weeks earlier
  4. Nasal and conjunctival secretions with irritability

C. Mucosal erosions plus a newly started drug (allopurinol is a classic cause) point to SJS or TEN. SSSS does not involve the mucosa and is caused by a staph toxin, not a drug.
Diffuse erythema before the blisters and profound skin tenderness can occur in both conditions, so they do not help. In fact, profound tenderness is a hallmark of SSSS.
Nasal and conjunctival secretions with irritability are part of the SSSS prodrome, so they favor SSSS, not TEN.

Drug-induced eruptions — "which has a drug etiology?" HIGH-YIELD 2028 #84, #86

A new drug with fever and rash can be one of three levels of severity. A plain drug exanthem is itchy with no organ damage. DRESS looks the same but adds facial swelling, eosinophilia and LIVER involvement. SJS/TEN adds skin sloughing and mucosal erosions. A separate reaction, AGEP, is a febrile patient on a new drug with tiny sterile pustules.

  • Who is prone to drug rashes
    • People with HIV given sulfa drugs: 50 to 60% get a rash.
    • People with EBV mononucleosis given ampicillin: 30 to 90% get a rash.
  • Why some people get DRESS (genetics)
    • Some cannot detoxify arene oxides, which are the toxic breakdown products of aromatic anticonvulsants.
    • Others are slow N-acetylators, so they clear sulfonamides poorly.
  • How to tell a drug exanthem from a viral rash
    • The history shows a new medication, and the patient is NOT prostrated (not looking very ill).
    • Drug rashes are usually redder and itchier than viral ones.
  • Rashes with NO drug cause in the trans (useful for "which has a drug etiology" items)
    • Erythema marginatum (GAS), erythema migrans (Borrelia), Still's disease and SLE (autoimmune), and Kawasaki disease (idiopathic).
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as:
    • "Started on carbamazepine 2 weeks ago", with facial edema, eosinophilia and liver involvement. The answer is DRESS.
    • "Which has drugs as etiology?" The answer is AGEP.
  • Trap: a simple drug exanthem and DRESS look identical at first.
    • How to tell them apart: organ involvement and facial edema mean DRESS.

A 28/M was started on cotrimoxazole 12 days ago. He now has an intensely pruritic, bright-red, symmetric maculopapular rash on trunk and limbs. He is alert and not prostrated, with no facial edema, liver enzymes normal, no mucosal lesions or pustules. What is the most likely diagnosis?

  1. Drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
  2. Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis
  3. Measles
  4. Exanthematous drug-induced eruption

D. A new drug, a very itchy bright-red symmetric rash, and a patient who is not prostrated, with no organ involvement, is a simple exanthematous drug eruption.
DRESS is the tempting choice because its rash looks the same at first, but DRESS needs facial edema and organ (especially liver) involvement, and his liver enzymes are normal.
AGEP needs pustules, which he does not have. Measles would come with a prodrome of cough, coryza and conjunctivitis and a prostrated patient.

D · Vesiculobullous: varicella vs smallpox vs mpox (and HSV) HIGH-YIELD 2028 #76, #80, #85 2027 #86, #94

Lesions at mixed stages, mostly on the trunk, is VARICELLA. Lesions all at the same stage, on the face and limbs including the palms and soles, is VARIOLA (smallpox). Umbilicated "doughnut" pseudopustules on the genitals, hands or face after intimate contact is MPOX. Painful vesicles in a GROUP on a red base is HSV.

    • "Same stage", "palms and soles" and "severe backache" mean variola.
    • "Umbilicated", "central depression", "doughnut", genital lesions and big lymph nodes mean mpox.
    • "Painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base" means HSV.

    • A picture of clustered vesicles on the lip, which is HSV (2027 #94).
    • Sexual contact with genital lesions, where you must choose between HSV, mpox and syphilis.
  • Trap: genital lesions after sex.
    • How to tell them apart: painful grouped vesicles mean HSV, a painless ulcer means a syphilis chancre, and umbilicated pseudopustules with big nodes mean mpox.

During an outbreak investigation, a non-immune patient has fever, severe backache and vomiting, followed by deep pustules prominent on the face, forearms, palms and soles. In any one region, all lesions are at the same stage. Which agent is most likely?

  1. Varicella-zoster virus
  2. Rickettsia akari
  3. Variola major virus
  4. Pseudomonas aeruginosa

C. Lesions all at the same stage, prominent on the face and limbs including the palms and soles, after a prodrome with backache and vomiting, is smallpox (variola major).
Varicella is the tempting choice, but it shows lesions at mixed stages and is concentrated on the trunk.
Rickettsia akari gives an eschar with fewer than 100 papulovesicles. Pseudomonas gives hot-tub folliculitis in swimsuit areas.

Mpox: test, infectivity, isolation HIGH-YIELD LECTURER 2028 #85 2027 #91, #92 quiz Q1

The test of choice is PCR for viral DNA taken from the LESION itself (skin, fluid or crusts, collected by vigorous swabbing). A patient is infectious from the start of symptoms until the rash has FULLY healed and a FRESH layer of skin has formed. Close contacts isolate for 21 days.

  • Timeline of the illness
    • Incubation is 3 to 21 days, during which the person feels fine.
    • Next, a flu-like illness with swollen lymph nodes starts 1 to 4 days before the rash.
    • Then the rash appears and each lesion sinks in the center (umbilicated pseudopustule), then scales or ulcerates, scabs and heals.
    • The whole illness lasts 2 to 4 weeks.
  • Some people can spread mpox 1 to 4 days before they have symptoms.
  • The 4 routes of spread
    • Close or intimate contact: touching the rash or scabs, saliva, respiratory secretions, sexual contact, or long face-to-face contact.
    • Contaminated objects, fabrics and surfaces.
    • Infected wild animals.
    • Pregnancy, from mother to fetus or newborn.
  • Advice for the patient
    • Notify close contacts and isolate for the whole infectious period.
    • Do not share towels or glasses, and disinfect shared spaces.
    • Cover upholstered furniture, wear a mask and cover the lesions around others.
  • Advice for a close contact: watch for symptoms. If none develop, complete 21 days of isolation. Twenty-one days is the upper end of the incubation period.
TRAP
  • Scabbed or crusted lesions are STILL contagious. Crusting is not the end point.
  • Being without fever for 24 hours, or feeling better, is also NOT the end point.
  • Serology or blood tests are not the preferred test, because the virus is best found in the lesion.
  • The trans also says "until lesions heal and scabs fall off". For the quiz and exam, the answer is a fresh layer of skin.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: when isolation ends, the preferred specimen, or the cause of umbilicated genital pseudopustules after sex.
  • New angles to expect: how long contacts isolate, the incubation range, and how the specimen is collected.

A clinician suspecting mpox in a man with umbilicated pustules on his genitals and thighs sends a serum antibody test and a throat swab. What is the BEST way to confirm the diagnosis?

  1. Repeat paired serum antibody titers in 2 weeks
  2. PCR for viral DNA on material vigorously swabbed from a skin lesion (fluid or crust)
  3. Tzanck smear of a vesicle base
  4. Blood PCR for viral load

B. The trans names PCR for viral DNA as the test of choice, using material taken directly from the rash (skin, fluid or crusts) by vigorous swabbing.
Antibody titers only show that the person was exposed, and they take weeks. Blood is not the best specimen because the virus is most reliably found in the lesions, so blood PCR is the tempting but weaker choice.

Exposure / host clue to diagnosis (Vibrio, hot tub, neutropenia) HIGH-YIELD 2028 #81, #87

Raw oysters or a wound in seawater, plus cirrhosis, hemorrhagic bullae and hypotension, is Vibrio vulnificus. A neutropenic patient with a bulla that becomes an eschar with a red halo in the armpit or groin is ecthyma gangrenosum (Pseudomonas).

Exposure or hostThink
Raw or undercooked seafood (oysters), or a wound in seawater

Redness, then hemorrhagic bullae, then necrotic ulcers
Mortality 50%
Neutropenia with Pseudomonas bacteremiaEcthyma gangrenosum (armpit, groin, perianal area)
Hot tub or swimming pool, in an outbreakP. aeruginosa folliculitis
Flood or water with animal urineLeptospirosis
Contaminated food or waterTyphoid (rose spots)
Body lice
Rat or cat flea
Mites
Mouse mites		Epidemic typhus
Murine typhus
Scrub typhus
Rickettsialpox

  • Vibrio versus ecthyma gangrenosum: both give hemorrhagic bullae with sepsis in a sick host. The host and the exposure separate them.
    • Vibrio: raw oysters or seawater, in a person with cirrhosis, diabetes or kidney failure. The bullae turn into necrotic ulcers, usually on the legs.
    • Ecthyma gangrenosum: a neutropenic patient with Pseudomonas bacteremia. A firm plaque becomes a bulla, then an eschar with a red halo, usually in the armpit, groin or perianal area.
  • Hot-tub folliculitis is also Pseudomonas, but in a healthy person. It comes in outbreaks after bathing and is usually self-limited.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "ate uncooked seafood… gram-negative curved rods". The answer is V. vulnificus.
  • Trap: both Vibrio and ecthyma gangrenosum give hemorrhagic bullae with sepsis.
    • How to tell them apart: seafood and cirrhosis mean Vibrio, neutropenia means ecthyma gangrenosum.

A 50/F with acute leukemia on chemotherapy (ANC 200) has fever and hypotension. In her axilla, an indurated plaque became a hemorrhagic bulla that sloughed into a black eschar with an erythematous halo. She has not eaten seafood. Which organism is most likely?

  1. Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  2. Vibrio vulnificus
  3. Bacillus anthracis
  4. Orientia tsutsugamushi

A. A neutropenic patient (ANC 200) with an armpit plaque that became a bulla and then an eschar with a red halo has ecthyma gangrenosum, usually caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Vibrio is tempting because it also gives hemorrhagic bullae with shock, but it needs raw seafood or seawater exposure, usually in cirrhosis, and she has not eaten seafood.
Anthrax needs animal exposure and gives a painless eschar with edema. Orientia needs a mite bite and comes with a truncal rash.

E · Urticaria-like & F · Nodular MUST KNOW 2028 #94 2027 #81

Fever with hive-like plaques that last 3 to 5 days and do NOT blanch under a glass slide (diascopy) is urticarial vasculitis. Very tender nodules on the shins of a young woman is erythema nodosum. Tender, swollen plaques on the face, neck and arms with a high white count is Sweet syndrome.

Classic urticariaUrticarial vasculitis
FeverUsually noneVariable
Fever with hive-like lesions most often means this
BlanchingBlanchesDoes not blanch under a glass slide, because blood has leaked out of the vessels
Each lesion lasts24 hours or less3 to 5 days
Itchy or burning
CausesHypersensitivitySerum sickness, hepatitis B, enterovirus, parasites, drugs, SLE, Sjögren's
  • Why urticarial vasculitis does not blanch: the vessel walls are inflamed and blood has leaked into the skin. Pressing with glass cannot push out blood that is already outside the vessels.
  • Clue words for urticarial vasculitis: "hive-like but lasting days", "non-blanching", "burning", plus hepatitis B, SLE or Sjögren's.
Nodular diseaseEtiologyMorphology and siteWho and clue wordsLook-alike
Erythema nodosum (septal panniculitis)Strep, fungi, TB, Yersinia
Sulfa, penicillin, oral contraceptives
Sarcoidosis		Violet-red nodules that do not ulcerate
Extremely tender
Lower legs		Women 15 to 30
Joint pain in 50%		Chronic meningococcemia (nodules not tender)
Sweet syndromeInfection, IBD, pregnancy, blood cancers, G-CSFTender red-blue plaques so swollen they look like blisters
Face, neck, arms		Women 30 to 60
Leukocytosis
20% have a malignancy		Erythema nodosum (on the legs)
Disseminated infectionFungi, mycobacteriaNodules under the skin up to 3 cm
Necrotic nodules suggest Aspergillus or Mucor
Molluscum-like lesions suggest Cryptococcus		Immunocompromised
Candidiasis triad: fever, muscle pain, nodules		—
Bacillary angiomatosisBartonella henselae or quintanaVascular nodules that bleed easilyAdvanced HIV

  • Telling the tender nodules apart
    • Erythema nodosum: young women 15 to 30, extremely tender nodules on the shins, often after strep, TB, sarcoidosis or oral contraceptives.
    • Sweet syndrome: women 30 to 60, swollen plaques mainly on the face, neck and arms, with leukocytosis and often a blood cancer or G-CSF. On the legs it can mimic erythema nodosum.
    • Chronic meningococcemia: purpuric leg nodules that look like erythema nodosum but are NOT very tender.
  • Nodules in the immunocompromised: think disseminated fungal or mycobacterial infection. In advanced HIV with friable vascular nodules, think bacillary angiomatosis.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "non-blanching urticaria-like lesions with hepatitis", which is urticarial vasculitis. It has been asked twice, so expect a new angle such as lesion duration or diascopy.
  • Trap: erythema nodosum and Sweet syndrome are tender too.
    • How to tell them apart: they are nodules or swollen plaques, not wheals.

A 48/F with acute myeloid leukemia receiving G-CSF develops fever and multiple tender, red-blue, very edematous plaques on her face, neck and arms that look almost blistered. CBC shows leukocytosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?

  1. Erythema nodosum
  2. Urticarial vasculitis
  3. Sweet syndrome
  4. Bacillary angiomatosis

C. Swollen plaques that look like blisters (pseudovesicular) on the face, neck and arms, with leukocytosis, in a woman with a blood cancer receiving G-CSF, is Sweet syndrome.
Erythema nodosum is the tempting choice because it is also tender, but it gives nodules on the shins of younger women (15 to 30).
Urticarial vasculitis gives non-blanching wheals. Bacillary angiomatosis gives friable vascular nodules in advanced HIV.

G · Purpuric: meningococcemia vs RMSF vs dengue vs DGI HIGH-YIELD LECTURER

Fever with petechiae that multiply quickly and low blood pressure must be treated as bacterial sepsis right away. This is acute meningococcemia until proven otherwise, and it cannot be reliably told apart from RMSF or echovirus 9 in time. Purpura fulminans reflects severe DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) and is an emergency.

Acute meningococcemiaRMSFDengue
Agent and vectorN. meningitidisR. rickettsii (tick)Dengue virus (Aedes)
HostChildren, people with no spleen, C5 to C8 complement deficiencyTick exposureTropics
Rash coursePink blanching spots or hives
Then many petechiae on trunk and limbs
Sometimes purpura fulminans		Starts at wrists and ankles, then spreads inward
Palms and soles late
Macules turn into petechiae		Flushing, then a maculopapular rash, then petechiae after the fever breaks
SyndromeHypotension, meningitisHeadache, muscle pain, abdominal pain
Mortality up to 40%		Breakbone pain, leukopenia, saddleback fever
  • Why you treat first and sort out later: the lecturer stresses that meningococcemia, RMSF and echovirus 9 may be impossible to separate quickly, and meningococcemia can kill within hours. So the safe move is to treat as bacterial sepsis immediately.
  • Telling the three apart when there is time
    • Meningococcemia: asplenia or complement deficiency, rapid shock and meningitis.
    • RMSF: a tick history and a rash that begins at the wrists and ankles.
    • Dengue: an Aedes exposure, leukopenia, and petechiae that appear after the fever breaks.
DiseaseEtiologyMorphologyClue wordsLook-alike
Purpura fulminansSevere DIC (from sepsis, cancer or trauma)Large irregular bruises, then blood-filled bullae, then black necrosisEmergency
High risk without a spleen		Retiform purpura
Chronic meningococcemiaN. meningitidisMixed lesions
Purpura with pale blue-gray centers
Leg nodules that are NOT tender		Complement deficiency, fevers that come and go, arthritisErythema nodosum, DGI
DGIN. gonorrhoeaeFew, countable (under 40) hemorrhagic pustules with gray necrotic centers
Near the joints, more often on the arms		Sexually active women
Tenosynovitis		Chronic meningococcemia
Enteroviral petechial rashEchovirus 9, coxsackievirus A9Widespread petechiaeOutbreaks
Aseptic meningitis		Meningococcemia
Viral hemorrhagic feverArenaviruses, bunyaviruses, filoviruses (Ebola), flavivirusesPetechiaeTravel
Fever, shock, and bleeding from the mucosa or gut		Dengue
TTP/HUSADAMTS13 deficiency, Shiga toxin (E. coli O157:H7), drugsPetechiaeHemolytic anemia with fragmented cells (MAHA), low platelets, kidney and brain involvement
Normal coagulation tests		DIC
Small-vessel vasculitis and HSPGAS, hepatitis B or C, drugs
IgA in HSP		Palpable purpura in crops on the lower legsHSP: a child with purpura, arthritis and abdominal pain—
  • Key clue words
    • "Asplenia" or "C5 to C8 deficiency" points to meningococcemia.
    • "Fewer than 40 pustules with gray centers near joints" plus tenosynovitis in a sexually active woman points to DGI.
    • "Blue-gray centers" and painless leg nodules point to chronic meningococcemia.
    • "Travel" with petechiae, shock and bleeding points to viral hemorrhagic fever.
    • "Palpable" purpura points to vasculitis, because the inflamed vessel wall makes it raised.
  • DIC versus TTP/HUS: both have low platelets and petechiae. In DIC the clotting tests are abnormal. In TTP/HUS the clotting tests are normal.
  • DGI versus chronic meningococcemia: the lesions can look identical. Tenosynovitis and a sexual history favor DGI.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: a host clue (no spleen, complement deficiency, sexually active) with a purpuric pattern, then name the organism. Or "next step", where the answer is to treat as sepsis.
  • Trap: the coagulation tests.
    • How to tell them apart: TTP/HUS has NORMAL coagulation, while purpura fulminans reflects DIC.

A 23/F, sexually active, has low-grade fever, pain along the extensor tendons of her wrist, and about a dozen scattered hemorrhagic pustules with gray necrotic centers near her wrists and fingers. What is the most likely etiology?

  1. Neisseria meningitidis
  2. Neisseria gonorrhoeae
  3. Rickettsia rickettsii
  4. Echovirus 9

B. A small, countable number (under 40) of hemorrhagic pustules with gray centers near the joints, plus tenosynovitis (pain along the tendons) in a sexually active woman, is disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI).
N. meningitidis is tempting because chronic meningococcemia can look the same, but it lacks the tenosynovitis and the sexual clue.
RMSF gives petechiae spreading inward from the wrists and ankles, not pustules. Echovirus 9 gives widespread petechiae.

H · Ulcers & eschars: tularemia vs anthrax (and every eschar) MUST KNOW quiz Q5

A TENDER necrotic ulcer with raised borders (the ulceroglandular form) is TULAREMIA. A PAINLESS ulcer ringed by vesicles that becomes a black eschar with swelling, with NO other rash anywhere, is ANTHRAX.

DiseaseEtiologyLesionExposureOther rash?
TularemiaFrancisella tularensisTender papule that becomes a tender necrotic ulcer with raised bordersTicks, biting flies, infected animals35% have other eruptions
AnthraxBacillus anthracisItchy papule
Then a 1 × 3 cm painless ulcer ringed by vesicles
Then a central eschar with swelling
Then a scar		Animals or animal products, sporesNone, the eschar is the only lesion
Scrub typhusO. tsutsugamushiEscharMitesMacular rash on the trunk
Spotted feversR. africae and othersEscharTicksMaculopapular rash on the upper limbs, then the trunk
RickettsialpoxR. akariEscharMouse mitesPapulovesicles
SodokuS. minusEscharRat biteBlotchy violet rash
Ecthyma gangrenosumP. aeruginosaEschar with a red haloNeutropenia—
  • Two questions sort every eschar
    • Is it painful? Tender points to tularemia. Painless points to anthrax.
    • Is there a rash elsewhere? An eschar with a generalized rash points to a rickettsial disease (scrub typhus, spotted fever, rickettsialpox) or Sodoku. An eschar alone, with swelling, points to anthrax.
  • Then use the exposure: animal hides and spores mean anthrax, ticks or biting flies mean tularemia, mites in Asia mean scrub typhus, mouse mites in a city mean rickettsialpox, and neutropenia means ecthyma gangrenosum.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: a lesion with an animal exposure, then name the organism.
  • Trap: tularemia versus anthrax versus rickettsial eschars.
    • How to tell them apart: tender means tularemia, painless means anthrax, and an eschar with a generalized rash means a rickettsial disease.

A 40/M who processes goat hides noticed an itchy papule on his forearm that became a painless ulcer ringed by small vesicles, then a black central eschar with marked surrounding edema. He has no other skin lesions. Which organism is responsible?

  1. Francisella tularensis
  2. Rickettsia akari
  3. Orientia tsutsugamushi
  4. Bacillus anthracis

D. A painless ulcer ringed by vesicles that becomes a black eschar with marked swelling, as the ONLY skin finding, in a man who handles goat hides, is cutaneous anthrax.
Tularemia is tempting because it also follows animal contact, but its ulcer is tender.
Rickettsia akari and Orientia do give eschars, but always together with a rash elsewhere, and he has none.

Clue word to diagnosis (one-liners) HIGH-YIELD

Her stems are built from these phrases. When you see the phrase, name the disease.

    • Nagayama spots belong to roseola, Forchheimer spots are not specific, and Koplik spots prove measles.
    • Rose spots are typhoid, while rose-pink papules with a white halo are roseola.
    • Strawberry tongue is in both scarlet fever and Kawasaki disease. Pastia's lines and sandpaper skin are scarlet fever only. Fissured lips and coronary aneurysm are Kawasaki disease only.
    • MIRM and SJS both affect the mucosa. MIRM has bloody lip crusts, a sparse rash on under 10% of the body and a good prognosis.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "Which pair is INCORRECT?" using these phrases.
  • Trap: the strawberry tongue.
    • How to tell them apart: it appears in BOTH scarlet fever and Kawasaki disease, but Pastia's lines appear only in scarlet fever.

Which clue–diagnosis pair is INCORRECT?

  1. "Grains of sand" on buccal mucosa opposite the premolars – measles
  2. Football-shaped erosions on palms and soles – hand-foot-and-mouth disease
  3. Accentuated petechiae in linear skin folds (Pastia's lines) – Kawasaki disease
  4. "Dewdrops on a rose petal" in mixed stages – varicella

C. Pastia's lines belong to scarlet fever, not Kawasaki disease. This pair is tempting to accept because the two diseases share a scarlet-fever-like rash and a strawberry tongue. Kawasaki disease is recognized instead by fissured lips, swelling of the hands and feet, and coronary artery vasculitis.
The other three pairs are correct: Koplik spots ("grains of sand") are measles, football-shaped erosions are HFMD, and "dewdrops on a rose petal" in mixed stages is varicella.

Practice drill — Dr. Co-Buenviaje style

A 29/M has 5 days of fever, myalgia and tender inguinal and cervical nodes, followed by the lesions shown, also on his genitals. Lesions are firm, some with central depression. His partner of the last month has similar lesions. His asymptomatic housemate asks how long he must stay isolated if he never develops symptoms. What is the correct advice?

  1. Until 24 hours without fever
  2. Complete 21 days of isolation
  3. Until the patient's lesions have crusted
  4. No isolation is needed without symptoms

B. The patient has mpox: a flu-like prodrome with swollen nodes, then firm umbilicated lesions including on the genitals, and a sexual partner with the same lesions. A close contact isolates while watching for symptoms. If none develop, he completes 21 days, which is the maximum incubation period.
"Until the lesions have crusted" is the tempting wrong choice. Crusted lesions are still contagious, and the patient stays infectious until a fresh layer of skin forms.
Being without fever for 24 hours is not an end point, and having no symptoms does not remove the need to isolate, since some people spread mpox before symptoms start.

A 6-year-old has 2 days of low fever and dry cough, then the intensely itchy eruption shown, which began on the face and is now densest on the trunk. Which feature best distinguishes this from smallpox?

  1. Lesions in different stages (macules, vesicles, crusts) are present together
  2. Lesions are most prominent on the palms and soles
  3. Lesions are all at the same stage in one area
  4. Red macules on the tongue and palate appear first

A. This is varicella, whose lesions come in crops, so macules, vesicles and crusts are all present together, mostly on the trunk.
Choices B, C and D all describe variola (smallpox): prominent on the palms and soles, all lesions at the same stage in an area, and red spots on the tongue and palate appearing first.

A 17/M had a painful cluster of vesicles on his lip one week ago. He now has the symmetric lesions shown (≤2 cm, central dusky zone, pale ring, outer red rim) on his elbows, knees, palms and soles, with no skin sloughing. Which is the most likely trigger?

  1. Borrelia burgdorferi
  2. Group A Streptococcus
  3. Treponema pallidum
  4. Herpes simplex virus

D. Symmetric target lesions of 2 cm or less on the elbows, knees, palms and soles are erythema multiforme. The painful lip vesicles a week earlier were herpes labialis, so HSV is the trigger.
Borrelia causes erythema migrans, a single ring of about 15 cm. Group A Streptococcus causes erythema marginatum, rings that vanish within hours.
Treponema pallidum is tempting because secondary syphilis also involves the palms and soles, but its lesions are copper-colored scaly papules, not targets.

A 61/M with alcoholic cirrhosis develops fever, hypotension and the lesions shown, a day after a seaside trip where he ate raw oysters. The lesions are evolving into necrotic ulcers. Which organism is most likely?

  1. Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  2. Staphylococcus aureus
  3. Vibrio vulnificus
  4. Neisseria meningitidis

C. Raw oysters, cirrhosis, hemorrhagic bullae turning into necrotic ulcers, and shock add up to disseminated Vibrio vulnificus, which has a mortality of 50%.
Pseudomonas is tempting because ecthyma gangrenosum also gives hemorrhagic bullae, but that is a lesion of neutropenic patients, not of people who ate seafood.

A 4-year-old and his sister had mild fever, sore mouth and the lesions shown. Six weeks later the mother returns worried about a new finding. Which late finding is expected from this illness?

  1. Shedding of the fingernails (onychomadesis)
  2. Splinter hemorrhages under the nails
  3. "Moth-eaten" alopecia
  4. Coronary artery aneurysm

A. Two siblings with mild fever, mouth sores and lesions on the palms is HFMD (coxsackievirus A16 or enterovirus 71). Nail shedding (onychomadesis) can follow 1 to 2 months after the illness.
Splinter hemorrhages belong to endocarditis. Moth-eaten alopecia belongs to secondary syphilis. Coronary artery aneurysm belongs to Kawasaki disease, which is tempting because it also affects young children and the hands, but it does not cause vesicles or erosions.

A 52/M started allopurinol 3 weeks ago. He has fever, purpuric targetoid macules, oral erosions and a positive Nikolsky sign. Using his palm, detached skin (bullae, erosions) equals 6 palms and Nikolsky-positive skin not yet blistered equals 8 palms. What is the classification?

  1. Stevens-Johnson syndrome
  2. SJS/TEN overlap
  3. Toxic epidermal necrolysis
  4. Erythema multiforme major

B. Each palm is 1% of the body surface. You add the detached skin and the detachable skin: 6 plus 8 gives 14%. A value between 10 and 30% is SJS/TEN overlap.
The trap is counting only the detached skin (6%), which would wrongly give SJS.
TEN needs more than 30%. Erythema multiforme major can involve the mucosa but lacks prominent skin sloughing.

Which eruption–drug pair is INCORRECT?

  1. Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis – antimicrobials
  2. DRESS – aromatic anticonvulsants
  3. SJS/TEN – allopurinol
  4. Erythema migrans – penicillin

D. Erythema migrans is the rash of Lyme disease, caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, not by a drug. Penicillin is listed as a trigger for erythema MULTIFORME. Do not mix up the "erythema M" names.
The other pairs are correct: AGEP with antimicrobials, DRESS with aromatic anticonvulsants, and SJS/TEN with allopurinol.

A 26-week pregnant woman's husband just returned from a tropical area with Zika transmission. He has a pruritic maculopapular rash, conjunctival injection and small-joint arthralgia. Apart from Aedes mosquito bites, which route puts the fetus at risk through him?

  1. Shared saliva
  2. Fecal-oral contact
  3. Sexual transmission
  4. Water contaminated with animal urine

C. Zika spreads mainly through Aedes mosquitoes, and less commonly through sex or blood transfusion. If the mother is infected, the virus can reach the fetus and cause microcephaly. So her husband can infect her sexually, which then puts the fetus at risk.
Shared saliva is the route for roseola. Fecal-oral is HFMD. Water with animal urine is leptospirosis.

A 38/F back from a safari in southern Africa has fever, headache, regional lymphadenopathy, a black crusted lesion with a red rim on her ankle where a tick was attached, and a maculopapular rash on her proximal limbs spreading to her trunk. Which is the most likely etiology?

  1. Orientia tsutsugamushi
  2. Rickettsia africae
  3. Rickettsia akari
  4. Bacillus anthracis

B. A tick bite in Africa, an eschar at the bite, and a maculopapular rash that starts on the upper limbs and spreads to the trunk is African tick-bite fever, one of the spotted fevers, caused by Rickettsia africae.
Orientia is tempting because scrub typhus also gives an eschar, but it is spread by mites in Asia and its rash starts on the trunk.
R. akari is spread by urban mouse mites and gives papulovesicles. Anthrax gives an eschar with no rash at all.

A 9-year-old with asplenia has 12 hours of fever and lethargy, BP 80/40, and a petechial eruption on the trunk and legs that is increasing by the hour. There is no travel or tick history. What is the best next step?

  1. Wait for blood culture results before antibiotics
  2. Skin biopsy to separate meningococcemia from RMSF
  3. Treat immediately as bacterial sepsis
  4. Observe whether the rash reaches the palms and soles

C. The lecturer stresses that meningococcemia, RMSF and echovirus 9 may be impossible to tell apart quickly. A child without a spleen, in shock, with petechiae multiplying by the hour must be treated as bacterial sepsis immediately. Asplenia also raises the risk of purpura fulminans.
Waiting for cultures, doing a biopsy, or watching the rash all waste time in a disease that can kill within hours.

A febrile woman with Sjögren's syndrome has hive-like plaques. All of the following support urticarial vasculitis EXCEPT:

  1. Each lesion resolves completely within 24 hours
  2. Lesions do not blanch under a glass slide
  3. Lesions burn rather than only itch
  4. Individual lesions persist for 3–5 days

A. Lesions that clear completely within 24 hours describe classic urticaria (hives), not vasculitis.
Urticarial vasculitis lesions last 3 to 5 days, do not blanch under a glass slide because blood has leaked out of the vessels, and may burn. Sjögren's syndrome is one of its listed causes.

Which pairing of rash timing and disease is INCORRECT?

  1. Roseola – rash appears after the fever resolves
  2. Still's disease – rash coincides with fever spikes
  3. Dengue – petechiae after defervescence
  4. Relapsing fever – rash at the onset of each febrile episode

D. Relapsing fever (Borrelia) gives a central rash at the END of each fever episode, not at the start.
The other pairs are correct: roseola appears after the fever resolves, Still's rash comes with the fever spikes, and dengue petechiae appear after the fever breaks.

A 45/F from the southern US recalls removing a Lone Star tick (Amblyomma americanum) a week ago. She has mild malaise and one annular lesion with central clearing about 8 cm across. Compared with the leading alternative, what is her diagnosis?

  1. Southern tick-associated rash illness (STARI)
  2. Lyme disease
  3. Erythema marginatum
  4. Erythema multiforme

A. A Lone Star tick, a smaller ring (about 8 cm), a remembered bite, and a mild illness point to STARI.
Lyme disease is the leading alternative because its ring looks almost the same. But Lyme erythema migrans averages 15 cm, comes from an Ixodes tick, and the illness is more severe.
Erythema marginatum (rings gone within hours) and erythema multiforme (small targets) do not fit a single expanding ring after a tick bite.

A kindergarten teacher who is 16 weeks pregnant was exposed to a 6-year-old with the rash shown, which appeared after the child's fever subsided. What fetal complication is she most at risk for?

  1. Microcephaly, congenital heart disease, deafness
  2. Coronary artery aneurysm
  3. Neonatal flaccid paralysis
  4. Fetal hydrops

D. Slapped cheeks and a lacy rash that appeared after the fever is erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19). In pregnancy, parvovirus B19 causes fetal hydrops.
Choice A is the tempting one, but microcephaly, congenital heart disease and deafness are congenital rubella (and microcephaly is also Zika).
Coronary artery aneurysm is Kawasaki disease.

A 4-year-old with nasal colonization by toxin-producing S. aureus has fever, irritability and diffusely red, extremely tender skin. Light lateral pressure forms bullae. He has no strawberry tongue and no circumoral pallor. Compared with TEN, where is the split in his skin and what causes it?

  1. Entire epidermis – drug hypersensitivity
  2. Superficial epidermis – toxin from S. aureus phage group II
  3. Dermal–epidermal junction – group A strep exotoxins
  4. Superficial epidermis – viral cytopathic effect

B. This is SSSS. A toxin from phage group II S. aureus splits the skin superficially within the epidermis.
Choice A describes TEN, where the whole epidermis dies, usually because of a drug.
Group A strep exotoxins cause scarlet fever, which is ruled out here because there is no strawberry tongue and no circumoral pallor.

Last-look cram sheet

  • The 8 eruption types are central maculopapular (the most common), peripheral, confluent desquamative, vesiculobullous, urticaria-like, nodular, purpuric, and ulcer or eschar.
  • Measles is a paramyxovirus. Its rash reaches the trunk in 2 to 3 days, lasts 3 to 5 days, and Koplik spots prove it.
  • Rubella is a togavirus. Its rash reaches the trunk in 1 day, clears as it spreads and lasts 2 to 3 days. It gives postauricular nodes, and in pregnancy it causes microcephaly, heart disease and deafness.
  • Fifth disease is parvovirus B19. Slapped cheeks come first, then a lacy rash. It can spread by transfusion and causes fetal hydrops.
  • Roseola is HHV-6 or HHV-7 in children under 3. The rash comes after the fever, spares the face, and spreads by shared saliva.
  • Transmission lines: varicella is airborne, HFMD is oral-oral and fecal-oral, typhoid is food or water, leptospirosis is water with animal urine, and Zika is Aedes plus sexual spread.
  • Dengue rash goes from flushing, to a maculopapular rash, to petechiae after the fever breaks. Still's disease gives salmon papules at the fever spikes. Relapsing fever gives a rash at the end of each episode.
  • Body lice mean epidemic typhus. Fleas mean murine typhus. Mites mean scrub typhus (with an eschar). Mouse mites mean rickettsialpox.
  • An Ixodes tick with a 15 cm ring means Lyme disease. A Lone Star tick with an 8 cm ring means STARI.
  • RMSF starts at the wrists and ankles and spreads inward. Secondary syphilis gives copper-colored scaly palms and is never vesicular in adults.
  • HFMD gives football-shaped erosions and later nail shedding. Erythema multiforme gives target lesions of 2 cm or less.
  • Osler nodes are tender (subacute, viridans strep). Janeway lesions are painless (acute, S. aureus). COVID-19 gives chilblains when mild and retiform purpura when severe.
  • Scarlet fever has sandpaper skin, Pastia's lines and circumoral pallor. Kawasaki disease is idiopathic and attacks the coronary arteries.
  • Staph TSS is TSST-1 with colonization only. SSSS gives tender skin and a positive Nikolsky sign but no tongue signs.
  • SJS is under 10%, overlap is 10 to 30%, and TEN is over 30% of the body surface. The palm is 1%, and you count detached plus detachable skin. The main drugs are allopurinol, anticonvulsants and antibiotics.
  • DRESS is an anticonvulsant or sulfa drug plus facial edema, eosinophilia and liver involvement. AGEP is a new drug plus fever plus sterile pustules. EBV patients given ampicillin get a rash 30 to 90% of the time.
  • Varicella shows mixed stages on the trunk. Smallpox shows one stage with palms and soles. Mpox shows umbilicated lesions with big nodes. HSV shows painful grouped vesicles.
  • Mpox is confirmed by PCR of a lesion swab. The patient is infectious until fresh skin forms. Contacts isolate for 21 days, and incubation is 3 to 21 days.
  • Raw oysters with cirrhosis mean Vibrio. Neutropenia with an eschar and red halo means ecthyma gangrenosum (Pseudomonas). A hot tub means Pseudomonas folliculitis.
  • Urticarial vasculitis lasts 3 to 5 days, does not blanch, burns, and is linked to hepatitis B and SLE. Erythema nodosum gives tender shin nodules in young women, sometimes from oral contraceptives. Sweet syndrome gives swollen plaques with leukocytosis, sometimes from G-CSF.
  • Meningococcemia with asplenia or C5 to C8 deficiency must be treated as sepsis right away. Purpura fulminans means DIC.
  • DGI gives fewer than 40 gray-centered pustules plus tenosynovitis. TTP/HUS has normal coagulation tests.
  • Tularemia gives a tender ulcer. Anthrax gives a painless eschar with no other rash.
  • Rat-bite fever is NOT Borrelia (a past answer key error). It is Spirillum minus or Streptobacillus moniliformis.

2.04 PE of the Skin / General Approach to Skin Disorders 19 items

Dr. Gilbert C. Yang · Recall 3 / Comp 4 / App 8 / Analysis 4 · Past-exam style source: 2028 LE2 #57–75 AND 2027 LE2 #59–77 (same professor all years) · Main source: 2026 trans 2.04 (25 pp.)

How Dr. Yang asks
  • Short case, then "name the lesion." You decide if it is a primary or secondary lesion, and the answer usually hinges on a size cutoff.
    • The usual cutoff is 1 cm. Purpura uses 0.5 cm. A tumor is above 5 cm.
    • In 2028 he gave the same case twice and changed only the size: 3 mm (vesicle) in one item and 3 cm (bulla) in the other.
  • A bedside sign, then "what disease or what depth?" Expect Auspitz, Darier, Nikolsky, Asboe-Hansen and the dimple sign.
    • Classic line: a negative Nikolsky sign means the blister split is subepidermal (below the epidermis).
  • "Which pair is INCORRECT?" He lists sign and disease pairs, or test and disease pairs, and you pick the wrong match. This was asked in both 2027 and 2028.
  • Picture matching.
    • Lesion photos: crust, scale, nodule, scar, ulcer, telangiectasia, wheal, pustule.
    • Nail photos: pitting, half-and-half nails.
  • Clue word to diagnosis. Learn these one-liners:
    • Exclamation-point hairs mean alopecia areata.
    • Carpet tacks mean discoid lupus.
    • A CKD (chronic kidney disease) patient points to half-and-half nails.
    • A steroid cream points to atrophy.
    • Leprosy points to loss of sensation (anesthesia).
    • A farmer or gardener points to a linear arrangement.
Past-exam concept map (2027 / 2028)
Concept20282027Covered in
Primary lesion by size (vesicle vs bulla)#61, #62—Size cutoffs
Primary lesion definitions / pictures (wheal, pustule, nodule)#69–70#75–76Primary lesions
Primary lesion = main diagnostic tool—#62Approach
Secondary lesions (ulcer, lichenification, fissure, scales, crust)#57, #69–70#59, #60, #61Secondary lesions
Scar / ulcer / telangiectasia pictures#73–75#77Erosion vs ulcer vs scar, Special lesions
Atrophy from topical steroid—#72Atrophy
Diascopy (vasculitis / purpura)—#63Special lesions + diascopy
Arrangement: linear = plant contact—#66Arrangement
Negative Nikolsky means a subepidermal split#63—Nikolsky vs Asboe-Hansen
Incorrect sign–disease pair#68#69, #71Bedside signs
KOH ("spaghetti/ziti and meatballs"), patch test#72#67Lab tests
Leprosy symptom (anesthesia)#65—Leprosy
Vitiligo association (thyroid)—#70Color disorders
Alopecia areata (exclamation-point hairs) and cicatricial alopecia (DLE)#58, #59#65Hair / alopecia
Nails: psoriasis, CKD (half-and-half), pictures#60#68, #73–74Nails
Psoriasis secondary lesion (scales)#57#69Psoriasis capsule
Ichthyosis vulgaris and pityriasis rosea#66#64NOT in 2026 trans (see trap box in Arrangement)

Primary lesions: flat, raised, fluid HIGH-YIELD 2028 #61–62, #69 2027 #75–76

A primary lesion is the ORIGINAL lesion of the disease, the first thing the disease produces on the skin. Sort it with three questions: Is it flat or raised? Is it solid or filled with fluid? How big is it (the usual cutoff is 1 cm)?

  • Flat lesions cannot be felt with the fingertip. Only the color is different.
  • Raised solid lesions can be felt. They differ by size and by shape (flat-topped vs domed).
  • Fluid-filled lesions are named by what is inside.
    • Clear or bloody serous fluid makes a vesicle (small) or bulla (big).
    • Pus makes a pustule, whatever the size.
  • The wheal is its own group. It is swelling (edema) in the skin, and it disappears within 24 to 48 hours.
FamilyLesionSizeDefining featureLecture example
Flat (not palpable)Macule< 1 cmColor change onlyFreckles
Patch≥ 1 cmA big macule—
Raised, solidPapule< 1 cmSmall, well-circumscribed solid bumpLichen planus
Plaque≥ 1 cmFlat-topped, like a plateauPsoriasis
Nodule≥ 1 cmDomed and deep (a "deep papule"), solid or cysticBasal cell carcinoma (BCC)
Tumor> 5 cmLarge solid mass, may be mobile or fixedSquamous cell carcinoma (SCC)
EdematousWhealAnyPale-red swollen plateau that is gone in 24–48 h (evanescent, meaning short-lived)Urticaria / allergy
Fluid-filledVesicle< 1 cmSerous fluid, clear or bloody (hemorrhagic)Chickenpox
Bulla≥ 1 cmSame kind of fluid, just bigger—
PustuleAnyVisible pus (white, yellow or green). Pustules can merge into "lakes" of pus—
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "fluid-filled lesions measuring X", and you name the lesion.
    • Or a definition in Column A matched to a photo. Example: 2027 #75 described the wheal as "short-lived edema".
  • Trap: wheal vs plaque.
    • How to tell them apart: a wheal is evanescent. Each lesion comes and goes within a day, while a plaque stays.
  • Trap: pustule vs vesicle.
