    • How to tell them apart: if you see pus (white or yellow), it is a pustule no matter how small or big it is.

A 26/F develops itchy, pale-red, raised, swollen lesions of various sizes and shapes after eating shrimp. Each lesion fades within hours, and new ones appear elsewhere. What is the primary lesion?

  1. Plaque
  2. Wheal
  3. Patch
  4. Bulla

B. The lesions are swollen (edematous), pale-red, change shape, and each one fades within hours. A lesion that disappears within 24–48 h is a wheal, the lesion of urticaria (here an allergic reaction to shrimp).
Why not a plaque: a plaque is a fixed, solid plateau that stays in place. It does not fade and reappear elsewhere.

Size cutoffs: the near-miss items HIGH-YIELD 2028 #61 vs #62

1 cm splits each small–big pair. Above 5 cm, a solid mass is a tumor. 0.5 cm splits petechiae from purpura. Always READ THE UNIT (mm vs cm).

  • Most lesion names come in pairs: one name for small, one name for big. The lesion type is the same, only the size changes.
  • Two lesions have no size cutoff.
    • A wheal is defined by being short-lived swelling.
    • A pustule is defined by containing pus.
PairSmallerCutoffBigger
FlatMacule1 cmPatch
Solid raisedPapule1 cmPlaque (flat top) or nodule (domed, deep)
Solid massNodule5 cmTumor (> 5 cm)
FluidVesicle1 cmBulla
Blood in skin (non-blanching)Petechiae0.5 cmPurpura
No cutoffWheal (any size)
Pustule (any size, defined by pus)
TRAP 2028 #61 and #62 were the same case: a 22/M with fever and painful fluid-filled lesions at the angles of the mouth. The only change was the size.
  • "3 mm" means a vesicle.
  • "3 cm" means a bulla.
  • Circle the number AND the unit before you read the choices.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: a size in mm or cm, plus a word that tells you the family (flat, raised, fluid or pus).
  • Trap: plaque vs nodule (both are 1 cm or bigger).
    • How to tell them apart: a plaque is a flat-topped plateau (psoriasis). A nodule is domed and deep (BCC, basal cell carcinoma).

A 28/F has multiple light-brown lesions on the trunk. They cannot be felt on palpation. The smallest is 4 mm, and the one being described measures 3 cm. What is the primary lesion being described?

  1. Macule
  2. Plaque
  3. Patch
  4. Nodule

C. "Cannot be felt" means the lesion is flat. A flat lesion 1 cm or larger is a patch, and this one is 3 cm.
Why not macule: the 4-mm lesions would be macules, but the question asks about the 3-cm one. That is the near-miss.
Plaque and nodule are raised, so they would be palpable.

Secondary lesions HIGH-YIELD 2028 #57, #69–70 2027 #59–61

A secondary lesion is what a primary lesion BECOMES. There are 9 types.

  • A primary lesion turns into a secondary lesion in three ways:
    • The natural course of the disease.
    • The patient scratches or rubs it.
    • It gets infected.
  • The 9 types are scales, crusts, lichenification, excoriations, erosions, ulcers, scars, fissures and atrophy.
LesionWhat it isClue word and example
ScalesFlakes of the stratum corneum (the outer dead layer)Silvery scales point to psoriasis.
Psoriasis skin sheds in 5 days instead of the normal 28, so flakes pile up.
CrustDried serum, blood or pus on the surface (a "scab")Honey-colored crust means impetigo 📌
The color tells you what dried: yellow is serum, green is pus, brown or dark red is blood.
LichenificationThickened skin with exaggerated skin linesComes from repeated rubbing or scratching (chronic itch).
ExcoriationPinpoint (punctate) or linear scrapeMade by fingernail scratching, as in atopic dermatitis.
ErosionLoss of the epidermis onlySuperficial burn or sunburn.
Heals with no scar.
UlcerDefect reaching the dermis or deeperLeg ulcer.
Heals with a scar.
ScarFibrous tissue that fills in an old defectCan be hypertrophic and hard, or atrophic and soft.
A keloid is a scar with claw-like extensions beyond the wound.
FissureLinear crack, often painfulPalms and soles, where the thick stratum corneum stretches the least.
Also dry lips.
AtrophyThinning: the epidermis is intact, but tissue under it is lostPotent topical steroid (clobetasol).
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: a symptom story, and you name the secondary lesion.
    • 2027: hair dye exposure with thick, lined skin was lichenification.
    • 2027: painful cracks on the soles were fissures.
  • Trap: lichenification vs scales.
    • How to tell them apart: lichenification is the skin itself becoming thick with deep lines. Scales are loose flakes sitting on the surface.
  • Trap: excoriation vs fissure.
    • How to tell them apart: an excoriation is a scratch made by a fingernail. A fissure is a crack that opens from tension or dryness.

A 6/M with atopic dermatitis scratches his antecubital folds at night. PE shows several superficial straight-line abrasions, some with pinpoint dried blood. What secondary lesion is this?

  1. Fissures
  2. Lichenification
  3. Erosions
  4. Excoriations

D. Straight-line scrapes made by fingernails are excoriations. The story says he scratches, and the marks are linear.
Why not lichenification: that needs long-term rubbing that leaves the skin thick with exaggerated lines.
Why not fissures: fissures are cracks from tension or dryness, not scratch marks.

Erosion vs ulcer vs scar HIGH-YIELD 2027 #59, #77 2028 #73–75

Ask one question: did the defect reach the DERMIS? If not, it is an erosion and leaves no scar. If yes, it is an ulcer and heals with a scar.

  • An erosion stays within the epidermis, so it heals without scarring.
  • Once the dermis is lost, the gap is filled with fibrous tissue. That fibrous tissue is the scar.
ErosionUlcerScarKeloid
DepthEpidermis onlyDermis, sometimes subcutis tooFibrous tissue filling an old defectA hypertrophic scar
HealsNo scarWith a scar—Grows beyond the wound (claw-like)
ExampleSunburn, ruptured blisterLeg ulcer, pressure ulcerHealed woundKeloid
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "loss of epidermis AND dermis, heals with scarring" (that is an ulcer).
    • Or picture matching: scar, ulcer, keloid, telangiectasia.
  • Trap: keloid vs ordinary hypertrophic scar.
    • How to tell them apart: a keloid extends into unaffected skin beyond the original wound.

A 19/M's sunburn blisters ruptured, leaving shallow, moist, red, weeping areas on the shoulders. Which statement about these lesions is CORRECT?

  1. They are erosions and are expected to heal without scarring
  2. They are ulcers and will heal with a scar
  3. They are fissures caused by decreased skin elasticity
  4. They are primary lesions, since they appeared within days

A. A shallow, moist area left after a blister breaks is a loss of epidermis only. That is an erosion, and it heals with no scar.
Why not ulcer: an ulcer needs loss of the dermis too.
Why not "primary lesion": erosions are secondary lesions. They form from ruptured vesicles or bullae, however quickly that happens.

Atrophy from topical steroids HIGH-YIELD 2027 #72

A patient uses an over-the-counter "cream" for 1–2 weeks that secretly contains a potent steroid (clobetasol). The result is ATROPHY, and it is IRREVERSIBLE.

  • Atrophy means the skin layers become thinner. The epidermis stays intact, but tissue underneath is lost.
  • Epidermal atrophy looks thin and shiny, with fine "cigarette-paper wrinkling".
  • Dermal atrophy is loss of connective tissue in the dermis.
    • Because tissue is missing, the lesion looks depressed (sunken).
  • No treatment reverses it p. 4. This is why the trans flags self-medication with steroid creams.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: a patient self-medicates with a topical steroid, a whitening cream or an "anti-itch" cream. What lesion results?
  • Trap: purpura or crust are offered as distractors.
    • Also watch for "reversible after stopping the cream". That is wrong, because atrophy is permanent.

A 32/F applied a friend's "anti-itch cream" to a facial rash daily for 3 weeks. The skin is now thin, shiny and finely wrinkled like cigarette paper. The cream contained clobetasol. Which statement is TRUE?

  1. This is lichenification from repeated rubbing
  2. The change resolves fully within weeks after stopping the cream
  3. This is epidermal atrophy and it is irreversible
  4. This is an erosion and will heal without scarring

C. A potent steroid (clobetasol) causes atrophy. Thin, shiny, cigarette-paper skin is epidermal atrophy, and the trans says it is irreversible with no treatment.
Why not B: this is the tempting choice, but the change does not resolve after stopping.
Why not A: lichenification is thickening of the skin, the opposite of thinning.

Special lesions + diascopy (blanch or not) HIGH-YIELD 2027 #63 2028 #74

Diascopy means pressing a glass slide on a red lesion. ERYTHEMA blanches (turns pale). PURPURA and PETECHIAE do NOT blanch.

  • Why erythema blanches: the redness comes from dilated capillaries. Pressing squeezes the blood out of the vessels, so the color fades.
  • Why purpura does not blanch: the blood has already leaked out of the vessels into the skin (extravasated). Pressure cannot push it away.
LesionDefinitionClue
PetechiaeSmall purpuric macules, usually groupedEach under 0.5 cm.
Do not blanch.
PurpuraBleeding into the skin (can be a macule up to a plaque)0.5 cm or larger. Does not blanch.
Palpable purpura calls for a comprehensive review of systems (ROS), because it can signal systemic disease.
TelangiectasiaDilated superficial blood vesselsSeen on the legs.
The lecturer said it also does not blanch.
CystA cavity whose lining makes its own contentsIt recurs, so you enucleate it (remove the whole capsule).
Example: epidermal inclusion cyst.
ComedoneKeratin plug in a hair follicle openingSeen in acne vulgaris.
Closed comedone is a whitehead. Open comedone is a blackhead.
  • Diascopy can also show glassy yellow-brown papules. This is the apple-jelly sign.
    • It points to sarcoidosis. It can also be seen in skin TB, lymphoma and granuloma annulare.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "which test tells if red lesions come from vessel inflammation or bleeding?" The answer is diascopy (2027 #63, a case of HSP, Henoch-Schönlein purpura).
    • New angles: which lesion blanches, and petechiae vs purpura by size.
  • Trap: tourniquet test or patch test offered as distractors.
    • How to tell: diascopy is the bedside test that uses a glass slide.

On diascopy, which of the following lesions is expected to BLANCH?

  1. Grouped 2-mm petechiae on the legs of a patient with low platelets
  2. Erythematous macules of a viral exanthem
  3. 1.5-cm purpuric patches on the shins
  4. Telangiectasia on the thighs

B. Erythema is caused by dilated capillaries. The blood is still inside the vessels, so pressure pushes it out and the lesion blanches.
Why not A or C: petechiae and purpura are blood that has leaked out of the vessels, so they do not blanch.
Why not D: the lecturer said telangiectasia also does not blanch.

Approach and how to state the derm PE LECTURER 2027 #62

In dermatology you do the PE FIRST, then take a focused history. The primary lesion is the main basis of the differential diagnosis.

  • The flow of the consult p. 2:
    • Chief complaint.
    • Physical exam 📌
    • Detailed history, focused on what the PE showed.
    • Impression, then tests, then plan.
  • Lighting: natural sunlight is ideal.
  • Inspect the whole skin, including the scalp, hair, nails, mucosa, palms, soles and web spaces.
    • Have a chaperone when the patient undresses.
  • Always check the palms and soles.
    • Copper-colored lesions there ("dimes and nickels") mean you should ask the sexual history, because this is secondary syphilis.
  • Check the lymph nodes when you suspect infection or malignancy.
  • State the findings as one sentence, in this order (N-A-M-C-S-P-S-L):
    • Number, Arrangement, Margination, Color, Shape.
    • Primary lesion, then Secondary lesion.
    • Location and distribution.
    • If the lesion is solitary, skip arrangement.
    • Do not start with the primary lesion. The lecturer stressed this.
Trans sample caseStatement (key words)
ChickenpoxMultiple erythematous round macules, papules and vesicles with surrounding erythema, disseminated on back and nape
Impetigo…erythematous plaques with erosions topped with scales and yellowish-brown crusts, grouped on the chin
PsoriasisWell-defined erythematous oval plaques, thick silvery-white scales, bilateral elbows
Tinea corporisSolitary … round annular plaque with prominent border and central clearing, scales, on the arm
Pityriasis versicolorMultiple coalescing well-defined hypopigmented oval thin plaques with fine scales
Herpes zoster (Table 14)Multiple, grouped … vesicles on erythematous base, dermatomal (T10), unilateral
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as:
    • "What is the main diagnostic tool?" The primary lesion.
    • "Which comes first?" The PE.
    • "Which statement follows the correct order?"
  • Trap: "take a detailed history first".
    • That is true elsewhere in medicine, but not in dermatology.

Which description of a 40/M's rash follows the recommended order for stating a dermatologic PE?

  1. Plaques, multiple, erythematous, well-defined, with scales, on the knees
  2. On the knees, multiple well-defined plaques, erythematous, topped with scales
  3. Erythematous scales on multiple plaques, well-defined, on the knees
  4. Multiple, well-defined, erythematous, oval plaques topped with scales on the knees

D. D follows the order: number (multiple), margination (well-defined), color (erythematous), shape (oval), primary lesion (plaques), secondary lesion (scales), and location (knees) last.
Why not A: it starts with the primary lesion, which the lecturer said not to do.
B starts with location, and C mixes up the order.

Shape, arrangement, distribution: clue words MUST KNOW 2027 #66

The pattern points to the disease. Clustered lesions suggest herpes. A line suggests plants or thorns. A dermatomal band suggests zoster. Palms and soles suggest secondary syphilis.

ClueTermThink
Clustered togetherHerpetiform (grouped)Herpes simplex or zoster
In a line, in a gardener or farmerLinearPlant contact or thorn trauma
BullseyeIris / targetoidErythema multiforme
Ring with central clearingAnnularTinea corporis (sample case)
Central dimple ("pimple na may dimple")UmbilicatedMolluscum contagiosum
Snake-likeSerpiginousElastosis perforans serpiginosa
Scattered, separate lesionsDisseminatedChickenpox
Lesions merge togetherConfluentMeasles (viral exanthem).
Molluscum is non-confluent.
Area supplied by one spinal nerveDermatomalHerpes zoster
Flexures or extensor surfacesFlexor / extensorFlexor: atopic dermatitis.
Extensor: psoriasis.
Trunk plus palms and soles, copper-colored—Secondary syphilis, so take a sexual history
Scalp—Seborrheic dermatitis.
If extensive or not responding to treatment, think of HIV.
  • Measuring extent: the patient's own palm is about 1% of body surface area (BSA).
    • Psoriasis severity uses this: mild is under 3%, moderate is 3–10%, severe is over 10%.
NOT IN 2026 TRANS Two past items came from outside the current trans. Know the one-liners only.
  • 2027 #64 asked pityriasis rosea: a "drooping pine-tree" or Christmas-tree pattern along the skin cleavage lines of the trunk.
  • 2028 #66 asked ichthyosis vulgaris: fine plate-like scales on the shins of an atopic patient (keyed from Fitzpatrick).

A 24/M has a rash on the trunk and copper-colored scaly papules on both palms and soles. After completing the skin exam, which part of the history is MOST important to take next?

  1. Sexual history
  2. Occupational exposure to plants
  3. Family history of atopy
  4. Recent use of topical steroids

A. This is the lecturer's boxed point. Copper-colored lesions on the palms and soles suggest secondary syphilis, so the next step is a sexual history.
Why not B: plant exposure explains a linear arrangement, not a palm-and-sole pattern.

Nikolsky vs Asboe-Hansen, PV vs TEN HIGH-YIELD 2028 #63, #68 2027 #71

Both signs are POSITIVE when the skin splits ABOVE the basement membrane, as in pemphigus vulgaris (PV) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). A NEGATIVE Nikolsky sign in a patient with blisters means the split is SUBEPIDERMAL.

  • Why: when the split is high in the epidermis, the top layer is loosely attached. Rubbing or pressing makes it slide off or makes the blister spread.
NikolskyAsboe-Hansen
Where you pressIntact, unblistered skinOn an existing bulla
DirectionLateral (rub sideways)Downward
Positive resultThe epidermis shears offThe blister spreads sideways
Seen inPemphigus vulgaris and TEN (the problem is above the basement membrane zone, BMZ)
Pemphigus vulgarisTEN
CauseAutoimmuneMainly drugs. It is a cell-mediated reaction, amplified mainly by granulysin.
LevelSuprabasal acantholysis (cells separate just above the basal layer, inside the epidermis)Widespread death (apoptosis) of keratinocytes, so the epidermis detaches
MucosaErosions almost always (oral, nasal)Involved
SkinFlaccid blisters and large erosions.
Spares palms and soles.		Purpuric macules first, then flaccid bullae, then sheets of skin detach.
Starts on the upper trunk.
Signs(+) Nikolsky, (+) Asboe-Hansen(+) Nikolsky
Numbers—Onset 4–28 days after the drug. Risk is highest in the first 8 weeks.
By detached BSA: SJS under 10%, overlap 10–30%, TEN over 30%.
  • Drugs that cause TEN: cotrimoxazole, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, lamotrigine, nevirapine, allopurinol and meloxicam (an oxicam).
  • Tense bullae in an elderly patient with a negative Nikolsky sign mean a subepidermal blister.
    • Example: bullous pemphigoid Harrison's. This disease is not named in the trans.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as:
    • A sign is given, and you name the depth of the split.
    • A maneuver is described, and you name the sign.
    • A drug started X days ago plus a BSA %, and you choose SJS (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), overlap or TEN.
  • Trap: Nikolsky vs Asboe-Hansen.
    • How to tell them apart: Nikolsky is done on intact skin. Asboe-Hansen is done on an existing blister.
    • 2027 #71 paired Asboe-Hansen with psoriasis. That pair was the incorrect one.
  • SSSS (staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome) vs TEN is taught in 2.05 Fever and Rash, not in this trans.

A 38/M started carbamazepine 2 weeks ago. He now has painful dusky macules, flaccid bullae and sheets of detached epidermis over about 40% of his BSA, with oral erosions. Lateral pressure on normal-looking skin peels the epidermis. What is the diagnosis?

  1. Stevens-Johnson syndrome
  2. SJS-TEN overlap
  3. Toxic epidermal necrolysis
  4. Pemphigus vulgaris

C. Carbamazepine is an aromatic antiepileptic that causes TEN. The onset at 2 weeks fits the 4–28 day window. Detachment of about 40% BSA is over 30%, which defines TEN.
Why not B: SJS-TEN overlap is only 10–30% BSA.
Why not D: pemphigus vulgaris is autoimmune and is not timed to a new drug.

Bedside signs and their diseases ("incorrect pair" items) HIGH-YIELD 2028 #68 2027 #69, #71

Match the MANEUVER to the disease. Scraping is for psoriasis. Rubbing is for mastocytosis. Pinching is for dermatofibroma. Pressing intact skin or a bulla is for PV and TEN.

SignManeuverPositiveDisease
AuspitzScrape off the scale (blunt glass slide)Pinpoint bleedingPsoriasis (but not specific)
DarierFirmly rub the lesion (finger or pen end)A wheal appears only within the lesion, after a few minutesCutaneous mastocytosis, including urticaria pigmentosa
Dimple (Fitzpatrick)Squeeze from the sides (thumb and index finger)The lesion dimples inwardDermatofibroma
NikolskySideways pressure on intact skinThe epidermis shears offPV, TEN
Asboe-HansenDownward pressure on a bullaThe bulla spreadsPV, TEN
KoebnerTrauma to normal skinNew lesions appear at the injury sitePsoriasis, vitiligo, warts, molluscum
Apple-jellyDiascopyGlassy yellow-brown colorSarcoidosis
  • Why the dimple appears: the epidermis is tethered (stuck down) to the lesion in the dermis, so squeezing pulls the surface inward.
MUST KNOW 📌 In mastocytosis, AVOID drugs that make mast cells degranulate. Young children can go into shock. p. 11
  • Drinks: alcohol.
  • Opioids: morphine, codeine.
  • Pain relievers: aspirin, NSAIDs.
  • Anesthesia and ICU drugs: d-tubocurarine, scopolamine.
  • IV fluids and antibiotics: dextran, polymyxin-B.
  • Dermatofibroma is a firm, button-like nodule in the dermis, 3–10 mm, usually on the extremities.
    • It is a late reaction to an arthropod (insect) bite.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "Which is the INCORRECT sign and disease pair?"
    • 2028: Darier sign with TEN was the wrong pair.
    • 2027: Asboe-Hansen sign with psoriasis was the wrong pair.
  • Trap: Darier sign belongs to mastocytosis, but it is often wrongly paired with TEN or urticaria.
    • Auspitz sign belongs to psoriasis, but it is often wrongly paired with PV.

A 35/F has a firm, 6-mm brown button-like nodule on the shin that appeared months after an insect bite. When the examiner squeezes the skin on either side of it, the lesion puckers downward. Which sign is this?

  1. Darier sign
  2. Auspitz sign
  3. Dimple (Fitzpatrick) sign
  4. Koebner phenomenon

C. Squeezing from the sides makes a dimple because the epidermis is tethered to the dermal lesion. A firm, button-like nodule after an insect bite is a dermatofibroma, and this is its sign.
Why not A: Darier sign needs rubbing and produces a wheal, in mastocytosis.
Auspitz needs scraping a scale, and Koebner is new lesions at a site of trauma.

Psoriasis capsule (appears in every topic) HIGH-YIELD 2028 #57, #60 2027 #69, #73

Psoriasis shows sharply marginated, dull-red PLAQUES with silvery-white SCALES on the EXTENSOR surfaces (elbows, knees, scalp). It spares the face. Auspitz sign and Koebner phenomenon are positive.

  • Why there are so many scales:
    • The keratinocyte cell cycle is shortened.
    • The epidermis makes cells at 28 times the normal rate.
    • The skin sheds in about 5 days instead of the normal 28, so scales pile up.
  • The primary lesion is a papule or plaque. The secondary lesion is scales.
  • Triggers: trauma, infection, medication.
  • Psoriatic arthritis occurs in 10–25%, so ask about joint pain in a focused review of systems.
  • Severity by BSA: mild under 3%, moderate 3–10%, severe over 10%.
    • Severe forms are pustular and erythrodermic psoriasis (the patient may have fever).
  • Nails are involved in 25%.
    • Pitting is the most frequent nail sign.
    • Oil spots are pathognomonic (seen only in psoriasis).
    • Others: onycholysis and subungual hyperkeratosis.

A 50/M with plaque psoriasis and joint pains has nail changes. Which nail finding is considered PATHOGNOMONIC of nail psoriasis?

  1. Salmon-colored "oil spots" under the nail plate
  2. Small, shallow pits on the nail plate
  3. Detachment of the nail plate from the distal nail bed
  4. Transverse grooves parallel to the lunula

A. Oil spots are the pathognomonic nail sign of psoriasis.
Why not B: pitting is the MOST FREQUENT sign, not the pathognomonic one. That is the near-miss.
C (onycholysis) is seen in psoriasis but is not pathognomonic. D describes Beau lines.

Wood's lamp and other examination aids HIGH-YIELD LECTURER

A Wood's lamp gives long-wave UV light (365 nm). Coral red means erythrasma. Yellow-green means pityriasis versicolor. Green-yellow means Microsporum. T. tonsurans does NOT glow. 📌

  • Why a negative lamp does not rule out tinea capitis:
    • Trichophyton tonsurans is an endothrix fungus, meaning it lives inside the hair shaft. It does not fluoresce.
    • Only the ectothrix Microsporum species (living on the outside of the hair) glow.
ConditionOrganismWood's lamp
Tinea capitis, ectothrixMicrosporum canis, M. audouiniiGreen to yellow
Tinea capitis, endothrix 📌Trichophyton tonsuransNo fluorescence.
A negative result does not exclude tinea.
ErythrasmaCorynebacterium minutissimumCoral red
Pityriasis versicolorMalasseziaYellow-green
Vitiligo, melasma, CALMs (café-au-lait macules)Change in melaninContrast is accentuated
AidUse
Hand lensFine detail, such as:
follicular plugging (lupus)
Wickham striae (lichen planus)
translucence and telangiectasia (BCC)
gray-blue color (melanoma)
Oblique light (dark room)Shows slight elevation or depression
Subdued lightImproves contrast of hypo- and hyperpigmented areas
Dermoscopy (10–30x)Helps separate benign from malignant pigmented lesions
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as:
    • An incorrect test and diagnosis pair.
    • A fluorescence color, and you name the organism.
    • "The Wood's lamp is negative. Is tinea excluded?" (No, if it may be T. tonsurans.)
  • Trap: coral red (erythrasma) vs yellow-green (pityriasis versicolor).
    • Mnemonic: Coral red goes with Corynebacterium.

A 7/M has scaly patches with broken hairs on the scalp. His older brother was treated for Trichophyton tonsurans tinea capitis. Wood's lamp shows no fluorescence. What is the correct interpretation?

  1. Tinea capitis is excluded, so consider seborrheic dermatitis
  2. The lamp is faulty, since all dermatophytes fluoresce green
  3. The finding suggests erythrasma
  4. Tinea capitis is not excluded, because T. tonsurans is an endothrix organism that does not fluoresce

D. This is a lecturer-pinned point. T. tonsurans lives inside the hair (endothrix) and does not glow, so a negative lamp cannot rule out tinea capitis. His brother had this same organism.
Why not A: it assumes a negative lamp excludes tinea, which is the trap.
Why not B: only ectothrix Microsporum glows, not all dermatophytes.

Lab tests: test, finding, disease HIGH-YIELD 2028 #72 2027 #67

KOH looks for fungi. Tzanck looks for herpesviruses. The patch test is the gold standard for allergic contact dermatitis. Biopsy is for tumors and blistering diseases.

TestSample / howPositive findingDisease
KOH smear (10–20%)Scrape scales outward from the advancing margin of the lesionLong, narrow, septate, branching hyphaeDermatophytes (tinea)
Pseudohyphae with budding yeastCandida
"Ziti/spaghetti and meatballs": short hyphae with round yeastPityriasis versicolor, Malassezia folliculitis
Tzanck smearScrape the base of a fresh vesicle.
Stain with Giemsa or Wright.		Multinucleated giant cells (10–12 nuclei)HSV, varicella, zoster
Patch testAbout 35 allergens plus 1 control, taped on for 48 h.
Final reading at 72 or 96 h.		Graded from + to ++++Allergic contact dermatitis (type IV reaction)
Gram stainCrystal violet, then iodine, then alcohol, then safraninGram (+) stains purple.
Gram (−) stains red.		Bacterial infection
CultureWedge biopsy split in half: half for histopathology, half for culture.
Fungi are grown on Sabouraud agar.		Organism growsBacteria, mycobacteria, fungi
Skin biopsy3–4 mm punch.
Formalin for H&E staining.
Michel's medium for immunofluorescence (IF).		Histology or IF patternTumors, bullous disease, unclear diagnosis
  • KOH gives a false negative about 15% of the time.
    • So if the picture strongly suggests fungus, still treat.
    • Get a culture before systemic (oral) therapy, for example in onychomycosis.
  • Common patch test allergens: nickel and cobalt, formaldehyde, fragrance, neomycin and bacitracin, latex, and PPD (para-phenylenediamine, found in hair dye).
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as:
    • A condition is given, and you pick the test.
    • A smear is described, and you name the diagnosis.
    • "Which test–disease pair is incorrect?"
  • Trap: Tzanck vs KOH for blistering or scaly lesions.
    • How to tell: Tzanck is for herpes vesicles. KOH is for scaly fungal lesions.

A 33/F hairdresser has itchy, scaly, lichenified dermatitis on both hands that flares after applying hair dye. You want to identify the specific allergen. Which test, and when is the FINAL reading done?

  1. KOH smear, read immediately
  2. Patch test, final read at the 72nd or 96th hour
  3. Tzanck smear, read after Giemsa staining
  4. Patch test, final read once the patches are removed at 48 hours

B. Patch testing is the gold standard for allergic contact dermatitis, and the likely allergen here is PPD in hair dye. Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed (type IV) reaction, so the final reading is late, at 72 or 96 hours.
Why not D: the patches are removed at 48 hours, but that is not the final reading. This is the near-miss.
KOH is for fungi, and Tzanck is for herpes.

Leprosy: sensitivity testing + spectrum HIGH-YIELD 2028 #65

Every suspected leprosy lesion gets a SENSITIVITY evaluation. By the time skin signs appear, the nerves are already damaged, so the lesions have reduced or absent feeling (hypesthetic or anesthetic) and reduced sweating (anhidrotic).

  • Why the nerves are already damaged: M. leprae and the body's immune response invade the peripheral nerves before the skin changes become visible.
  • So expect LOSS of function: less sensation and less sweating, never more.
FunctionHow tested
VasomotorAxon-reflex erythema (capillary dilatation)
SweatingIodine-starch test.
Expect decreased sweating, not hyperhidrosis.
ThermalHot vs cold (about 45 °C)
PainTip vs base of a needle
TouchCotton wisp or Semmes-Weinstein monofilament
Tuberculoid (TT)Lepromatous (LL)
Cell-mediated immunity (CMI)GoodAbsent
LesionsFew, well-defined plaques, hypopigmented or red.
They are hypesthetic (reduced feeling), with raised edges, often annular.		Many nodules, diffuse thickening (infiltration) of the skin
ExtrasLimited to one body segmentMadarosis (loss of lateral eyebrows and eyelashes).
Leonine facies (thickened, lion-like face).
Extensive nerve damage.
  • M. leprae is an obligate intracellular acid-fast bacillus (AFB).
    • It cannot be cultured in a lab dish (in vitro). It is grown in the armadillo footpad instead.
    • It spreads by respiratory droplets.
    • Incubation is 2–40 years, usually 5–7.
  • The spectrum runs TT, BT, BB, BL, LL, and where a patient falls depends on their CMI.
    • Good CMI keeps the disease limited (TT). No CMI lets it spread widely (LL).
  • Indeterminate leprosy shows a few hypopigmented macules.
  • Disability persists even after multidrug therapy (MDT), because the nerve damage is already done.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as:
    • What symptom or finding goes with the lesions? (Anesthesia.)
    • Which test do you use?
    • TT vs LL, based on immunity.
  • Trap: hyperhidrosis or itching offered as distractors.
    • Leprosy causes LOSS of sweating and LOSS of sensation.

A 45/M has multiple skin-colored nodules on the face and ears, thickened facial skin and loss of the lateral eyebrows. Which statement about his condition is CORRECT?

  1. He has a complete lack of cell-mediated immunity against the organism
  2. He has strong cell-mediated immunity, so lesions are few and well-defined
  3. The organism is readily cultured on Sabouraud agar
  4. Sensitivity testing is unnecessary because nerves are spared in this form

A. Leonine facies, madarosis and many nodules mean lepromatous leprosy (LL). LL develops because the patient has no cell-mediated immunity against M. leprae.
Why not B: that describes tuberculoid leprosy (TT).
Why not C: M. leprae cannot be cultured in vitro.
Why not D: LL has the MOST nerve involvement, so sensitivity testing is essential.

Skin color and pigment disorders MUST KNOW 2027 #70

Depigmented skin (chalk-white, with no melanocytes) means vitiligo, so check the THYROID and screen for diabetes (DM). Hypopigmented skin with scales suggests pityriasis versicolor or leprosy.

  • Depigmented means the pigment is completely gone (chalk-white). Hypopigmented means the pigment is only reduced (lighter than normal).
ClueThinkKey point
Chalk-white, sharply marginated, Koebner positiveVitiligo (depigmented)Autoimmune, with no melanocytes left.
Associated with thyroid disease (Hashimoto, Graves), so request thyroid function tests (TFT), and with DM.
Hypopigmented scaly patches on neck, chest or back, in humid weather ("an-an")Pityriasis versicolorMalassezia makes dicarboxylic acid, which blocks tyrosinase, the enzyme melanocytes need to make pigment.
Not contagious.
6 or more tan macules, each over 5 mm before puberty or over 15 mm after pubertyNF1 (café-au-lait macules, CALMs)Melanocyte number is normal, but they make more melanin.
Dark palmar creases, darkening at sun-exposed and pressure sites, salt-wastingAddison's diseaseHigh ACTH stimulates the MC1R receptor on melanocytes.
Yellow skin with the sclera spared, first on the face, then palms and solesCarotenemiaCarotene over 250 mcg/dL.
Not liver disease, and reversible.
Yellow skin plus yellow scleraJaundiceBilirubin over 3 mg/dL.
The sclera is the best site to look.
Bronze skin with cirrhosisHemochromatosisHFE gene. About 70%.
Blue-gray color on sun-exposed skin, in a patient on an antiarrhythmicAmiodaroneOther drug colors: clofazimine (part of leprosy MDT) gives orange-pink.
Minocycline over 100 mg/day also discolors skin.
  • Skin turgor: the best site to test is the sternum.
    • The wrist skin loses elasticity with age, so it can falsely look dehydrated.
    • Slow return of a pinched fold means dehydration.
  • Tyndall effect: melanin deep in the dermis looks blue-gray. Examples are the Mongolian spot and the blue nevus.
  • Why carotenemia spares the sclera: carotene deposits in the lipid-rich stratum corneum of the skin, which the sclera does not have. Bilirubin in jaundice does stain the sclera.

A 4/F has yellow-orange palms, soles and nasolabial folds. Her mother feeds her mashed squash and carrots daily. The sclerae are white and she is active and well. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

  1. Obstructive jaundice, so request a liver ultrasound
  2. Hemolytic jaundice, and total bilirubin is likely > 3 mg/dL
  3. Addison's disease from ACTH excess
  4. Carotenemia, which spares the sclera and is not a sign of liver disease

D. Look at the sclera first. White sclera with yellow skin means carotenemia. Mashed and cooked foods make carotene easier to absorb, which raises the carotene level.
Why not A or B: jaundice stains the sclera yellow, and this child's sclerae are white.
Why not C: Addison's causes dark pigmentation, not yellow skin.

Alopecia: type from the clue HIGH-YIELD 2028 #58, #59 2027 #65

Exclamation-mark hairs mean alopecia areata. Carpet-tack plugs with lost follicle openings mean discoid lupus, which scars and is permanent.

  • The key question is scarring vs non-scarring.
    • In non-scarring alopecia, the follicle stem cells survive, so you can still see the follicle openings and hair can regrow.
    • In scarring (cicatricial) alopecia, the stem cells are destroyed and replaced by fibrous tissue. The openings disappear and the loss is permanent.
TypeScarring?ClueOutcome
Alopecia areataNoRound or oval coin-like bald patches on normal-looking skin.
Exclamation-mark hairs at the edges (broken hairs whose distal end is wider than the base).
Fine nail pitting ("hammered brass").
Associated with autoimmune thyroid disease.		Hair regrows because the stem cells are spared.
Poor outlook if extensive or if it starts in childhood.
AndrogeneticNoThe most common type. Follicles shrink (miniaturization).
Men: frontotemporal and vertex loss (Hamilton scale).
Women: later and milder (Ludwig scale).		Progressive
Telogen effluviumNoFollows fever, surgery, weight loss, or childbirth (3–5 months after delivery).
Hair pull (50–60 hairs) shows all telogen (club) bulbs.		Complete regrowth
Anagen effluviumNoCaused by chemotherapy, radiation, thallium or mercury, protein malnutrition.
Rapid, diffuse loss with tapered hair fractures.		Regrows after chemo
Discoid lupus (cicatricial)YesMore common in females.
Scaly red plaques on the face, scalp and ears.
Carpet tacks under the scale.
Follicle openings are wiped out (effaced).		Irreversible.
1–5% progress to SLE.
  • Alopecia areata variants:
    • Totalis: all scalp hair lost.
    • Universalis: all scalp and body hair lost.
    • Ophiasis: a band of loss along the edge of the scalp.
  • Hair cycle:
    • Anagen (growth): 3–5 years, 85–90% of hairs.
    • Catagen (transition): about 2 weeks, about 1% of hairs.
    • Telogen (rest): 3–5 months. These are the club hairs that shed.
  • Hirsutism vs hypertrichosis:
    • Hirsutism is excess hair in women at androgen-dependent sites (for example in PCOS).
    • Hypertrichosis is excess hair at non-androgen sites, caused by drugs such as minoxidil, cyclosporine and phenytoin.
    • Acquired lanugo hair ("malignant down") is a sign of internal malignancy.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as:
    • A coin-shaped bald patch with exclamation-mark hairs (2027 and 2028).
    • Lupus features with hair loss, so cicatricial alopecia (2028 #59).
  • Trap: "moth-eaten" alopecia is secondary syphilis (from the 2028 key, not in the 2026 trans).
  • Trap: telogen vs anagen effluvium.
    • How to tell them apart: telogen follows childbirth or fever. Anagen follows chemotherapy.

A 34/F has scaly, red, round plaques on the cheeks, ears and scalp. Under a lens, the scale's undersurface shows spines like carpet tacks. The bald areas of the scalp are smooth with no visible follicular openings. Which statement is TRUE?

  1. This is alopecia areata, and regrowth is expected
  2. Hair pull test will show all telogen bulbs
  3. This is a scarring alopecia, and the hair loss is irreversible
  4. This is anagen effluvium from autoimmune attack on the matrix

C. Carpet tacks and scaly plaques on the face and scalp mean discoid lupus (DLE). DLE destroys the follicle stem cells, which are replaced by fibrous tissue, so the hair loss is permanent.
Why not A: in alopecia areata the follicle openings are still visible. Here they are gone, which means scarring.
B describes telogen effluvium, and D misdescribes anagen effluvium (which follows chemo or toxins).

Nail changes and their diseases HIGH-YIELD 2028 #60 2027 #68, #73–74

Half-and-half nails mean kidney disease (CKD, dialysis). Terry nails mean liver disease. Spoon nails mean iron deficiency. Clubbing points to heart, lung or GI disease. Pitting, oil spots and onycholysis mean psoriasis.

  • Memory aids from the trans:
    • Half-and-half: "half your kidneys are gone".
    • Terry: "Terrible liver", a white nail with a pink tip.
Nail signLookDisease
PittingSmall, shallow depressionsPsoriasis (the most frequent nail sign).
Fine "hammered brass" pitting is seen in alopecia areata.
Oil spotsSalmon or yellow-brown spots under the nail platePsoriasis (pathognomonic)
OnycholysisThe plate separates from the distal nail bedPsoriasis
KoilonychiaSpoon-shaped, concave nailIron deficiency anemia, Plummer-Vinson syndrome
ClubbingNail angle over 180°, bulbous tip, "rockable" nailCardiovascular (congenital heart disease).
Pulmonary (cancer, suppurative disease).
GI (IBD).
Methemoglobinemia.
Half-and-halfProximal half white, distal half pink or brownChronic renal insufficiency, hemodialysis
Terry nailsAlmost the whole nail is white, with a thin pink band at the tipSevere liver disease
Beau linesTransverse groove parallel to the lunulaA short pause in nail growth: high fever, chemotherapy cycles, zinc deficiency
OnychomadesisThe nail separates at the base and may shedA longer pause in nail growth, for example after hand-foot-mouth disease
Acute paronychiaPainful, red, swollen nail fold, sometimes with pusS. aureus
  • Nail growth: a fingernail grows 0.1 mm a day and takes 4–6 months to fully replace. A big toenail takes 12–18 months.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as:
    • A CKD patient, and you pick the nail finding.
    • A nail photo, and you name the associated disease.
    • "Which nail change is seen in psoriasis?" (onycholysis).
  • Trap: half-and-half vs Terry nails.
    • How to tell them apart: look at how much of the nail is white. Half white means kidney. Nearly all white means liver.

Which nail finding–condition pair is INCORRECT?

  1. Koilonychia – iron deficiency anemia
  2. Terry nails – chronic renal insufficiency on hemodialysis
  3. Onychomadesis – recent hand-foot-mouth disease
  4. Clubbing – cyanotic congenital heart disease

B. Terry nails go with severe liver disease, not kidney disease. The nail of chronic renal insufficiency and hemodialysis is the half-and-half nail.
The other three pairs are correct: spoon nails with iron deficiency, onychomadesis after hand-foot-mouth disease, and clubbing with congenital heart disease.

Practice drill — Dr. Yang style

A 45/M has painful, grouped, clear fluid-filled lesions on an erythematous base in a band on the left side of the trunk (T10). Each lesion measures 2–4 mm. What is the primary lesion?

  1. Bullae
  2. Vesicles
  3. Pustules
  4. Papules

B. The lesions are fluid-filled and under 1 cm, so they are vesicles. The grouped (herpetiform) and dermatomal pattern fits herpes zoster.
Why not pustules: the fluid is clear, not pus.
Why not bullae: those are 1 cm or larger.

Same patient, 3 days later: several lesions have merged into tense, clear fluid-filled blisters measuring 1.5 cm. How should these new lesions be described?

  1. Bullae
  2. Vesicles
  3. Wheals
  4. Erosions

A. Fluid-filled lesions 1 cm or larger are bullae. It is the same disease, only the size changed. This is the 2028 trick.
Why not vesicles: vesicles are under 1 cm.
Erosions would appear only after the blisters break.

A 9/F with dengue has many grouped, flat, red, 2-mm dots on the legs that do not fade when pressed with a glass slide. What are these lesions?

  1. Purpura
  2. Erythematous macules
  3. Telangiectasia
  4. Petechiae

D. The dots do not blanch, so the blood is outside the vessels. Non-blanching spots under 0.5 cm are petechiae.
Why not purpura: purpura is 0.5 cm or larger.
Why not erythematous macules: erythema would blanch under the slide.

The lesion shown is on the leg of a 70/M with poor circulation. Which statement correctly describes it?

  1. An erosion: loss of epidermis only, heals without scar
  2. A fissure: linear crack from decreased elasticity
  3. An ulcer: defect into the dermis or deeper, heals with a scar
  4. A crust: dried serum and blood on the surface

C. A deep crater on the leg is an ulcer, and the leg ulcer is the trans example. It reaches the dermis, so it will heal with a scar.
Why not A: an erosion is shallow and moist and leaves no scar.

A 5/M has the lesions shown on the chin, which started as small blisters. What does the golden-yellow material on top represent, and what is the likely diagnosis?

  1. Crust (dried exudate) – impetigo
  2. Scales (stratum corneum) – psoriasis
  3. Lichenification – atopic dermatitis
  4. Pustules – acne vulgaris

A. 📌 A honey-colored crust means impetigo (trans sample case 3). A crust is dried serum, pus or blood, and it is a secondary lesion.
Why not B: scales are flakes of the outer skin layer, typically silvery in psoriasis, not golden.

Identify the primary lesion shown.

  1. Vesicles
  2. Pustules
  3. Nodules
  4. Wheals

B. Raised lesions with visible white-yellow pus are pustules, at any size.
Why not vesicles: vesicles contain clear or serous fluid, not pus.

A 20/M basketball player has the lesions shown on the upper back, worse in hot humid months. They are hypopigmented, oval, coalescing, with fine scales. Which bedside finding is expected?

  1. KOH: long, narrow, septate, branching hyphae without constriction
  2. Wood's lamp: coral-red fluorescence
  3. KOH: short hyphae and yeast forms ("ziti and meatballs"), Wood's lamp yellow-green
  4. Tzanck: multinucleated giant cells

C. Hypopigmented, finely scaly, coalescing patches on the back in humid weather mean pityriasis versicolor (trans case 6). Its KOH shows "ziti and meatballs", and it glows yellow-green.
Why not A: long septate branching hyphae are dermatophytes (tinea).
Why not B: coral red is erythrasma.
D (Tzanck) is for herpes.

These nails (almost entirely white and opaque, with only a narrow pink band at the tip) were seen in a 58/M. Which condition should you look for?

  1. Iron deficiency anemia
  2. Chronic renal insufficiency
  3. Psoriasis
  4. Severe liver disease

D. A nail that is almost all white with a thin pink tip is a Terry nail, which goes with severe liver disease.
Why not B: that is the near-miss. Kidney disease gives half-and-half nails, where only the proximal half is white and the distal half is pink or brown.

A 50/F has flaccid blisters on the trunk and painful oral erosions for 2 months, with no new medications. When the examiner presses straight down on an intact blister, the blister extends into the surrounding skin. Which sign is this, and where is the split?

  1. Nikolsky sign, subepidermal
  2. Asboe-Hansen sign, above the basement membrane (suprabasal)
  3. Darier sign, dermal mast cells
  4. Auspitz sign, papillary dermis

B. Pressing straight down on an existing blister and watching it spread is the Asboe-Hansen sign. It is positive in pemphigus vulgaris, where the split is just above the basal layer (suprabasal acantholysis). Flaccid blisters, oral erosions and no drug trigger fit PV.
Why not A: Nikolsky uses sideways pressure on unblistered skin, and a positive sign means a split above, not below, the epidermis.

Which test or sign and its finding is INCORRECTLY matched?

  1. Wood's lamp coral-red fluorescence – pityriasis versicolor
  2. Diascopy apple-jelly sign – sarcoidosis
  3. Tzanck smear multinucleated giant cells – herpes zoster
  4. Darier sign – urticaria pigmentosa

A. Coral-red fluorescence means erythrasma (Corynebacterium). Pityriasis versicolor glows yellow-green, so this pair is wrong.
The other three pairs are correct: apple-jelly with sarcoidosis, giant cells with herpes zoster, and Darier with urticaria pigmentosa.

A 29/F gave birth 4 months ago and now notices large amounts of hair on her pillow and comb, all over the scalp. No bald patches or scalp inflammation are seen. A hair pull test yields hairs with depigmented, rounded club ends. What is the diagnosis?

  1. Alopecia areata
  2. Anagen effluvium
  3. Telogen effluvium
  4. Androgenetic alopecia

C. After childbirth, many hairs enter the resting (telogen) phase together and shed 3–5 months later as club hairs. This is telogen effluvium, and the hair fully regrows.
Why not B: anagen effluvium follows chemotherapy or toxins.
Why not A: alopecia areata makes round bald patches, and there are none here.

A 40/M from an endemic area has a few well-defined, hypopigmented plaques with raised edges on one arm. Which finding on sensitivity evaluation of the lesions would SUPPORT your suspected diagnosis?

  1. Increased sweating on the iodine-starch test
  2. Intense pruritus on stroking
  3. Hyperalgesia to the tip of a needle
  4. Inability to feel a cotton wisp

D. A few well-defined hypopigmented plaques with raised edges in one body area fit tuberculoid leprosy. The nerves are already damaged, so the lesions have reduced or absent sensation (cannot feel a cotton wisp).
Why not A, B or C: these all describe MORE function. Leprosy causes less sweating and less sensation, not more.

A 3/M has many tan-brown macules and papules on the trunk. Rubbing one lesion with a pen end produces a wheal limited to that lesion after a few minutes. He needs pain relief after a minor fracture. Which of the following is a mast-cell degranulator that must be AVOIDED?

  1. Codeine
  2. Paracetamol
  3. Cetirizine
  4. Plain normal saline

A. A positive Darier sign with many tan-brown lesions means urticaria pigmentosa (mastocytosis). 📌 Drugs that make mast cells degranulate must be avoided, because young children can go into shock. Codeine is one of them, along with morphine, aspirin, NSAIDs and alcohol.
The other choices are not on the trans list of degranulators.

A 62/M on long-term hemodialysis is referred for skin and nail changes. Which nail finding is MOST expected?

  1. Spoon-shaped concave nails
  2. Proximal half whitish, distal half pinkish-brown
  3. Salmon-colored oil spots
  4. Swollen, tender, pus-filled lateral nail fold

B. Half-and-half nails go with chronic renal insufficiency and hemodialysis.
Why not the others: A (spoon nails) is iron deficiency. C (oil spots) is psoriasis. D is acute paronychia, caused by S. aureus.

A 27/F has depigmented, chalk-white, sharply marginated patches around the mouth and on the fingertips that also appeared on a recent scratch. Diascopy and KOH are negative. Which work-up is MOST appropriate?

  1. Patch test for allergic contact dermatitis
  2. Slit-skin smear for acid-fast bacilli
  3. Thyroid function tests and blood sugar
  4. Serum carotene level

C. Chalk-white (depigmented) patches, the Koebner phenomenon (new lesion on a scratch), and a lips-and-fingertips pattern mean vitiligo. Vitiligo is associated with thyroid disease (Hashimoto, Graves) and diabetes, so check thyroid function and blood sugar.
Why not B: leprosy lesions are hypopigmented (lighter), not chalk-white.

Last-look cram sheet

  • 1 cm splits macule from patch, papule from plaque or nodule, and vesicle from bulla. A solid mass over 5 cm is a tumor. 0.5 cm splits petechiae from purpura. Wheals and pustules have no size cutoff.
  • Fluid-filled at 3 mm is a vesicle. Fluid-filled at 3 cm is a bulla. READ THE UNIT.
  • A wheal is gone in 24–48 h. A nodule is domed and deep. A plaque is a flat-topped plateau. A pustule contains pus.
  • Honey-colored crust means impetigo 📌. Silvery scales mean psoriasis. Thick skin with deep lines is lichenification (from rubbing). Linear scratch marks are excoriations. Cracks on the soles are fissures.
  • An erosion involves the epidermis only and leaves no scar. An ulcer reaches the dermis and leaves a scar. A keloid is a scar that grows beyond the wound.
  • An OTC cream hiding clobetasol causes atrophy (cigarette-paper skin), and it is irreversible.
  • On diascopy, erythema blanches. Purpura, petechiae and telangiectasia do not. The apple-jelly sign means sarcoidosis.
  • In derm, do the PE BEFORE the history 📌. The primary lesion is the main basis of diagnosis. State findings in the order N-A-M-C-S-P-S-L.
  • Copper-colored palms and soles mean secondary syphilis, so take a sexual history. Linear lesions suggest plants. Herpetiform means herpes. Umbilicated means molluscum. Target lesions mean erythema multiforme. The patient's palm is about 1% BSA.
  • Nikolsky (intact skin, sideways pressure) and Asboe-Hansen (on a bulla, downward pressure) are positive in PV and TEN. A negative Nikolsky means a subepidermal split.
  • TEN starts 4–28 days after the drug. SJS is under 10% BSA, overlap is 10–30%, and TEN is over 30%.
  • Auspitz sign suggests psoriasis but is not specific. Darier sign means mastocytosis, so avoid opioids, aspirin, NSAIDs and alcohol 📌. The dimple sign means dermatofibroma.
  • Wood's lamp: coral red is erythrasma. Yellow-green is pityriasis versicolor. Green-yellow is Microsporum. T. tonsurans does NOT glow 📌.
  • KOH: septate branching hyphae mean tinea. Pseudohyphae with budding yeast mean Candida. "Ziti/spaghetti and meatballs" means pityriasis versicolor.
  • Tzanck: multinucleated giant cells mean herpes. Patch test: for allergic contact dermatitis, patches off at 48 h, final reading at 72 or 96 h.
  • In leprosy, test sensation (cotton, needle, temperature, iodine-starch). Lesions are numb and do not sweat. TT has good CMI. LL has no CMI, with leonine facies and madarosis.
  • Vitiligo calls for thyroid tests and a DM screen. Yellow skin with white sclera is carotenemia. Test turgor at the sternum. Six or more CALMs suggest NF1.
  • Exclamation-mark hairs mean alopecia areata, which regrows. Carpet tacks mean DLE, which scars permanently. Hair loss after childbirth or fever is telogen effluvium. Hair loss after chemo is anagen effluvium.
  • Nails: pitting (most frequent), oil spots (pathognomonic) and onycholysis mean psoriasis. Half-and-half means CKD. Terry means liver. Spoon means iron deficiency. Clubbing means heart, lung or GI disease. Beau lines mean a growth arrest (chemo, fever). Onychomadesis follows hand-foot-mouth disease.

2.03 Approach to Malignancy, Cancer Screening & Prevention 19 items

Dr. Arthur Jason Go (NEW, no past exam from him) · Recall 4 / Comp 5 / App 4 / Analysis 6 · Past-exam style source: none. The 2027/2028 items were written by a different professor, so use them for TOPICS only and follow the 2026 trans.

How Dr. Go will likely ask
  • His whole trans follows one frame, which he underlined: Diagnosis, then Stage, then Plan, then Support.
    • So expect many "next best step" cases. The answer is usually the next step in this order.
    • Tissue before treatment. You never treat a cancer that has not been proven by biopsy.
    • Staging before the plan. You cannot choose a treatment until you know how far the cancer has spread.
    • Fix reversible causes before calling the patient "too frail". A patient who looks weak may only be dehydrated or in pain.
  • For the prevention part, he will likely ask three things:
    • Which level of prevention is being described (primary, secondary or tertiary).
    • Which agent is used (chemoprevention, immunoprevention or surgical prevention) and what harm it carries.
    • Who qualifies for which screening under PHEX (Philippine Periodic Health Examination): the ages, the intervals and the tests.
  • He wrote four cases himself in the trans. Know the answer to each:
    • The smoker who asks for a "complete cancer blood test". The answer is to address tobacco first.
    • The lung nodule found on screening. The answer is to follow a standard diagnostic pathway.
    • The ECOG 3 lymphoma patient with hypercalcemia. The poor function is reversible, so correct it first.
    • The new breast mass. The order is mammogram and biopsy first, then CT for extent, then the treatment plan.
  • Numbers he may test:
    • Response criteria: RECIST 30% shrinkage, WHO more than 50% shrinkage, progression at 20% growth.
    • Pain causes 70-20-10, nausea timing, nutrition cut-offs and PHEX screening intervals.
Past-exam concept map (2027 / 2028) — different professor, topics only
Concept20282027Covered in
First / priority step in the cancer patient#19, #28#23, #28Framework, Diagnosis
TNM, stage = best prognostic factor#20, #21—Staging
Role of a CT after treatment (surveillance vs staging)—#24Staging
Performance status: why, which scale, ECOG matching#25, #35#36–38ECOG vs Karnofsky
Tumor markers (CA-125, CEA, AFP, CD30)—#20, #33–35Tumor markers
Cancer pain (most common cause)#29#30Supportive care
Chemo side effect / cachexia#23, #24—Supportive care
Recurrent malignant pleural effusion—#31Effusions
Smoking cessation 30–50%—#32Prevention levels
Carcinogen (benzene causing leukemia)#34—Carcinogens
HPV vaccine preventing oropharyngeal cancer#31—Immunoprevention
Purpose of screening, lead-time bias#26, #33#21 (sensitivity)Screening biases
Low-dose CT eligibility (repeated)#30#22, #29LDCT
Mammogram age / breast screening (repeated)#27#25, #29PHEX table
Spinal cord compression (emergency)—#27Emergencies (Harrison's)

The 4-step frame: Diagnosis, Stage, Plan, Support HIGH-YIELD LECTURER 2028 #19, #28 2027 #23, #28

Always go in this order: (1) establish the diagnosis, (2) find the extent of disease (stage), (3) make a treatment plan, (4) manage the complications of the disease and its treatment.

  • Step 1, Diagnosis. No treatment is given until there is tissue proof (a biopsy) that the patient has cancer.
  • Step 2, Stage. No plan is made until the patient is staged, meaning you know where the cancer has spread.
    • This step also looks at the patient's physiologic reserve, which is measured as performance status (how well the patient functions day to day).
    • It also looks at tumor biology, meaning how aggressively the cancer behaves.
  • Step 3, Plan. The plan needs an explicit goal. It is either curative (aiming for cure) or palliative (aiming for comfort and longer, better life).
  • Step 4, Support. This is supportive care, checking whether the treatment is working (response assessment), and end-of-life care.
  • He closes the lecture with the same four words, underlined: "Diagnosis, stage, plan, support". p. 1, 3
TRAP: "priority once cancer is established"
  • Both the 2027 (#28) and 2028 (#28) keys chose "disclosure of diagnosis to the patient". They picked it over "extent of disease" and "treatment plan".
  • The current trans does not list disclosure as a step. It does stress telling the patient the truth.
  • How to answer:
    • If the stem says the diagnosis is already established and "disclosure" is one of the choices, that was the old key.
    • If disclosure is not a choice, pick the next step in the frame, which is extent of disease (staging).
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "newly diagnosed via biopsy… next step?" or "a mass is seen on imaging… next step?"
  • Trap: choosing "start chemo" or "PET-CT" before there is tissue.
    • How to tell them apart: ask yourself "do we have a biopsy yet?"
    • If there is no biopsy, the answer is biopsy.
    • If there is already a biopsy, the answer is staging.

A 61/M had a core-needle biopsy of a colonic mass showing adenocarcinoma. His physician now orders a CT of the chest and abdomen to look for liver and lung lesions. In the approach to the cancer patient, this CT belongs to which step?

  1. Establishing the diagnosis
  2. Determining the extent of disease
  3. Making the treatment plan
  4. Managing treatment complications

B. The diagnosis is already proven, because the biopsy showed adenocarcinoma. So step 1 is finished.
A CT that looks for spread to the liver and lungs is finding out how far the cancer has gone. That is staging, or determining the extent of disease.
The treatment plan (C) only comes after the extent is known, so the CT cannot belong to the planning step.

Step 1: Diagnosis needs tissue, and Cancer of Unknown Primary MUST KNOW

An invasive tissue biopsy is the starting point. Imaging or a tumor marker alone does not diagnose cancer.

  • FNAB (fine-needle aspiration biopsy) is the biopsy method named for thyroid cancer.
  • CUP (cancer of unknown primary) means a metastasis is found but the original tumor is not known. The approach has three parts:
    • Take a detailed history.
    • Do a focused search for the primary.
    • Biopsy the nearest accessible tissue, meaning the lesion that is easiest and safest to reach.
  • What is done with the tissue:
    • IHC (immunohistochemistry) is his example of how tumor markers are used on tissue.
    • Consider gene expression testing or NGS (next generation sequencing) to see which mutations the cancer carries.
    • NGS can find a driver mutation, the mutation that makes the cancer grow. If one is found, a matching targeted drug can be given.
  • He underlined that NGS is predictive, not only prognostic.
    • Predictive means it tells you whether a specific treatment will work.
    • Prognostic means it tells you how the disease will behave.
  • A multidisciplinary team improves the quality of decisions. For example, a colon problem goes to a gastroenterologist and a lung problem goes to a pulmonologist. p. 1–2
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: a lymph node or liver mass with no obvious primary, or "the marker is elevated, should we start treatment?"
  • Trap: choosing a whole-body PET-CT or "repeat tumor markers".
    • How to tell them apart: the trans says to biopsy the nearest accessible tissue. Tissue is what gives the diagnosis.

A 66/F has a hard, fixed 3 cm left supraclavicular lymph node. Breast, pelvic and skin exams are unremarkable, and she has no localizing symptoms. Which is the most appropriate next step?

  1. Start empiric chemotherapy for a presumed lung primary
  2. Request CEA, CA-125 and AFP to identify the primary
  3. Observe and repeat the exam in 3 months
  4. Biopsy the lymph node, with IHC on the tissue, after a detailed history

D. This is cancer of unknown primary. The trans approach is a detailed history, a focused search, and a biopsy of the nearest accessible tissue, which here is the lymph node. IHC on that tissue helps point to the primary.
B is tempting, but tumor markers rarely diagnose cancer and are elevated by many benign conditions.
A is wrong because no treatment is given without tissue proof.
C is wrong because a hard, fixed node needs a diagnosis now, not observation.

Step 2: Staging systems and TNM HIGH-YIELD 2028 #20, #21 2027 #24

Treatment outcome depends on 3 things: the extent of disease, the patient's physiologic reserve and the tumor biology. TNM (from the AJCC, American Joint Committee on Cancer) is the most common staging system.

  • The three factors in plain words:
    • Extent of disease asks "where did it spread?"
    • Physiologic reserve asks "how well does the patient function?" Is the patient working, sedentary or bedridden?
    • Tumor biology asks "how does this cancer behave?" Is it aggressive or more benign in behavior?
Clinical stagingPathologic staging
Based onPhysical exam, imaging and other pre-treatment informationOperative and tissue findings
Tells youWhether disease is early or advanced
Whether body function is good or bad		Tumor biology (how aggressive the cancer is)
MemoryBefore the knifeAfter the knife
SystemUsed for
TNM (AJCC)Most cancers
T = primary tumor (size or depth)
N = regional lymph nodes
M = distant metastasis
Ann ArborHodgkin's lymphoma
DukesColorectal cancer (but TNM is still what is used in practice)
FIGOGynecologic cancers
  • How T is graded depends on the organ:
    • Breast is graded by tumor size.
    • Colorectal and uterine cancer are graded by depth of penetration into the wall.
    • In both cases, the bigger or deeper the tumor, the higher the T. The more nodes involved, the higher the N. p. 1
Past-exam extra (not in the 2026 trans). These three words describe different times of scanning:
  • Surveillance means scans after treatment is finished, to look for recurrence (2027 #24).
  • Staging means scans at first diagnosis, to find the extent.
  • Screening means testing people without symptoms who are not known to have the disease.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: matching a staging system to a cancer, clinical vs pathologic stage, or how T is graded.
  • Trap: Dukes for colorectal cancer.
    • Dukes is the correct name of the colorectal system, but the lecture says TNM is still what is used in practice.

Which staging system and cancer pairing is INCORRECT?

  1. Ann Arbor — Hodgkin's lymphoma
  2. Dukes — colorectal cancer
  3. FIGO — non-Hodgkin lymphoma
  4. TNM — most solid tumors

C. FIGO is the system for gynecologic cancers, not lymphoma. Lymphoma is staged with Ann Arbor.
B may look wrong because TNM is used in practice for colorectal cancer, but Dukes is still a correct colorectal pairing by name.

Performance status: ECOG vs Karnofsky, and poor PS may be reversible HIGH-YIELD LECTURER 2028 #25, #35 2027 #36–38

Performance status (PS) estimates physiologic reserve. It tells you whether the patient can tolerate treatment. Karnofsky (KPS) counts up toward health, where 100 is normal. ECOG (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group) counts up toward death, where 5 is dead.

ECOGMeaningKarnofsky (trans anchors)
0Fully active100 normal, no complaints
1Restricted to light work—
2Walks around and cares for self, but cannot work70 cares for self, unable to work
3Limited self-care, in bed or chair more than 50% of waking hours50 needs considerable assistance
4No self-care, completely disabled—
5Dead0 dead

The trans lines up the rows by direction only (both scales get worse going down). It gives no exact KPS-to-ECOG conversion. p. 1

  • The lecturer's rule: ECOG 3 or 4 at baseline means limited treatment options.
    • Why: a patient who is usually in bed most of the day has little reserve to survive the side effects of treatment.
  • Exception: if the cancer itself is causing the poor PS and the patient has a chance to improve, treating the cancer may still be worth it, as long as the patient will respond.
  • His trans case shows this:
    • A 58-year-old woman with newly diagnosed lymphoma is ECOG 3. She also has hypercalcemia, dehydration and severe pain.
    • Before calling her "too frail", treat the reversible problems first (the high calcium and the dehydration).
    • Clarify her baseline, meaning how well she functioned before she got sick.
    • Reassess her PS after she is stabilized.
  • He underlined: "PS is a clinical finding, not a verdict." It describes how the patient is now, and that can change. p. 2
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: a description of the patient's day, and you pick the score. Or "why assess PS?" The answer is to know whether the patient can tolerate treatment.
  • Trap: ECOG 2 vs ECOG 3.
    • How to tell them apart: up and about more than half of the day is ECOG 2. In bed or chair more than half of the day is ECOG 3.
    • Also remember that PS does not measure the extent of disease. Staging does that.

A 70/M with prostate cancer can no longer care for himself without frequent help and needs regular medical care, but he is not bedridden all day. Which Karnofsky score from the lecture best fits?

  1. 50
  2. 70
  3. 100
  4. 0

A. KPS 50 means the patient needs considerable assistance. This man needs frequent help even for self-care, so 50 fits.
B is the tempting choice, but KPS 70 means the patient still cares for himself independently and is only unable to work.
100 is normal and 0 is dead, so C and D do not fit.

Tumor markers monitor, they rarely diagnose MUST KNOW 2027 #20, #33–35

Use tumor markers after the diagnosis is made: to set a baseline, to follow the response to treatment and to raise concern for recurrence. Do not use them to make the diagnosis, and do not use them to screen the patient who asks for a "complete cancer blood test".

MarkerCancerBenign causes (trap)
AFPHCC (hepatocellular carcinoma), gonadal germ-cell tumorCirrhosis, hepatitis
CEAAdenocarcinomas: colon, pancreas, lung, breast, ovaryPancreatitis, hepatitis, IBD (inflammatory bowel disease), smoking
CA-125Ovarian cancer, some lymphomasMenstruation, pregnancy, peritonitis
PSAProstate cancerProstatitis, BPH (benign prostatic hypertrophy)
  • Why markers cannot diagnose:
    • A marker can be normal even when cancer is present. For example, a patient can have colon cancer with a normal CEA.
    • A marker can be high without cancer. For example, a high CEA in a patient with Crohn's disease is not automatically cancer.
  • What markers are useful for, after the diagnosis:
    • Baseline. A pre-operative CEA gives a patient-specific starting value to guide treatment.
    • Response. In stage 4 colon cancer, a CEA that starts at 50 and keeps falling suggests the treatment is working.
    • Recurrence. A rising marker in a patient on follow-up after treatment raises concern that the cancer has come back.
    • Markers complement imaging, they do not replace it.
  • Common pitfalls:
    • Benign conditions can raise markers.
    • Not every tumor secretes a marker.
    • Results vary with the lab assay and with timing.
    • So the rule is: never treat a number alone. p. 2
Old exam keys used some Harrison's markers that are not in this trans:
  • CD30 points to Hodgkin's lymphoma and anaplastic large-cell lymphoma.
  • CD25 points to hairy-cell leukemia.
  • CA 19-9 points to pancreatic and colon cancer. Harrison's
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: an elevated marker in a patient with a benign condition, or "what is an appropriate use of a tumor marker?"
  • Trap: "the CEA is high, so diagnose colon cancer".
    • How to tell: markers only support decisions once tissue has already proven the cancer.

Each of the following can raise CA-125 without cancer, EXCEPT:

  1. Menstruation
  2. Pregnancy
  3. Smoking
  4. Peritonitis

C. In the trans, smoking is listed as a benign cause of a high CEA, not CA-125.
Menstruation, pregnancy and peritonitis are the three benign causes listed for CA-125, so A, B and D can all raise it.

Step 3–4: Curative vs palliative intent, and response criteria MUST KNOW

The goal of treatment must be stated. Early-stage disease is treated with curative intent. Advanced-stage disease is treated with palliative intent. Response to treatment is measured with objective, repeatable tools such as RECIST (Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors) and tumor markers.

CurativePalliative
StageEarlyAdvanced
ToxicityAccepts short-term toxicity in exchange for cureLow tolerance for toxicity
Aggressive chemo is not recommended
DeliveryPrecise protocol
Often combined modalities (surgery plus radiotherapy)		Controls symptoms and disease
Keeps comfort and continuity of care
GoalCure, with a planned definitive assessmentQuality and length of life
  • Why the toxicity tolerance differs: in curative treatment, a hard few months is worth it if the patient is cured. In palliative treatment, cure is not possible, so side effects that ruin quality of life defeat the purpose.
ResponseDefinition
CompleteAll evidence of disease is gone (a sum of 10 falls to 0)
PartialA decrease of at least 30% (RECIST) or more than 50% (WHO) in the summed diameters
ProgressiveA 20% increase in the summed diameters, or any new lesion
StableNeither enough shrinkage for partial response nor enough growth for progression
  • During treatment, any new symptom is treated as reversible until proven otherwise. Always look for a fixable cause before blaming the cancer. p. 2
Solved example The masses measure 4 + 3 + 3 cm, a total of 10. After 2 cycles they measure 2 + 2 + 3 cm, a total of 7.
  1. (10 − 7) ÷ 10 = 0.30, which is a 30% decrease.
  2. RECIST needs at least 30%, so this is a partial response by RECIST.
  3. WHO needs more than 50%, so the WHO threshold is not met.
  4. If any new lesion had appeared, the answer would be progressive disease, even though the sum fell.
Shortcut / trap
  • Add up only the original lesions. Leave any new lesion out of the sum.
  • A new lesion means progression all by itself, no matter what the sum does.
  • Do not mix up the three numbers: 30 (RECIST partial), 50 (WHO partial) and 20 (progression).

Which feature belongs to a PALLIATIVE treatment plan?

  1. Accepts short-term toxicity in exchange for cure
  2. Lower tolerance for toxicity, with focus on symptom control
  3. Combined surgery and radiotherapy delivered by a precise protocol
  4. Plans a definitive assessment of cure

B. Palliative intent has a lower tolerance for toxicity and focuses on symptoms and quality of life, because cure is not the goal.
A, C and D are all features of curative intent: accepting toxicity for cure, combined modalities by a precise protocol, and a planned assessment of cure.

Supportive and end-of-life care: pain, nausea, depression, nutrition HIGH-YIELD 2028 #23, #29 2027 #30

Treat the person, not only the tumor. This covers symptoms, nutrition, psychological needs and end-of-life care. Most cancer pain (70%) comes from the tumor itself.

TopicTrans numbers
Causes of pain70% from the tumor
20% from treatment
10% from other causes
Nausea timingAcute: within 24 hours of treatment
Delayed: 1 to 7 days after treatment
Anticipatory: before the chemo is even given
Prophylaxis for highly emetogenic chemoOndansetron 8 mg by mouth every 6 hours the day before, then IV on the treatment day
Dexamethasone 20 mg IV before treatment
Aprepitant 125 mg on day 1, then 80 mg on days 2 and 3
These are continued for a few days after treatment
DepressionAbout 25% of patients, and risk rises with more disease
Screen for at least 2 weeks of low mood or loss of interest (anhedonia)
Treat with an SSRI or a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA)
Allow 4 to 6 weeks for a response
Nutrition triggersWeight loss of more than 10%
Transferrin below 150 mg/dL
Albumin below 3.4 g/dL
Prefer enteral (oral or tube) feeding over parenteral (IV)
Megestrol may help
End of lifeInfection is the #1 cause of death in cancer patients
About 70% develop shortness of breath before death
Be truthful and promise the patient will not be abandoned
TRAP: "most common side effect/complication of therapy"
  • 2028 #23 keyed nausea and vomiting as the most common side effect of chemo.
  • The trans review-question key says the most common complication of cancer therapy is myelosuppression (low blood counts from bone marrow suppression). This is in the answer key only, not in the lecture body.
  • How to tell them apart: read the exact wording. If it says "complication of therapy", answer myelosuppression.
  • 2028 #24 (cachexia from the metabolic effects of the tumor) came from Harrison's.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: a story about when the vomiting started, and you name the nausea type. Or lab values, and you decide whether to start nutrition support.
  • Trap: anticipatory vs acute nausea.
    • How to tell them apart: anticipatory nausea begins before the drug is given. Acute nausea begins after the drug, within 24 hours.

A 45/F on her fourth cycle of cisplatin starts vomiting in the clinic waiting room while waiting for the infusion to be hung. Which type of chemotherapy-related nausea is this?

  1. Acute
  2. Delayed
  3. Breakthrough from the previous dose
  4. Anticipatory

D. No drug has been given yet in this cycle. Nausea that starts before the chemo is given is anticipatory.
Acute nausea (A) happens within 24 hours after the drug is given, and delayed nausea (B) happens 1 to 7 days after. Neither fits, because the infusion has not started.

Malignant effusions: step-up management 2027 #31

Pleural effusion steps up from thoracentesis, to a chest tube (if symptoms come back within 2 weeks), to pleurodesis. Pericardial tamponade is treated with a pericardial window. Ascites is treated with small-volume paracentesis.

  • Malignant effusions can collect in the pleural cavity, the pericardium and the peritoneum.
  • Lung cancer, breast cancer and lymphoma together cause 75% of malignant effusions.
  • Deciding whether to treat:
    • An effusion without symptoms may need no treatment.
    • If it causes symptoms, first consider whether the cancer will respond to systemic therapy and how long the patient is expected to live.
  • The pleural steps in order:
    • Start with thoracentesis (draining the fluid with a needle).
    • If symptoms come back within two weeks, place a chest tube (chest tube thoracostomy or pigtail catheter).
    • Then do pleurodesis, which seals the pleural space so the fluid cannot re-collect.
  • Other sites:
    • Pericardial: a window for tamponade, or stripping, or chemical sclerosis.
    • Ascites: small-volume paracentesis, or shunts in selected patients. p. 2
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: metastatic breast or lung cancer with an effusion. The patient feels better after a tap, but the shortness of breath returns in under 2 weeks. What next?
  • Trap: "repeat thoracentesis".
    • How to tell: symptomatic recurrence within 2 weeks calls for a chest tube, followed by pleurodesis.

A 59/M with stage IV lung cancer has hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds. Echo shows a large pericardial effusion with tamponade. Per the trans, which site-specific palliation fits?

  1. Pericardial window
  2. Pleurodesis
  3. Small-volume paracentesis
  4. Observation, since malignant effusions may not need treatment

A. The trans pairs pericardial tamponade with a pericardial window.
D is tempting, but "no treatment" applies only to effusions that cause no symptoms. This patient has tamponade, which is life-threatening.
Pleurodesis (B) is for the pleural space and paracentesis (C) is for ascites, so they are the wrong site.

Levels of prevention, carcinogenesis steps, tobacco first HIGH-YIELD LECTURER 2027 #32

Primary prevention is for people with no cancer yet (change their exposures). Secondary prevention is screening people without symptoms. Tertiary prevention is treating cancer that already causes symptoms. Stopping tobacco is the single highest-yield prevention action.

Carcinogenesis stepWhat interrupts itLevel
1 Initiation (injury to DNA or epigenetic changes)Exercise, stopping smoking, sun avoidancePrimary
2 Promotion (signals that make the damaged cells grow)VaccinationPrimary
3 Progression (invasion and malignant behavior)ScreeningSecondary
  • He underlined that prevention can interrupt more than one of these steps.
  • Why tobacco comes first:
    • About 1 in 3 smokers die early from tobacco-related disease.
    • Smoking shortens life by about 10 years.
    • Quitting gives a 30–50% lower 10-year lung-cancer mortality compared with continuing to smoke.
    • This benefit happens even after mutations have already occurred, so it is never too late to quit.
  • What the clinician does (the 3 A's):
    • Ask every patient about all tobacco and vaping products.
    • Advise complete cessation. Switching to "light" cigarettes is not enough.
    • Assist with counseling plus medicines (such as nicotine patches and drugs that reduce craving), or refer.
  • Counseling points:
    • Cigars and smokeless tobacco are not safe substitutes.
    • Secondhand smoke is carcinogenic.
    • Prevention starts in adolescence. p. 3
His Case 1
  • A 52/M smokes 20 cigarettes a day, has a BMI of 31, rarely exercises and has no symptoms. He asks for a "complete cancer blood test".
  • The answer is to address his tobacco use first.
  • After that, check if he qualifies for evidence-based screening, and address weight, activity, vaccination and sun exposure.
  • Avoid tumor markers, whole-body CT and MCED (multi-cancer early detection) blood tests. None of these has been shown to help.
  • His take-home line: "Prevention earns priority. Screening earns scrutiny." p. 3, 5

Which of the following is an example of SECONDARY cancer prevention?

  1. HPV vaccination of a 12-year-old girl
  2. Chest tube and pleurodesis for a malignant effusion
  3. Annual FIT in an asymptomatic 55-year-old
  4. Smoking-cessation counseling for a 30-year-old smoker

C. Secondary prevention means screening people who have no symptoms. A yearly FIT (fecal immunochemical test) in a person without symptoms is screening.
A (vaccination) and D (quitting smoking) are primary prevention, because they act before any cancer exists.
B treats a cancer that is already causing symptoms, which is tertiary prevention.

Carcinogens and lifestyle evidence 2028 #34

Know which exposure causes which cancer. Lifestyle advice is strongest when it also has broad health benefits beyond cancer.

CarcinogenCancers
TobaccoUpper aerodigestive tract, lung, and also bladder and kidney
AsbestosLung, pleura (mesothelioma), peritoneum
AlcoholBreast, liver, esophagus, head and neck
UV radiationSkin cancers
The lecturer stresses it causes more SCC (squamous cell carcinoma) than melanoma
Actinic keratosis can turn into SCC
Aromatic aminesBladder
Ionizing radiationMany solid and blood cancers
  • Lifestyle evidence that is supported:
    • Physical activity lowers the risk of colon and breast cancer.
    • A higher BMI modestly raises the risk of several cancers.
    • Sun protection lowers UV exposure and actinic keratosis.
  • Lifestyle evidence that is uncertain:
    • Observational diet studies are confounded by other factors.
    • Low-fat, high-fiber diet trials did not clearly reduce cancer.
    • Supplements beyond a balanced diet have no established anticancer value. p. 3
  • Extras from old keys:
    • Benzene causes leukemia (2028 #34).
    • Schistosomiasis causes squamous cell bladder cancer, through chronic parasitic inflammation of the bladder lining (trans review key). Harrison's

A 58/M who worked 25 years in a dye factory presents with painless gross hematuria. Which carcinogen and cancer pair is most likely?

  1. Asbestos — mesothelioma
  2. Aromatic amines — bladder cancer
  3. Alcohol — kidney cancer
  4. UV radiation — squamous cell carcinoma
