B. Dye factory work means exposure to aromatic amines, and aromatic amines cause bladder cancer. Painless blood in the urine fits bladder cancer.
C is a trap: kidney cancer is on the tobacco list, not the alcohol list.
A and D are real pairs, but they do not fit a dye worker with hematuria.

Chemoprevention: benefit must beat harm LECTURER

Chemoprevention means giving a natural or synthetic agent BEFORE invasive cancer develops, to reverse, suppress or prevent carcinogenesis (he underlined this). An agent that makes sense on paper can still cause more harm than good.

AgentEffectHarm / lesson
Beta caroteneLooked protective in observational dataRandomized trials in smokers found MORE lung cancer
Lesson: a plausible idea is not the same as a proven outcome
AspirinLowers adenomas and colorectal cancer after long follow-upBleeding
Net benefit depends on age, cardiovascular risk and bleeding risk
Tamoxifen (SERM)Lowers ER-positive breast cancerVTE (venous thromboembolism), endometrial cancer, cataracts, hot flashes
Raloxifene (SERM)Lowers invasive breast cancer in postmenopausal womenLess uterine toxicity, but still VTE
Aromatase inhibitorsLarge relative reduction in trialsMusculoskeletal symptoms, osteoporosis
FinasterideAbout 25% fewer prostate cancers diagnosedMore high-grade cancers seen
Changes prostate volume and PSA results
Not FDA-approved for prevention
  • SERM means selective estrogen receptor modulator.
  • The four ways chemopreventive agents work:
    • Antimutagenic: they reduce DNA damage.
    • Hormonal: they remove growth signals.
    • Anti-inflammatory: they change the environment that promotes tumors.
    • Antiproliferative or proapoptotic: they limit abnormal clones of cells.
  • Breast chemoprevention is a preference-sensitive decision:
    • First take a history to confirm high risk (family history of breast cancer or a genetic predisposition).
    • Then make an individualized risk estimate and decide together with the patient (shared decision-making). p. 3

A 50/F heavy smoker read that carrots "fight cancer" and asks to start high-dose beta-carotene supplements to prevent lung cancer. Best advice?

  1. Discourage it: randomized trials in smokers showed more lung cancer
  2. Encourage it: observational studies showed lower lung cancer rates
  3. Allow it only with yearly chest X-ray screening
  4. Recommend aspirin instead, which prevents lung cancer

A. This is the beta-carotene lesson. Randomized trials in smokers found more lung cancer, so a plausible idea should not be trusted over actual outcomes.
B is tempting because observational data did look protective, but the randomized trials overruled it.
D is wrong because aspirin's evidence is for colorectal cancer, not lung cancer. C is wrong because chest X-ray screening does not lower lung-cancer deaths.

Immunoprevention (vaccines) and surgical prevention 2028 #31

Vaccines prevent cancers that are caused by chronic infection. Surgery is powerful but cannot be undone, and some cancer risk remains afterwards.

TypeIntervention and the cancer it prevents
ImmunoHBV vaccine prevents chronic hepatitis B, which lowers hepatocellular carcinoma risk
ImmunoHPV vaccine (types 16 and 18) lowers cervical cancer and other HPV-related cancers such as oropharyngeal cancer
Infection controlH. pylori eradication may lower gastric adenocarcinoma risk (in selected settings)
SurgicalProphylactic mastectomy and salpingo-oophorectomy in hereditary breast-ovarian cancer syndromes (BRCA)
SurgicalColectomy in FAP (familial adenomatous polyposis)
  • Before preventive surgery, weigh these:
    • How large the inherited risk really is.
    • The cancer risk that remains even after surgery.
    • Effects on fertility, hormones, sexual function and mental health, plus the risks of surgery itself.
  • Lecture example: Angelina Jolie carries a BRCA1 mutation and had a bilateral mastectomy and oophorectomy.
    • Why the oophorectomy: removing the ovaries removes the main source of estrogen, which lowers the risk of estrogen-driven cancer. p. 3–4

A 22/M has hundreds of colonic adenomas and an APC mutation (familial adenomatous polyposis). Which cancer-preventive strategy from the lecture applies?

  1. Finasteride chemoprevention
  2. HBV vaccination
  3. Prophylactic colectomy
  4. Annual FIT starting at age 50

C. The lecture lists colectomy in FAP as a surgical prevention strategy. With hundreds of adenomas, his colon cancer risk is near-certain.
D is tempting because FIT is colon screening, but population screening from age 50 is for average-risk people and does not fit a hereditary, near-certain risk.
Finasteride (A) is for prostate cancer and HBV vaccine (B) is for liver cancer.

Screening is a program, and screening biases HIGH-YIELD 2028 #26, #33

Judge screening by whether it lowers deaths from that cancer (disease-specific mortality). Do not judge it by longer survival after diagnosis, because longer survival can be an artifact of bias.

Lead-time biasLength biasOverdiagnosisSelection (volunteer) bias Harrison's — not in 2.03 trans
What happensDiagnosed earlier, but dies at the same timeSlow tumors stay detectable longerFinds a cancer that would never have caused harmPeople who volunteer for screening are healthier to begin with
EffectSurvival looks longer on paper, but life is not longerScreening mostly finds favorable disease
Fast-growing cancers are missed		More diagnoses and treatment, with no benefitThe screened group looks better for reasons that have nothing to do with screening
MemoryThe clock started earlierSlowNeverWho signed up
  • Screening is a program, not a single test. Every link must work:
    • An eligible population without symptoms.
    • An accurate test that people accept.
    • Timely confirmation of abnormal results.
    • Effective treatment that works better when given earlier.
    • The benefit can fail at any link, and harms can pile up at every link.
  • Harms of screening:
    • False positives, which lead to invasive work-ups.
    • False reassurance after a false negative.
    • Overdiagnosis and overtreatment.
    • Procedures, radiation, anxiety and cost. p. 4
  • Test terms (from 2.01): sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive (2027 #21).
TRAP
  • 2028 #26 keyed "diagnose at an early stage" as the purpose of screening.
  • The current trans adds that early detection only counts if it lowers mortality and morbidity.
  • How to answer: if both are choices, "reduce disease-specific mortality" is the trans answer.

In a new screening program, the tumors found by the screening test are mostly low-grade and slow-growing, while aggressive cancers keep appearing between screening rounds. This pattern illustrates:

  1. Lead-time bias
  2. Length bias
  3. Overdiagnosis
  4. False-negative reassurance

B. Slow tumors stay detectable for a long time, so the screening test keeps catching them. Fast tumors grow and cause symptoms between rounds, so they show up as interval cancers. That is length bias.
C is tempting, but overdiagnosis means cancers that would never matter. Here the issue is about slow vs fast tumors being found.
Lead-time bias (A) is about the survival clock starting earlier, which is not described here.

Who gets screened for what: PHEX adult recommendations HIGH-YIELD MUST KNOW 2028 #27 2027 #25, #29

Screening has been shown to lower mortality for 4 cancers (memory aid CBCL): Cervical, Breast, Colorectal and Lung. In the PHEX table, every row is green (recommended) except prostate, which is blue (shared decision-making).

CancerWhoTest · interval
CervicalWomen 30–65Cytology every 3 years, OR high-risk HPV test every 5 years
VIA (visual inspection with acetic acid) every 3 years is an alternative
BreastWomen 50–69Mammography every 1–2 years
Yearly if there is a family history of breast cancer or a BRCA mutation
BreastWomen ≥50Clinical breast exam every 2 years
ColonAdults 50 and older (in the Philippines)
45–50 abroad		FOBT/FIT yearly
A positive result needs a colonoscopy
Sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, or colonoscopy every 10 years, if normal
LungHigh risk, age 50–80, more than 20 pack-yearsAnnual low-dose CT
LiverAt risk for HCC, with or without cirrhosisUltrasound plus AFP every 6 months
NasopharyngealFirst-degree relative with NPC (nasopharyngeal carcinoma)EBV DNA test and/or nasopharyngoscopy
Prostate (blue)Men 50–64 without symptomsShared decision before PSA plus DRE (digital rectal exam) every 2 years
  • Breast MRI is only for selected high-risk, younger patients. It is not used for population screening. Mammography is the standard test.
  • Two screening tests are controversial:
    • Ovarian cancer screening with CA-125 plus transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) did not lower mortality in average-risk women, and false positives can lead to major surgery.
    • PSA for prostate cancer has a small or uncertain benefit, so it needs shared decision-making.
  • MCED (multi-cancer early detection) blood tests have not been shown to improve health outcomes, so they are not routine. p. 4–5
TRAP: old keys vs current trans
  • Mammography:
    • 2027 #25 keyed mammography starting at age 40 (USPSTF/ACS guidelines).
    • 2028 #27 keyed ages 50–74, every 2 years.
    • The current trans (PHEX) says ages 50–69, every 1–2 years.
  • Pap smear:
    • 2027 #29 keyed a yearly Pap smear.
    • PHEX says cytology every 3 years (or HPV test every 5 years) for ages 30–65.
  • Follow the trans.

A 54/F with no symptoms has a mother who had breast cancer at age 60. She has never been screened. Per the PHEX recommendations in the trans, what breast screening should she get?

  1. Mammography every 2 years
  2. Annual breast MRI alone
  3. Clinical breast exam only, since she is under 70
  4. Yearly mammography

D. Women 50–69 get mammography every 1–2 years. A family history of breast cancer (or a BRCA mutation) moves this to yearly. Her mother had breast cancer, so she gets yearly mammography.
A is the average-risk interval and ignores her family history.
B is wrong because MRI is not routine population screening.

Lung screening: low-dose CT eligibility and what happens after HIGH-YIELD 2028 #30 2027 #22, #29

Only low-dose CT (LDCT), not chest X-ray, lowers lung-cancer mortality. It works only in high-risk smokers: age 50–80 with more than 20 pack-years, screened yearly.

Formula Pack-years = packs per day × years smoked.
  1. Example: 1.5 packs a day × 18 years = 27 pack-years.
  2. Then check three things in order: is the age 50–80, is it more than 20 pack-years, and can the patient undergo curative treatment?
Shortcut / trap
  • A family history, radon exposure or asbestos exposure alone does not make someone eligible.
  • Chest X-ray screening has no mortality benefit in randomized trials.
  • In the NLST (National Lung Screening Trial), LDCT gave about 3 fewer lung-cancer deaths per 1,000 people screened compared with chest X-ray.
  • Eligibility depends on age, smoking exposure, overall health, and the ability to undergo curative treatment.
    • Why the last point matters: finding an early cancer only helps if the patient is fit enough to have it treated.
  • Harms of LDCT: false positives, incidental findings, radiation, invasive procedures, anxiety and cost.
  • His Case 2: a 62-year-old current smoker has a small nodule on screening LDCT. What next?
    • Estimate the chance that it is malignant, using features of the nodule and the patient.
    • Follow a standardized diagnostic pathway.
    • Do not dismiss the finding, and do not rush to invasive treatment.
    • Keep supporting smoking cessation. Screening quality includes what happens after the scan. p. 4–5
TRAP: changing criteria
  • 2027 #29 rationale used ages 55–80 with at least 30 pack-years, and 2028 #30 keyed "30 pack-years".
  • 2027 #22 used ages 50–80, at least 20 pack-years, and quit within the last 15 years.
  • The current trans says ages 50–80, more than 20 pack-years.
  • The "quit within 15 years" rule is not in the trans.

Which asymptomatic patient qualifies for annual low-dose CT screening per the current trans?

  1. 48/M, 2 packs/day for 20 years
  2. 58/F, half a pack/day for 30 years
  3. 63/M, 1.5 packs/day for 18 years, still smoking
  4. 82/M, 2 packs/day for 40 years

C. 1.5 × 18 = 27 pack-years, which is more than 20, and he is 63, which is within 50–80. He qualifies.
A has 40 pack-years but is too young (48).
B is the right age but has only 0.5 × 30 = 15 pack-years.
D has heavy exposure but is over 80.

Oncologic emergencies (compact) Harrison's — not in 2.03 trans 2027 #27

Past exams included emergency cases, but Dr. Go's trans does not cover them. Learn only these 4 short summaries.

EmergencyClueKey move
Spinal cord compressionKnown cancer (lung, breast, prostate, myeloma)
Back pain that is worse lying flat, later followed by leg weakness
Thoracic spine in 70%		Give high-dose dexamethasone now
Then get an MRI of the whole spine
Then radiation plus steroids (surgery first if the spine is unstable)
SVC syndrome (superior vena cava)Swollen face and neck, dilated veins on the chest, worse lying down
Lung cancer causes about 85%
In young adults, think lymphoma		Confirm with CT
NSCLC (non-small-cell lung cancer): radiation
SCLC, lymphoma, germ cell tumor: chemo
Stent if severe
The real danger is compression of the trachea
Tumor lysis syndromeBurkitt lymphoma or ALL, 1 to 5 days after chemo
High uric acid, high potassium, high phosphate, low calcium, acute kidney injury		Prevent it with allopurinol plus IV fluids
Rasburicase if high risk (never in G6PD deficiency)
HypercalcemiaThe most common paraneoplastic syndrome
Can make PS look worse than it really is		Correct it (and the dehydration), then reassess PS (trans case)
  • Why each key move:
    • Cord compression: dexamethasone reduces swelling around the cord. MRI is the test of choice because plain X-rays often miss it. Patients do best when treated while they can still walk and control their bladder.
    • SVC syndrome: SCLC, lymphoma and germ cell tumors respond well to chemo, which is why they get chemo instead of radiation.
    • Tumor lysis: chemo kills many fast-growing cells at once, and they spill their contents into the blood. Uric acid crystals form in the kidney tubules, which is why fluids and allopurinol are given before chemo. Rasburicase is avoided in G6PD deficiency because it produces hydrogen peroxide, which these patients cannot handle.
  • Neutropenia with infection is the most common serious complication of treatment. Infection is the #1 cause of death in cancer patients (trans).

A 68/M with metastatic prostate cancer has 2 weeks of mid-back pain that is worse at night when lying flat, and today cannot climb stairs because of leg weakness. What should be done FIRST?

  1. Give high-dose dexamethasone, then MRI of the whole spine
  2. Plain X-ray of the thoracic spine, then decide
  3. Start NSAIDs and reassess in 2 weeks as mechanical back pain
  4. EMG/NCV of the lower extremities

A. Back pain that is worse lying flat plus new leg weakness in a cancer patient suggests spinal cord compression. Give steroids right away to reduce swelling, then get an MRI of the whole spine.
B is tempting, but plain X-rays often miss cord compression and waste time.
C treats it as a slipped disk, but disk pain is not worse lying flat. Waiting is dangerous because outcome depends on treating while he can still walk.
D (a nerve study) looks at the wrong thing.

Practice drill — Dr. Go style (framework and prevention cases)

A 57/M smoker has a 4 cm right hilar mass on CT and a CEA of 28 ng/mL. His family asks that chemotherapy be started this week. What is the next best step?

  1. Start chemotherapy, since the CEA confirms adenocarcinoma
  2. Repeat CEA in 4 weeks to see the trend
  3. Obtain tissue (biopsy) to establish the diagnosis
  4. Refer to palliative care because of the high CEA

C. The diagnosis always starts with tissue. Without a biopsy, you do not even know the cancer type, so you cannot choose a treatment.
A is wrong because CEA never confirms cancer on its own. It can also be high just from smoking, and this patient smokes.
B and D both act on a number alone, which the trans says never to do.

A 41/F has a right breast mass enlarging over 4 months, unrelated to her cycle. Mammogram and core biopsy show invasive ductal carcinoma. What comes next?

  1. Modified radical mastectomy right away
  2. Determine extent with physical exam and imaging (e.g., CT) before planning treatment
  3. Start tamoxifen chemoprevention
  4. Repeat mammogram in 6 months

B. This matches the trans case. The diagnosis is made with mammogram and biopsy. The next step is the extent of disease (physical exam plus CT), and only then the treatment plan.
A is tempting, but surgery before staging skips a step.
C is wrong because chemoprevention is for people who do not yet have invasive cancer.

A 63/F with newly diagnosed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma has been bedbound for 10 days with severe bone pain, confusion, serum calcium 13.8 mg/dL and dry mucosa. Her daughter says she was gardening daily a month ago. The resident labels her ECOG 3, "not a candidate for therapy." Best next step?

  1. Agree and refer for hospice only
  2. Give full-dose chemotherapy today regardless of status
  3. Repeat the ECOG score tomorrow without other changes
  4. Correct the hypercalcemia and dehydration, control pain, then reassess performance status

D. PS is a clinical finding, not a verdict. Her poor function comes from reversible problems: high calcium, dehydration and pain. Her baseline was good, since she was gardening a month ago. So fix the reversible causes, then reassess.
A gives up on a patient who may do well once stabilized.
B gives chemo before stabilizing her, which skips the step in the trans case.
C changes nothing, so the score will not change either.

A patient with stage IV colon cancer had CEA 50 at diagnosis, which fell to 6 after chemotherapy. On follow-up it is now 34, and he feels well. What is the most appropriate interpretation and action?

  1. Concern for recurrence/progression, so confirm with imaging before changing treatment
  2. Diagnostic of progression, so switch chemotherapy now
  3. Meaningless, because CEA is not useful after diagnosis
  4. Probably lab error, so stop monitoring markers

A. A rising marker after treatment raises concern for recurrence or progression. But markers complement imaging, they do not replace it, so confirm with imaging first.
B is tempting, but switching chemo on the number alone breaks the rule "never treat a number alone".
C is wrong because following response and recurrence after diagnosis is exactly what markers are for.

Three liver metastases measured 5, 3 and 2 cm before treatment. After 3 cycles they measure 4, 3 and 2 cm, and a new 1 cm lesion appears in the lung. The response category is:

  1. Partial response
  2. Stable disease
  3. Progressive disease
  4. Complete response

C. Any new lesion means progressive disease, no matter what happens to the original tumors.
B is tempting: the original sum fell from 10 to 9, only a 10% drop, which by itself would be stable disease. But the new lung lesion overrides that.

A 36/F asks how often she needs cervical screening. Her co-tested cytology and high-risk HPV test today are both negative. Per PHEX in the trans, when is her next screen?

  1. In 1 year
  2. In 5 years
  3. In 3 years
  4. No further screening needed after one negative HPV test

B. When an HPV test is used, the interval is every 5 years. Cytology alone would be every 3 years.
C is the cytology-only interval, but she also had an HPV test.
A (a yearly Pap) was an old exam key and is not the trans interval. D is wrong because screening continues until age 65.

A 52/M, average risk, did a FIT for screening and it came back positive. What is the next step?

  1. Repeat the FIT next year
  2. Serum CEA to decide if work-up is needed
  3. CT colonography as the definitive test
  4. Colonoscopy

D. Any positive stool test (or positive CT colonography) needs a colonoscopy.
A is wrong because a screening program fails if abnormal results are not followed up.
C is wrong because a positive CT colonography itself also needs a colonoscopy, so it cannot be the definitive test. B uses a marker to decide, which markers cannot do.

A 58/M without urinary symptoms asks for a PSA test "to be safe." Per PHEX, what is the most appropriate approach?

  1. Discuss benefits and harms (shared decision-making) before biennial PSA + DRE
  2. Order annual PSA, since it is a green (recommended) test
  3. Refuse, since PSA is never used for screening
  4. Order PSA with CA-125 and CEA as a cancer panel

A. Prostate is the only blue (shared decision-making) row in PHEX. For men 50–64, discuss the benefits and harms, including overdiagnosis, before doing PSA plus DRE every 2 years.
B is wrong because prostate is blue, not green, and the interval is every 2 years, not yearly.
C is too absolute, since PSA can be offered after shared decision-making. D is a tumor-marker panel, which is not a screening tool.

Which screening pairing for an asymptomatic adult is INCORRECT per the trans?

  1. Chronic hepatitis B, no cirrhosis — ultrasound + AFP every 6 months
  2. Brother with nasopharyngeal carcinoma — EBV DNA and/or nasopharyngoscopy
  3. Average-risk 50/F — CA-125 + transvaginal ultrasound for ovarian cancer
  4. 60/M, 30 pack-years — annual low-dose CT

C. CA-125 plus transvaginal ultrasound did not lower mortality in average-risk women, and false positives can lead to major surgery. So it is not a recommended screen.
A is correct because HCC screening applies to at-risk patients with or without cirrhosis.
B and D match the PHEX rows for nasopharyngeal and lung cancer.

A screening study reports that 5-year survival after diagnosis rose from 40% to 65% in the screened group, but the age-adjusted death rate from that cancer did not change. The best explanation is:

  1. Screening is effective, and survival is the right endpoint
  2. Lead-time bias: diagnosis came earlier but death did not come later
  3. Selection of sicker patients into the screening arm
  4. False-negative results lowering survival

B. Survival rose but deaths did not fall. That means the cancer was found earlier, so the survival clock started earlier, but the patients did not live any longer. That is lead-time bias.
A is the trap: screening must be judged by mortality, not by survival after diagnosis.
C would make the screened group look worse, not better.

An 84/M in a nursing home has a small low-grade prostate cancer found on routine PSA. He dies 2 years later of heart failure with no prostate symptoms. This case best illustrates:

  1. Lead-time bias
  2. Length bias
  3. False-positive result
  4. Overdiagnosis

D. This was a real cancer, but it would never have harmed him. He died of something else first. That is overdiagnosis.
B is tempting, but length bias is about slow tumors being found more often than fast ones. It is not about cancers that never matter.
C is wrong because the cancer was real, so the result was not a false positive.

A side effect shared by tamoxifen and raloxifene used for breast cancer chemoprevention is:

  1. Venous thromboembolism
  2. Endometrial cancer
  3. Osteoporosis
  4. Bleeding

A. Both SERMs raise the risk of VTE. A simple way to remember: raloxifene spares the uterus but not the veins.
B is tempting, but endometrial cancer belongs to tamoxifen only. Osteoporosis (C) belongs to the aromatase inhibitors. Bleeding (D) belongs to aspirin.

Match the intervention with the step of carcinogenesis it mainly interrupts, per the lecture. Which pairing is correct?

  1. Screening — initiation
  2. Smoking cessation — progression
  3. HPV vaccination — promotion
  4. Sun avoidance — progression

C. In the lecture, vaccination interrupts promotion.
Initiation is interrupted by exercise, quitting smoking and sun avoidance, so B and D are wrong.
Progression is interrupted by screening, so A is wrong.

A 9-year-old Burkitt lymphoma patient starts induction chemotherapy. Two days later: K 6.4, phosphate high, calcium low, uric acid 14, creatinine rising. Which measure should have been the priority beforehand? Harrison's

  1. Urine alkalinization with bicarbonate
  2. Allopurinol with aggressive IV hydration before chemotherapy
  3. High-dose dexamethasone
  4. Calcium gluconate infusion before each cycle

B. This is tumor lysis syndrome: high potassium, high phosphate, low calcium, high uric acid and kidney injury after chemo for Burkitt lymphoma. Prevention with allopurinol plus IV fluids before chemo is the most important step.
A is tempting, but urine alkalinization is no longer advised. It helps uric acid dissolve but makes other crystals (xanthine, calcium phosphate) form.

Last-look cram sheet

  • The frame is Diagnosis (tissue), then Stage, then Plan, then Support. If there is no tissue yet, biopsy. If tissue is already in hand, stage.
  • Old keys said the "priority once cancer is established" is disclosure of the diagnosis (2027 and 2028).
  • FNAB is the biopsy for thyroid cancer. For cancer of unknown primary, take a history, do a focused search and biopsy the nearest accessible tissue. NGS is predictive.
  • TNM is the most common staging system. Ann Arbor is for Hodgkin's lymphoma. Dukes is for colorectal cancer, but TNM is still used. FIGO is for gynecologic cancers.
  • T is graded by size in breast cancer and by depth in colorectal and uterine cancer.
  • Clinical stage comes before the knife. Pathologic stage comes after the knife.
  • ECOG 0 is fully active, 1 is light work only, 2 is up and caring for self but not working, 3 is in bed or chair more than 50% of the day, 4 is completely disabled, and 5 is dead. Karnofsky anchors are 100 (normal), 70 (self-care, no work), 50 (considerable help) and 0 (dead).
  • ECOG 3–4 means limited treatment options, unless the cause is reversible (hypercalcemia, dehydration, pain). PS is a finding, not a verdict.
  • Tumor markers monitor and rarely diagnose. CEA rises with IBD and smoking. CA-125 rises with menses and pregnancy. AFP rises with cirrhosis. PSA rises with BPH.
  • Curative intent is for early disease, accepts toxicity and uses combined modalities. Palliative intent is for advanced disease and has a low tolerance for toxicity.
  • Partial response is at least 30% shrinkage by RECIST or more than 50% by WHO. Progression is a 20% increase or any new lesion.
  • 70% of cancer pain comes from the tumor. Acute nausea is within 24 hours, delayed is days 1–7, and anticipatory happens before chemo. Depression affects about 25%.
  • Start nutrition support with weight loss over 10%, albumin below 3.4 g/dL or transferrin below 150 mg/dL. Use enteral feeding first.
  • For pleural effusion, tap first, then a chest tube if it recurs within 2 weeks, then pleurodesis. Tamponade gets a window. Lung, breast and lymphoma cause 75% of malignant effusions.
  • Infection is the #1 cause of death in cancer patients. Heart disease is #1 overall and cancer is #2. Age is the #1 risk factor.
  • Primary prevention is before any cancer, secondary is screening, and tertiary is treatment. Tobacco comes first. Quitting lowers 10-year lung-cancer mortality by 30–50%.
  • Lifestyle changes interrupt initiation, vaccines interrupt promotion, and screening interrupts progression.
  • Asbestos causes mesothelioma. Aromatic amines cause bladder cancer. Alcohol causes breast, liver, esophageal and head and neck cancer. UV causes mostly SCC.
  • Beta carotene caused more lung cancer in smokers. Aspirin lowers colorectal cancer but causes bleeding. Tamoxifen causes endometrial cancer and VTE. Raloxifene still causes VTE. Finasteride is not FDA-approved for prevention.
  • HBV vaccine prevents HCC. HPV 16/18 vaccine prevents cervical and oropharyngeal cancer. H. pylori eradication may prevent gastric cancer. FAP gets colectomy. BRCA carriers may get mastectomy and salpingo-oophorectomy.
  • Lead-time bias means the clock started earlier. Length bias means slow tumors are found more. Overdiagnosis means a cancer that would never matter. Judge screening by mortality.
  • PHEX intervals:
    • Cervix, ages 30–65: cytology every 3 years or HPV test every 5 years.
    • Breast, ages 50–69: mammogram every 1–2 years, yearly with family history or BRCA.
    • Colon, age 50: FIT yearly, and a positive result needs colonoscopy.
    • Lung, ages 50–80 with more than 20 pack-years: LDCT yearly.
    • HCC risk: ultrasound plus AFP every 6 months.
    • Relative with NPC: EBV DNA test.
    • Prostate is the only blue row, so it needs a shared decision.
  • Chest X-ray screening has no benefit. MCED, whole-body CT and tumor-marker panels are not used for screening.

2.06 Introduction to Radiology I 5 items

Dr. Christine Carlos-Depaynos · Recall 3 / Comp 2 / App 0 / Analysis 0 · Past-exam style source: 2028 #95–100 and 2027 #96–100 (same professor, so trust both)

How Dr. Carlos-Depaynos asks
  • Her stems are short, one-line recall questions. There are no patient cases.
    • Typical forms: "How does X appear on Y?", "Which modality…?", "What do you call…?"
  • Her favorite topics:
    • Density words: radiolucent vs radiopaque vs hyperdense.
    • Radiation: which modality is high dose, and which ones have no radiation at all.
    • Best modality for a given job (soft tissue, fracture, meniscus).
    • Fluoroscopy.
    • The marker and the teleroentgenogram.
  • Her distractors are usually the same idea written in another modality's vocabulary.
    • Example: hyperdense, radiopaque, hyperintense and hyperechoic all mean "white", but each belongs to a different modality.
    • Strategy: first identify the modality in the stem, then pick the word that belongs to it.
  • The teleroentgenogram came up in both years, even though it is not in the 2026 2.06 trans. Learn its 4 criteria.

The 5 X-ray densities HIGH-YIELD 2028 #95 2027 #98

From whitest to blackest, the order is bone/calcium, then soft tissue, then water, then fat, then air. Metal is whiter than all five.

Rank (white to black)DensityOn X-ray
0 (brightest)Metal (coin, orthopedic device)Bright white, the most opaque of all
1Bone / calciumWhite, the most radiopaque of the 5
2Soft tissueLight gray
3Water / fluidGray
4FatDark gray
5 (darkest)Air (lungs, trachea, bowel gas)Black, the most radiolucent
It lets the most X-rays through.
  • Why things look white or black:
    • Dense tissue absorbs X-rays, so fewer X-rays reach the film. That area looks white.
    • Thin tissue like air lets X-rays pass through to the film. That area looks black.
    • This is why air is the darkest: it absorbs (attenuates) the fewest X-rays.
  • Mnemonic, read from black to white: Andrew Felt Sorry For Cursing Mammography. p. 4
    • Air, Fat, Soft tissue/Fluid, Calcium, Metal.
    • Note that this mnemonic groups soft tissue and fluid together, while the trans figure lists them as separate steps.
  • "Density" simply means how black or white something looks on the image. The word is used especially for CT. p. 4
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "How does [air / calcium / bone] appear on a conventional radiograph?"
  • Trap: hyperdense or hypodense appear among the choices.
    • How to tell them apart: those are CT words. On a plain X-ray the answer is always radiolucent (black) or radiopaque (white).
  • Trap: the direction of the order.
    • The mnemonic runs from black to white, but the trans figure runs from white to black. Read which direction the question asks for.

On a plain abdominal radiograph, which structure is expected to be more radiolucent than fat?

  1. Urine in the bladder
  2. Gas in the colon
  3. Liver
  4. Calcified gallstone

B. "More radiolucent" means blacker. In the density order, air is the only thing blacker than fat, and colon gas is air.
Urine is water and the liver is soft tissue. Both sit on the whiter side of fat.
A calcified gallstone contains calcium, which is radiopaque (white), the opposite of what was asked.

Black vs white: each modality has its own word MUST KNOW 2028 #98

"Hypo" means black and "hyper" means white. X-ray is the exception: radiolucent means black and radiopaque means white.

ModalityBlack (dark)White (bright)Root word
X-rayRadiolucent ("a lucency")Radiopaque ("an opacity")lucent / opaque
CTHypodenseHyperdensedensity
UltrasoundHypoechoicHyperechoic (echogenic)echo
MRIHypointenseHyperintensesignal intensity
  • Link each word to what the machine measures. p. 3
    • CT measures density, so it uses hypodense and hyperdense.
    • Ultrasound records echoes, so it uses hypoechoic and hyperechoic.
    • MRI reads signal intensity, so it uses hypointense and hyperintense.
    • X-ray is the odd one out with lucent and opaque.
  • How a radiologist writes it in a report: "There is a lucency noted in the right lower lung field" (black area) or "There is a hazy opacity" (white area).
  • "Echogenic" means the same thing as hyperechoic. It is a common ultrasound word, but it is not in the trans table.
  • "Isodense" (the same shade as the surrounding tissue) can show up as a distractor. It is not in the trans.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: "What do you call a structure that is white / dark on [modality]?" or "Which pairing is INCORRECT?"
  • Trap: all 4 choices describe the same color.
    • How to tell them apart: ignore the color and look at the root word. Pick the one that matches the modality named in the stem.

A renal cyst looks dark on ultrasound. In the sonologist's report, the cyst is described as:

  1. Hypoechoic
  2. Hypodense
  3. Radiolucent
  4. Hypointense

A. Ultrasound describes brightness by echoes, so a dark structure is hypoechoic.
All the other choices also mean "dark", but in a different modality's language. Hypodense is the CT word, radiolucent is the X-ray word, and hypointense is the MRI word.

Not in the 2026 trans: MRI T1 vs T2, CT Hounsfield units (skim only)

The trans says MRI physics will not be tested (p. 3). This is here only in case a distractor uses these words. Standard radiology, not trans

T1T2
FatBright (hyperintense)Bright to intermediate
Water / fluid (CSF, edema)Dark (hypointense)Bright ("T2 = water white")
Cortical bone, airDarkDark

CT Hounsfield units: air is about −1000, fat about −100, water 0, soft tissue +20 to +80, and bone +400 to +1000 or more. This follows the same order as the 5 densities.

Gadolinium (the MRI contrast agent) makes protons realign with the magnetic field faster. Faster realignment makes the tissue look brighter. This part is in the trans. p. 3

Modality summary: radiation, strengths, weaknesses LECTURER 2027 #97

Ionizing: X-ray (low dose) and CT (high dose). No ionizing radiation: MRI and ultrasound. The lecturer emphasized this point.

ModalityRadiation?Best forPoor for / problemContrast
X-rayYes, low doseBones
Metal (orthopedic devices)
Calcium
Cheap and readily available		Cartilage and soft tissue (they contain no calcium)
Intra-abdominal organs
2D images only		None
(angiography uses iodinated contrast)
CTYes, high doseGood soft tissue contrast
Detailed bone evaluation
Calcification (better than X-ray)		Cartilage and ligaments
Metal causes streak artifact
Quite expensive		Iodinated
MRINone
(uses magnetic fields, radio waves and field gradients)		Superior soft tissue contrast: ligaments, bone marrow, spinal cord
Images in any plane		Motion artifact because the scan is slow
Unsafe with non-MRI-compatible metal or electronic devices and shrapnel
Claustrophobia and anxiety (narrow tunnel)
Most expensive, not in all hospitals		Gadolinium
UltrasoundNone
(uses high-frequency sound by the pulse-echo technique)		Solid organs
Fluid-filled organs
Superficial small parts

Bone and anything behind bone

  • How to remember the radiation split:
    • X-ray and CT both use X-rays, so both are ionizing. CT is the high-dose one.
    • MRI uses magnets and radio waves, and ultrasound uses sound. Sound and magnets do not ionize.
  • Why each weakness happens:
    • X-ray shows soft tissue poorly because cartilage and soft tissue contain no calcium, so they absorb few X-rays.
    • MRI gets motion artifact because image acquisition is slow, so the patient must stay very still.
    • Ultrasound needs sound to travel through tissue. Air and bone block it, so lungs and organs encased in bone are poorly seen.
TRAP
  • Fluoroscopy is an X-ray study, but its continuous beam increases radiation exposure. Do not call it low dose just because it is "an X-ray".
  • Metal changes the answer depending on the modality.
    • On X-ray, metal is a strength (good for orthopedic devices).
    • On CT, metal causes streak artifact.
    • On MRI, metal is a safety problem.
p. 2–3

A 24-year-old pregnant woman needs abdominal imaging. Which pair of modalities avoids ionizing radiation completely?

  1. CT scan and fluoroscopy
  2. X-ray and ultrasound
  3. CT scan and MRI
  4. Ultrasound and MRI

D. Ultrasound uses sound waves and MRI uses magnets and radio waves, so neither is ionizing.
Every other pair contains at least one X-ray–based modality. B looks tempting because ultrasound is safe, but it is paired with plain X-ray, which is ionizing. C pairs MRI with CT, which is the high-dose one.

Pick the modality HIGH-YIELD 2027 #96 2028 #99 2028 #100

Soft tissue contrast gets better as you move from X-ray (poor) to CT (good) to MRI (superior). For fine bone detail and calcification, choose CT.

Stem says…Answer
Superior soft tissue contrast
Ligament, meniscus or cartilage, spinal cord, bone marrow		MRI
Fracture or detailed bone evaluation (when plain X-ray is not a choice)
Calcified lesion in a patient with a non-MRI-compatible device		CT
Bones, metal implants, calcium
A cheap first look		X-ray
Solid or fluid-filled organ, superficial part
Vessels by Doppler, real-time imaging		Ultrasound
Moving structures: peristalsis, diaphragm, heart, barium studies, catheter placementFluoroscopy
Contrast flowing through vessels in real timeConventional angiography
Operating room, patient cannot be moved to radiology (ORIF, intraoperative cholangiogram)C-arm X-ray
TRAP
  • In 2028 #99, the key for "best for bone fractures" was CT.
    • Why: plain X-ray was not among the choices, and the trans lists "detailed bone evaluation" as a CT strength (p. 3).
    • If both X-ray and CT are offered, read the stem. "Cheap" or "initial" points to X-ray. "Detailed" or "complex" points to CT.
  • A meniscus is cartilage.
    • Cartilage is listed as a CT weakness, so the answer for a meniscus is MRI.

A 19-year-old basketball player twisted his knee and now has instability. An anterior cruciate ligament tear is suspected. Which imaging best shows it?

  1. Plain radiograph
  2. CT scan
  3. MRI
  4. Fluoroscopy

C. A ligament is soft tissue, and MRI has the superior soft tissue contrast. The trans names ligaments specifically as an MRI strength.
CT is tempting because it has "good" soft tissue contrast, but cartilage and ligaments are listed as CT weaknesses. Plain X-ray has poor soft tissue contrast, and fluoroscopy is for watching motion.

Fluoroscopy and the other X-ray types 2028 #96

Fluoroscopy is "real-time X-ray". A continuous beam passes through the patient onto a fluorescing screen or monitor, so you can watch structures move.

TypeKey feature
FluoroscopyContinuous beam
Shows moving structures: GI peristalsis, diaphragm, cardiac action, barium studies, catheters
More radiation
Conventional angiographyFluoroscopy plus iodinated contrast injected into the vessels
Used to study blood vessels as the contrast passes through
CR vs DRCR (computed radiography) uses a phosphor plate that must be read manually, so it is slower.
DR (digital radiography) uses a fixed electronic detector or CCD (charge-coupled device). It is cassette-less and gives an immediate image.
C-armAn X-ray machine brought into the operating room
CT typesConventional: one slice at a time (about 15–30 min for a plain cranial study)
Helical: continuous scanning, faster
MDCT (multi-detector CT): multiple rows of detectors, so a cranial CT fits in one breath hold
  • Fluoroscopy vs angiography:
    • Both are real time. The difference is contrast in the vessels.
    • If the stem mentions iodinated contrast passing through vessels, it is angiography. If it only mentions watching something move, it is fluoroscopy.
  • CR vs DR: think "plate means CR, detector means DR".

A patient with suspected left phrenic nerve palsy is asked to sniff while the radiologist watches the hemidiaphragms move on a monitor. This study is:

  1. Conventional angiography
  2. Fluoroscopy
  3. Digital radiography
  4. Helical CT

B. Watching the diaphragm move in real time needs a continuous beam, which is fluoroscopy. Diaphragm movement is one of its listed uses.
Angiography is also real time, but it requires contrast injected into vessels, which is not described here. Digital radiography and helical CT do not show live motion.

Marker, orientation and teleroentgenogram HIGH-YIELD 2027 #99 2027 #100 2028 #97

The marker always goes on the patient's right. You view the film as if you are facing the patient, so the patient's right appears on the viewer's left. A teleroentgenogram is taken in the PA view.

  • Position and projection are different things. p. 4
    • Position is the patient's posture: upright, supine, prone or lateral decubitus.
    • Projection is the direction the beam travels from source to surface: AP (anteroposterior), PA (posteroanterior) or lateral.
  • Axial CT follows the same left-right rule. The patient's right is on the viewer's left, anterior is at the top, and posterior is at the bottom. p. 5
  • Swallowed coin in the neck: p. 4
    • On an AP film, you can see the coin but cannot tell whether it is in the trachea or the esophagus.
    • On the lateral view, the air-filled trachea shows as a dark tube. If the coin sits behind it, it is in the upper esophagus, because the esophagus lies behind the trachea.
TELEROENTGENOGRAM criteria (not in the 2026 2.06 trans. Source: the 2028 #97 rationale and the 2027 Radiology III trans.)
  • PA projection.
  • Patient upright.
  • Arms akimbo: hands on the waist or behind the head.
    • Why: this moves the scapulae off the lung fields.
  • Taken at mid or full inspiration.
  • The usual 6-ft (72 in) tube-to-film distance reduces magnification of the heart. Standard radiology, not trans
TRAP
  • "Supine", "AP" and "hands at the sides" are all wrong for a teleroentgenogram.
  • In 2028 #97 the key was "PA view" rather than "chest in full expansion".
    • So when only one choice is accepted, PA is the defining criterion.

Which radiographic technique is NOT appropriate when taking a teleroentgenogram?

  1. Patient supine with the beam entering anteriorly
  2. Patient upright
  3. Arms akimbo
  4. Film taken at full inspiration

A. A supine patient with the beam entering from the front gives an AP film. A teleroentgenogram must be an upright PA film, so this choice breaks two criteria at once.
Upright position, arms akimbo and full inspiration are all correct teleroentgenogram criteria.

Practice drill — Dr. Carlos-Depaynos style

On a plain radiograph, which order goes correctly from most radiolucent to most radiopaque?

  1. Fat, air, water, soft tissue, bone
  2. Air, water, fat, soft tissue, bone
  3. Air, fat, water, soft tissue, bone
  4. Bone, soft tissue, water, fat, air

C. Most radiolucent means blackest, so start with air and end with bone: air, fat, water, soft tissue, bone.
D lists the correct sequence but runs from white to black, the opposite of what was asked. B swaps fat and water. A puts fat before air, but air is always the blackest.

Which modality–term pair for a bright/white structure is INCORRECT?

  1. CT – hyperdense
  2. Ultrasound – hyperechoic
  3. MRI – hyperintense
  4. Plain radiograph – radiolucent

D. Radiolucent means black on X-ray. The X-ray word for white is radiopaque, so this pair is wrong.
The other three correctly match a "hyper" (white) word to its own modality.

A 68-year-old man with a hip prosthesis is followed up to check where the metal hardware sits. Which modality images the metal well at the lowest cost?

  1. CT scan
  2. Plain radiograph
  3. MRI
  4. Ultrasound

B. X-ray is listed as good for metals such as orthopedic devices, and it is cheap and readily available.
CT is more expensive and metal causes streak artifact on it. On MRI, metal is a safety problem. Ultrasound cannot see through bone, and the prosthesis sits in bone.

Which of the following is a limitation of ultrasound?

  1. Poor visualization of air-filled lungs
  2. High dose of ionizing radiation
  3. Unsafe with metallic shrapnel
  4. Cannot image in real time

A. Sound waves cannot travel well through air or bone, so air-filled lungs are poorly seen.
Ultrasound is non-ionizing (B is the CT description) and is a real-time study (D is wrong). The shrapnel problem in C belongs to MRI.

A patient with a non-MRI-compatible cardiac pacemaker has a suspected calcified intracranial lesion. Best modality?

  1. MRI with gadolinium
  2. Ultrasound
  3. CT scan
  4. Fluoroscopy

C. CT evaluates calcification better than X-ray does, and it is safe with the pacemaker.
MRI is tempting for brain imaging, but it is unsafe with a non-MRI-compatible device. Ultrasound cannot see through the skull. Fluoroscopy is for moving structures.

Which statement about MRI is TRUE?

  1. It uses low-dose ionizing radiation
  2. Its contrast agent is iodinated
  3. Its main artifact is the streak artifact from metal
  4. It gives superior soft tissue contrast, such as for the spinal cord

D. Superior soft tissue contrast, including the spinal cord, is MRI's main strength.
The others describe the X-ray family: MRI is non-ionizing (A is X-ray), its contrast is gadolinium (iodinated in B is for CT), and its typical artifact is motion. Streak artifact from metal (C) is a CT problem.

Which X-ray–based study exposes the patient to more radiation because of its continuous beam?

  1. Computed radiography
  2. Fluoroscopy
  3. Digital radiography
  4. Film radiography

B. Fluoroscopy keeps the beam on continuously so motion can be watched in real time, and that increases exposure.
Computed, digital and film radiography each take a single exposure. They differ only in the detector used (phosphor plate, electronic detector, or film).

Last-look cram sheet

  • From whitest to blackest: bone, soft tissue, water, fat, air. Metal is brighter than all of them. Air is the most radiolucent.
  • Words for black and white:
    • X-ray uses radiolucent / radiopaque.
    • CT uses hypodense / hyperdense.
    • Ultrasound uses hypoechoic / hyperechoic.
    • MRI uses hypointense / hyperintense.
  • Ionizing modalities are X-ray (low dose) and CT (high dose). Fluoroscopy gives more exposure. MRI and ultrasound are non-ionizing.
  • Superior soft tissue, ligament, meniscus, spinal cord or bone marrow means MRI.
  • Detailed bone, fracture (when X-ray is not a choice) or calcification means CT. Metal on CT causes streak artifact.
  • Metal implants, bones and a cheap first look mean X-ray. It gives only 2D images and has poor soft tissue contrast.
  • Ultrasound is good for solid, fluid-filled and superficial organs, Doppler and real time. It is poor for air and bone, and it is operator dependent.
  • A continuous beam showing real-time motion is fluoroscopy. Add iodinated contrast in the vessels and it becomes angiography.
  • Contrast: CT and angiography use iodinated contrast. MRI uses gadolinium, which makes tissue brighter.
  • The marker goes on the patient's right, which appears on the viewer's left.
  • Teleroentgenogram: PA, upright, arms akimbo, taken at inspiration.
  • A coin behind the tracheal air on the lateral view is in the upper esophagus.

LE1 Rapid Recall 10 items

2 items each: Communication (Dr. Castillo) · History Taking (Dr. Rosario) · PE / General Survey / Vitals (Dr. Lista) · Ophthalmology (Dr. Aclan) · ENT (Dr. Miura) · Past-exam style source: 2027 LE2 #101–110, 2028 LE2 #101–110, 2029 LE1

How LE1 recall shows up in LE2
  • Each LE1 lecture gets 2 short items, placed at the very end of the exam (#101–110). They are mostly recall or one-step application.
  • Communication and history questions quote a line the doctor says and ask you to name the technique.
    • Examples: summarization, topic tracking, empathic response.
  • PE questions ask about positions and technique, BMI, or precautions.
    • Examples: standing to check the spine, supine with knees bent for the abdomen.
  • Ophthalmology questions give a finding and ask for the test or the diagnosis.
    • Examples: confrontation test, oscillopsia, episcleritis, macular degeneration.
  • ENT questions ask you to interpret the tuning-fork tests, to pick the structure or maneuver that does NOT belong, or to name a duct.

Physician–Patient Communication HIGH-YIELD 2028 #101–102 2027 #101

Patient-centered (biopsychosocial) communication is the gold standard. Physician-centered (biomedical) communication is the fastest in acute cases. Best practice is to let the patient talk first, then shift to questions led by the clinician.

Biomedical (physician-centered)Biopsychosocial (patient-centered)
Who directsThe clinician takes charge to identify a disease. 70% of doctors use it.The patient tells what matters most to them. This is the gold standard.
StrengthEfficient for a quick diagnosis, so it fits acute casesBrings out the personal context, feelings and concerns
WeaknessDepersonalizing
Misses psychosocial factors
Lowers patient satisfaction and shared decision-making		Takes more time
TechniqueHow to recognize it
Continuers (facilitation)"Mm-hmm… go on… I'm listening"
EchoingRepeats one of the patient's words: "Spread?" "Going to die?"
Graded response"How many steps can you climb before you get short of breath?"
Multiple-choice answers"Aching, sharp, burning…?" This is acceptable. 2027 #101
ValidationTreats the emotion as legitimate ("anyone would feel that way"). This builds connection.
ReassuranceComes only after the feelings are acknowledged. Be careful not to give false hope.
PartneringCommits to an ongoing relationship ("we'll work on your asthma together")
Transitions"Next I'll ask about…"
Tells the patient the interview is changing direction, for example before questions about STDs.
SummarizationA capsule summary of the story. It shows you were listening carefully. 2028 #101
EmpoweringDraws out the patient's view, makes your reasoning transparent, and admits the limits of what you know
  • The 7 goals of communication (LE1 asked you to match quotes to goals):
    • Fostering the relationship, gathering information, providing information, decision-making.
    • Enabling treatment-related behavior, responding to emotions, managing uncertainty.
  • The 3 components of a message: verbal, nonverbal and paraverbal.
    • Verbal (the words) is only 10% of the message.
    • Nonverbal and paraverbal (tone, pitch, pace) make up the other 90%.
  • The most important barrier is lack of insight, meaning poor knowledge and training in communication skills.
  • Rapport breaks the initial barrier between doctor and patient. 2028 #102
    • Why it matters: it builds trust, so the patient becomes willing to share sensitive information.
EXAM APPLICATION
  • Asked as: a quoted doctor line, and you name the technique or goal.
  • Trap: validation vs reassurance.
    • How to tell them apart: validation says "your feeling makes sense". Reassurance says "it will be OK".
  • Trap: summarization vs echoing.
    • How to tell them apart: summarization restates the whole story. Echoing repeats a single word.

History Taking, Symptom Analysis, Temporal Profile HIGH-YIELD 2028 #103 2027 #102–104

Start with rapport, then ask open-ended questions before focused ones. Describe each symptom with PQRSTU. Write the chief complaint as a symptom plus its duration, never a diagnosis. Draw the temporal profile after the ROS (review of systems) and before the PE.

ItemKey points
Interview sequence1. Greet the patient and build rapport (this is first)
2. Invite the story
3. Set the agenda
4. Expand the story and test your hypotheses
5. Reach a shared understanding
6. Negotiate a plan
7. Follow-up and closing
Mindful practiceObserving your own thought process. Example: pausing before lecturing a non-compliant patient.
Topic trackingKeeping to a topic you both agreed on, using summaries, process transparency and goal alignment ("Should we stay with your diabetes or shift to your back pain?") 2027 #103
Empathic clue acknowledgement"It sounds like you're afraid… tell me more."
An empathic response sounds like: "How did you feel about that?" 2027 #102
Question typesLoaded: biased, with unjustified assumptions
Leading: "Isn't it true that…"
Simple direct: answered yes or no
Neutral: "Tell me more…"
Focusing: steers back to a topic the patient already raised
PQRSTUP: Provocative or Palliative factors
Q: Quality or Quantity
R: Region or Radiation
S: Severity (out of 10)
T: Timing
U: Understanding ("What do you think is causing it?")
Write-up orderPatient profile, then source and reliability (poor, fair, good, or a %), then CC (chief complaint), HPI (history of present illness), past health, family history, ROS, and finally the temporal profile
Chief complaintBrief, one or two symptoms at most, in the patient's own words, with the duration, and with no diagnostic labels
Correct: "Chest heaviness, 2 hours"
Wrong: "Unstable angina, r/o MI"
Sensitive historyIf relatives are present, ask the patient if he is comfortable answering in front of them. If not, politely ask them to step out. 2027 #104
CAGE screens for alcohol use.
Pack-years = packs per day × years smoked.
Temporal patternClue
IntermittentComes and goes, and stops completely in between (can happen several times a day)
ContinuousNo break at all
RemittentGoes up and down but never returns to baseline
RecurrentThe whole episode repeats at intervals of hours or days
PeriodicEpisodes come in clusters lasting days, weeks or months
The symptom-free period is longer than the symptomatic period
  • How to draw the temporal profile:
    • Use 1–2 symptom lines (3 at most), and a separate diagram for each illness.
    • The order of symptoms changes the diagnosis. Fever, then abdominal pain, then jaundice suggests viral hepatitis. Abdominal pain, then jaundice, then fever suggests a gallstone with cholecystitis.
  • The 4 phases of the HPI:
    • (1) Let the patient give an open-ended, neutral account.
    • (2) Analyze each symptom in detail with closed, neutral questions.
    • (3) Test the possible diagnoses by asking about other symptoms.
    • (4) Do the ROS.
  • Pertinent negatives narrow the differential diagnosis. Subjective data (the history) and objective data (PE and labs) complement each other.
Note: the 1.02 trans uses PQRSTU. The 1.01 and ENT lectures use CLITAAA instead: Character, Location, Intensity, Timing, Associated symptoms, Aggravating and Alleviating factors. "OLDCARTS" is not in the trans.

Complete PE, General Survey, Vital Signs HIGH-YIELD 2028 #105–106 2027 #105–106

Examine from the patient's right. Use the same head-to-toe order every time. Change the patient's position only when needed. Use IPPA (inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation) everywhere except the abdomen, which is IAPP (auscultation comes before palpation).

Vital signTechnique / cutoff
BPKeep the cuff at heart level.
Palpate the systolic first, then inflate 30 mmHg above it.
Listen with the bell, because Korotkoff sounds are low-pitched.
Deflate at 2–3 mmHg per second.
Systolic is the first of at least 2 consecutive sounds. Diastolic is when the sounds disappear.
Orthostatic BPMeasure supine after 3–10 min of rest, then again within 3 min of standing.
Positive if SBP falls by 20 or more or DBP falls by 10 or more mmHg.
Heart rateUse the radial pulse.
If regular, count for 30 s and multiply by 2.
If too fast, too slow or irregular, count a full 60 s.
Normal range is 60 to 90–100/min.
Respiratory rateCount quietly, by watching or by listening over the trachea, while still appearing to "take the pulse".
Why: patients change their breathing once they notice it is being counted.
TemperatureOral, rectal, axillary, tympanic or temporal
BMI (kg/m²)WHOAsia-Pacific (lecturer: "more applicable")
<18.5UnderweightUnderweight
18.5–22.9Healthy (up to 24.9)Normal
23–24.9HealthyOverweight, at risk
25–29.9OverweightObese I
30–34.9 / 35–39.9 / ≥40Obese I / II / IIIObese II (≥30)
  • The general survey begins the moment you meet the patient. It covers:
    • Apparent state of health, level of consciousness (LOC) and signs of distress.
    • Skin color, dress, grooming and hygiene, facial expression and odors.
    • Posture, gait and motor activity, and height, weight and BMI.
    • If the BMI is above 35, measure the waist circumference just above the hips. The risk of diabetes, hypertension and cardiovascular disease rises if the waist is above 35 in for women or above 45 in for men. per 1.03 trans
    • Bates uses above 40 in for men, so answer with the trans number.
  • Why examine from the right side:
    • JVP (jugular venous pressure) estimates are more reliable.
    • Your hand rests comfortably on the apical impulse.
    • The right kidney is more often palpable.
    • Tangential light helps show the JVP, the thyroid and the apical impulse.
  • Positions:
    • Cardiovascular exam: patient at 30°. Left lateral decubitus to hear an S3 or mitral stenosis. Sitting, leaning forward and exhaling to hear aortic regurgitation.
    • Abdomen: supine with the knees bent, which relaxes the abdominal muscles. 2028 #105
    • Standing: varicose veins, spine alignment 2027 #105, hernias, gait and the Romberg test.
  • Forgot a step? Go back to it calmly, even if it is out of sequence.
  • Drape so only the area being examined is exposed. For example, cover the right breast again before exposing the left.
  • Precautions and hand hygiene:
    • Standard precautions cover all body fluids except sweat.
    • Universal precautions cover fluids that carry bloodborne pathogens (blood, semen, vaginal secretions, CSF, pleural fluid and others).
    • Use soap and water if hands are visibly soiled or after contact with C. difficile or norovirus. Otherwise an alcohol rub is fine.
    • Contact precautions: gloves and gown, to protect staff and other patients. 2028 #106
    • Droplet precautions (influenza, meningococcus, pertussis): surgical mask.
    • Airborne precautions (TB, measles, varicella): N95 mask and a negative-pressure room.
    • After a needlestick, wash the area and report it immediately.
TRAP
  • BMI has been asked before with WHO cutoffs (2027 #106, LE1 #52).
  • If the stem says "Asian" or "more applicable", use the Asia-Pacific table.
    • Example: a BMI of 25.5 is "overweight" by WHO but "obese I" by Asia-Pacific.

Ophthalmic History and PE from LE1 exam rationales — ophtha trans unavailable 2027 #107–108 2028 #107–108

Visual acuity (VA) is the "vital sign of the eye" and is done first, before the eye is manipulated. This matters most in trauma or an open globe. For the other questions, match the finding to the test.

TestChecks
Confrontation testVisual fields, meaning lesions along the visual pathway (for example, a pituitary adenoma causing temporal field loss). Asked twice.
Corneal light reflex (Hirschberg)Alignment of the eyes
RetinoscopyRefractive error, measured objectively
Swinging flashlightRAPD (relative afferent pupillary defect), also called Marcus Gunn pupil
The affected pupil dilates when the light swings to it. This points to the optic nerve, as in optic neuritis.
Tonometry (eye pressure)Goldmann applanation is the gold standard.
iCare (rebound) and air-puff are screening tools.
Never do digital tonometry on an open globe.
Direct ophthalmoscopy (dark room)Checks the media and red reflex, the optic disc (cup-disc ratio, color, borders), the vessels, the retinal background (hemorrhages, exudates) and the macula.
It does not assess the limbus or retinal thickness.
  • VA ladder:
    • Snellen chart at 20 ft (6 m). If the patient cannot read it, they walk closer.
    • If they still cannot read it at 1 m, step down in order: count fingers, then hand movement, then light projection, then light perception.
    • The near card (Jaeger) is held at 14 in (35 cm). Use the tumbling E chart for patients who cannot read.
  • Light projection grading: all 4 quadrants is good, 2–3 of 4 is fair, 1 of 4 is poor, and 0 of 4 is negative.
  • Red reflex:
    • Absent or dull when something clouds the media, such as a cataract or a corneal scar.
    • It stays bright in myopia, dry eye and mild diabetic retinopathy.
  • Near response has 3 parts: the pupils constrict, the eyes converge (medial recti), and the eye accommodates (the ciliary muscle contracts so the lens becomes more convex).
  • Discharge type points to the cause:
    • Allergic: clear and stringy, with itching.
    • Bacterial: mucopurulent, with crusting.
    • Viral: watery, with redness.
  • Red eye:
    • Red eye with pain is scleritis. The pain is deep and boring and worse with eye movement.
    • Episcleritis is localized and usually painless. 2028 #107
    • Subconjunctival hemorrhage is painless.
    • A hordeolum is a painful, tender, red lump on the lid margin. A chalazion is painless.
  • Symptom clues:
    • Nystagmus causes oscillopsia (the world seems to bounce). 2027 #108
    • Trouble recognizing faces while side vision is intact points to macular degeneration. 2028 #108
    • Blurry distance vision in a young adult points to myopia. Blurry near vision with age points to presbyopia.
  • Previous eye surgery or trauma and use of glasses belong in the past ocular history, not the past medical history.

PE of ENT HIGH-YIELD 2028 #109–110 2027 #109–110

In conductive loss, Weber lateralizes to the bad ear and Rinne is negative (BC > AC). In sensorineural loss, Weber lateralizes to the good ear and Rinne stays positive (AC > BC). AC is air conduction and BC is bone conduction.

Weber (fork on the midline: vertex, glabella, nasal bridge or mentum, not the mastoid)Rinne (fork on the mastoid, then beside the ear canal with the tines parallel to it)
NormalHeard equally in both earsAC > BC (positive)
ConductiveLouder in the affected earBC > AC (negative)
If negative or equal, do threshold testing
SensorineuralLouder in the normal earAC > BC, but heard for a shorter time
  • Setup:
    • The patient sits upright. Never straddle the patient.
    • A 100-W unfrosted bulb is placed behind the patient. The head mirror goes over your dominant eye (focal length 14 in).
    • A 512 Hz tuning fork is best. Strike it near its base on your hand.
  • Ear exam:
    • Examine the healthy ear first.
    • Pull the pinna up, back and out in adults, and back and down in children.
    • Use the largest speculum that fits, so it cannot slide into the painful bony part of the canal.
    • The cone of light sits anteroinferiorly and is only a reflection.
    • Finger rub test is positive if more than 2 of 6 attempts are missed.
  • Maneuvers that test TM mobility: 2028 #110
    • Pneumatic (Siegel) otoscope.
    • Valsalva: pinch the nose and blow.
    • Toynbee: pinch the nose and swallow.
    • Epley is not one of them. It is a treatment for BPPV (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo).
  • Anterior rhinoscopy:
    • Hold the nasal speculum in your non-dominant hand.
    • Open the blades sideways, away from the septum, and withdraw it with the blades partly open.
    • Kiesselbach's plexus is on the anterior septum.
    • Pale, boggy turbinates with watery discharge suggest allergy. Purulent discharge suggests bacterial infection. A mass or polyp needs endoscopy.
  • Posterior rhinoscopy: 2027 #110
    • Press down the front two-thirds of the tongue and use a small nasopharyngeal mirror facing up.
    • The patient breathes through the nose, so the soft palate drops and you can see behind it.
    • You see the choanae, septum, middle turbinate, eustachian tube opening, tubal tonsil and fossa of Rosenmüller.
    • You do not see Kiesselbach's plexus, because it is at the front of the septum.
  • Indirect laryngoscopy:
    • Patient in the sniffing position, breathing through the mouth.
    • Hold the tongue with gauze. The laryngeal mirror faces down and is warmed so it does not fog.
    • Avoid touching the back third of the tongue, which triggers gagging. Touching the uvula is OK. Use xylocaine if the patient gags a lot.
    • A high-pitched "eee" makes the vocal folds adduct (close). "Hee-hee" makes them abduct (open). A fold that does not move suggests paralysis.
  • Mouth and neck:
    • Stensen's duct (parotid gland) opens opposite the upper 2nd molar.
    • Wharton's duct (submandibular gland) opens in the floor of the mouth. 2027 #109
    • The thyroid rises when the patient swallows and is examined from behind.
    • Lymph drainage: the lips drain to level IA, the front two-thirds of the tongue and the floor of the mouth drain to IB, and the nasopharynx drains to level II.
TRAP
  • "Weber lateralizes to the right" is ambiguous on its own. It can mean right conductive loss OR left sensorineural loss.
  • The Rinne result decides.
    • If Rinne is negative (BC > AC) on the side Weber points to, the loss is conductive on that side.

Practice drill — LE1 recall (2 per lecture)

A 50/F caring alone for her bedridden mother cries during the interview. The physician says: "Anyone looking after a sick parent by herself would feel exhausted. What you're feeling makes complete sense." Which skilled-interviewing technique is this?

  1. Validation
  2. Reassurance
  3. Partnering
  4. Summarization

A. Validation tells the patient that her emotion is legitimate, and "what you're feeling makes complete sense" does exactly that.
Reassurance (B) would promise a good outcome, like "everything will be all right", and the trans warns it can give false hope. Partnering commits to working together, and summarization restates the story. Neither fits this line.

A 62/M is brought to the ER pale, diaphoretic and clutching his chest. Which communication approach is most appropriate for the initial interview, and why?

  1. Biopsychosocial, because it is the gold standard and must always come first
  2. Biopsychosocial, because it gives the quickest diagnosis
  3. Biomedical, because it is efficient for quick diagnosis in acute situations
  4. Biomedical, because it raises patient satisfaction and shared decision-making

C. This is an acute emergency, and the physician-centered (biomedical) style is the efficient one for a quick diagnosis.
D picks the right style but gives the wrong reason. Its known weakness is lower satisfaction and less shared decision-making, so D has it reversed. The biopsychosocial style is the gold standard, but it takes more time, so A and B do not fit here.

A 24/M has had fever for 6 days. His temperature swings between 37.9 and 39.6 °C each day but never returns to normal between the peaks. Which temporal profile pattern does this show?

  1. Intermittent
  2. Periodic
  3. Recurrent
  4. Remittent

D. Remittent means the symptom goes up and down but never returns to baseline. That matches a fever that swings daily without touching normal.
Intermittent (A) is the tempting choice, but in an intermittent pattern the symptom stops completely between episodes.

On admission, a 58/F tells the clerk she "has a heart problem and high blood" and has felt dizzy for 3 days, with nausea since yesterday. Which chief complaint is written correctly?

  1. "Hypertensive urgency, rule out stroke"
  2. "Dizziness, 3 days"
  3. "Heart problem and high blood"
  4. "Dizziness, nausea, vomiting, headache, and weakness"

B. A chief complaint is a concrete symptom (two at most) with its duration, in the patient's words. "Dizziness, 3 days" meets all of these.
A and C are diagnostic labels, not symptoms. D lists too many symptoms and gives no duration.

A 45/M Filipino office worker weighs 72 kg and is 168 cm tall. Using the BMI classification the lecturer called more applicable in clinical practice, how is he classified?

  1. Overweight
  2. Overweight, at risk
  3. Obese I
  4. Obese II

C. BMI = 72 ÷ 1.68² = 25.5 kg/m². The lecturer's "more applicable" table is Asia-Pacific, where 25–29.9 is obese I.
"Overweight" (A) is the WHO class for this BMI, which is the trap. "Overweight, at risk" (B) is the Asia-Pacific class for 23–24.9 only.

A 72/M on antihypertensives reports lightheadedness on getting up. After 5 minutes supine his BP is 130/84. Two minutes after standing it is 116/72. What is the correct interpretation?

  1. Orthostatic hypotension, because diastolic pressure fell by at least 10 mmHg within 3 minutes
  2. Normal, because systolic pressure fell by less than 20 mmHg
  3. Not interpretable, because he must stand for at least 10 minutes
  4. Not interpretable, because he must rest supine for at least 15 minutes first

A. SBP fell by 14, which is less than 20. But DBP fell by 12, which is at least 10. Meeting either criterion within 3 minutes of standing is enough to call it positive.
B is the trap because it looks only at the systolic drop. C and D are wrong because the trans uses 3–10 minutes supine and a reading within 3 minutes of standing.

A 26/F has had blurred vision and pain on moving her right eye for 4 days. When the light is swung from her left eye to her right eye, both pupils dilate. What does this finding mean?

  1. A normal near response
  2. A left relative afferent pupillary defect from cataract
  3. Right ocular misalignment detected by the Hirschberg test
  4. A right relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil), suggesting an optic nerve problem

D. In the swinging flashlight test, pupils that dilate when the light reaches an eye mean that eye has an RAPD. Here it is the right eye, consistent with optic neuritis of the right eye.
B puts the defect in the wrong eye. C is wrong because the Hirschberg test checks alignment, not pupils. A near response involves constriction, not dilation.

Which finding–diagnosis pair is INCORRECT?

  1. Clear, stringy discharge with intense itching: allergic conjunctivitis
  2. Mucopurulent discharge with lid crusting: bacterial conjunctivitis
  3. Painless, non-tender nodule at the lid margin: hordeolum
  4. Images that seem to bounce when fixating: nystagmus

C. A hordeolum is an acute infection, so it is a painful, tender, red lump on the lid margin. A painless lid nodule is a chalazion.
The other three pairs are correct: clear stringy discharge with itch is allergic, mucopurulent with crusting is bacterial, and bouncing images (oscillopsia) come from nystagmus.

A 35/F says her hearing is muffled in the left ear. Weber lateralizes to the LEFT. Rinne shows BC > AC on the left and AC > BC on the right. What is the most likely cause?

  1. Right sensorineural loss from noise exposure
  2. Cerumen impaction in the left ear
  3. Left sensorineural hearing loss
  4. Right otitis media

B. Weber goes to the affected ear and Rinne is negative on that same side, so this is a left conductive loss. Cerumen impaction is a conductive cause (others include otitis media and TM or ossicle disease).
Right sensorineural loss (A) would also send Weber to the left, but then the left Rinne would stay positive. Left sensorineural loss (C) would send Weber to the right.

During indirect laryngoscopy, the examiner wants to see the vocal folds open (abduct) to check their movement. What should the patient be asked to do?

  1. Breathe through the nose
  2. Swallow repeatedly
  3. Say a high-pitched "eee"
  4. Say "hee-hee"

D. Saying "hee-hee" makes the folds abduct (open) during the short breath between sounds.
A high-pitched "eee" (C) does the opposite and makes them adduct (close). Breathing through the nose (A) is the instruction for posterior rhinoscopy. For laryngoscopy the patient breathes through the mouth.

Last-look cram sheet

  • The gold standard is patient-centered communication. Biomedical is fast in acute cases but misses psychosocial factors. Words are only 10% of communication.
  • Name the technique:
    • A capsule summary of the story is summarization.
    • Repeating one word ("Spread?") is echoing.
    • "Stay with diabetes or shift to back pain?" is topic tracking / goal alignment.
    • Pausing to check your own assumptions is mindful practice.
  • The first interview step is to greet and build rapport. The chief complaint is a symptom plus its duration, with no diagnosis. The temporal profile comes after the ROS and before the PE.
  • Periodic means the symptom-free period is longer than the clusters. Remittent means it never returns to baseline. Intermittent means it stops completely in between.
  • BP: palpate first, inflate 30 mmHg above, use the bell, deflate 2–3 mmHg per second. Orthostatic hypotension is an SBP drop of 20 or more or a DBP drop of 10 or more within 3 min of standing.
  • Examine from the right. The abdomen is IAPP, done supine with knees bent. Spine alignment and varicose veins are checked standing.
  • Asia-Pacific BMI: 23 or more is overweight, 25 is obese I, 30 is obese II. Use soap and water for C. difficile. Standard precautions exclude only sweat.
  • Eye: VA comes first. Confrontation tests the fields. Hirschberg tests alignment. Swinging flashlight finds an RAPD. Goldmann is the gold standard for eye pressure. An absent red reflex suggests cataract. Nystagmus causes oscillopsia.
  • Ear: healthy ear first, pinna up, back and out, largest speculum that fits. Weber toward the bad ear plus a negative Rinne means conductive loss. Epley does NOT test TM movement.
  • Nose breathing and a mirror facing up mean posterior rhinoscopy. Mouth breathing, sniffing position and a mirror facing down mean indirect laryngoscopy. Wharton's duct belongs to the submandibular gland.
